Source: Citi Research, Statistics Canada Euro Area Remarkable Endurance Likely to Continue – Despite the energy shock, subdued sentiment and growing competition from Chinese products for European producers, the economy has remained remarkably resilient so far this year. An export recovery took hold since the spring related, we think, to a stockpiling cycle (both domestic and global) amid tight supply conditions and fears of future price hikes. Also, manufacturing is benefitting from the global AI-related investment cycle. We expect European firms’ several ‘capex needs’ towards the digital transformation, AI, green targets, more resilient supply chains, diverse energy sources will continue to support demand ahead. Headwinds may be rising – i.e., tighter financial conditions, rising unemployment in core countries, shrinking fiscal space – but we think for now these are not strong enough to derail the moderate but steady growth pace of just above 1% (and roughly in line with potential). A higher and longer inflation ‘hump’ – Since the July GEOS update, we account for much higher crude oil and especially natural gas prices, which imply an almost mechanical increase in headline inflation – the inflation “hump” now looks taller and longer than before, peaking at just above 4% YY by Dec-26/Jan-27

That would lead Treasury to run down its cash balance over subsequent months, alongside the use of extraordinary measures to create borrowing headroom to cover Federal outlays. As a result, that would increase the supply of reserves and mitigate the need for the Fed to ramp up RMPs further. However, with the eventual resolution of the debt ceiling, Treasury would likely rebuild the TGA quickly by issuing bills, thereby draining liquidity from the banking system and threatening the reemergence of scarcity conditions. In the meantime, conclusions from the balance sheet task force and potential progress on regulatory reform are also likely to shape how the Fed considers optimal balance sheet policy, including the desired size and composition. Higher rates, as we describe in the next section, are also a headwind. It is our understanding that the more recent RDMICH bond had more investors involved in the primary process than RPLDCI and thus reason for different index providers to draw this line in the sand differently, but this shows the frailty of this criteria altogether. Our view is that when there is public disclosure pointing to limited syndication, this should be supplemented with some sort of objective criteria. Those criteria could be spread related. For example, if a bond issued with limited syndication tightens more than say 5% of its issuance spread over the first five days then it should be excluded; if not, it should be included, so long as its secondary market volumes are in line with similar size/rating broadly syndicated, registered securities. Or to keep it simple, benchmark indices could tighten their definition of limited syndication to exclude just deals with very little immediate secondary liquidity, or provide the marketplace with objective criteria to define this constraint, such as a requirement to syndicate to X number of investors per Y billion of bonds. Taking into account the aforementioned arguments both in favor and against 144A inclusion into the US Agg index, our conclusion is that adding 144A for Life securities to the US Aggregate index is a logical decision at this juncture. If the bill purchase operations were spread out, it would introduce a timing gap between the coupon maturity date and the bills purchase which could drive undesirable, additional volatility in the TGA and reserve balances. Given these considerations, we think the Fed is unlikely to take that route. Importantly, the main benefit of the Fed’s current reinvestment approach is that reinvestments are done passively as noncompetitive bids at auction. A decision to shift its reinvestments from across the curve to the front end would have zero first-order effect on duration held by private investors. The transmission to the market depends on whether Treasury responds to the shift in purchases by issuing more long-term debt, in order to prevent a shrinking of WAM of its outstanding debt. Historically, Treasury has managed to a target WAM and T-bill share, based on TBAC’s debt optimization framework. The easiest way to accelerate the shortening of SOMA duration would be to reinvest maturing coupon Treasuries into 2- and 3-year notes, instead of across the curve.

records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 25 September 2026 17 SARB devoted considerable attention to the risk of second-round effects. Its alternative scenarios assessed the impact of higher inflation expectations and stronger wage growth. Both scenarios produced a materially tighter policy path, requiring one to two additional hikes relative to the baseline. While evidence of building wage pressure remains partly qualitative and informed by business engagement, policymakers clearly signalled growing concern that inflation could become more entrenched. The September scenarios mark an important shift from July. Whereas the July MPC focused heavily on oil-price uncertainty and considered both favourable and adverse outcomes, the adverse scenario has now effectively materialised. SARB’s focus has consequently shifted towards higher global interest rates, elevated inflation expectations and stronger wage growth. Deteriorating global conditions amplifies domestic inflation risks The global backdrop has deteriorated noticeably since July. SARB highlighted: • Intensifying disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz. • Interruptions to Saudi oil exports linked to the conflict in Yemen. • Continued Russia-Ukraine-related supply disruptions. • A resumption of Federal Reserve tightening. • Rising global bond yields amid larger fiscal deficits and persistent inflation concerns. records.text: US Rates Weekly 25 September 2026 Citi Research 4 Overview: Neutrals are back in style for fall Few catalysts to shift out of neutral in the near term Last week we moved neutral on duration after trying to dip our toe into a long 20y position in August following Treasury’s increased buybacks (see US Rates Weekly - Only hawks outside the window). We shifted neutral after Chair Warsh’s September FOMC press conference, which was littered with support for the bond bears, giving our previous bullish view very little to work with. Without any expectation for a near-term Fed pause, it is challenging to argue for a near-term rally in the long end. The market apparently agreed and sharply repriced both Fed expectations and long-end yields higher this week given the large uncertainty on the Fed policy path. In other words, the market knows that cuts are not on the table, so there is a hard floor on forwards (perhaps as high as 4.5%), hikes are somewhat unbounded from above and thus the path of least resistance was higher. In our view the Treasury market is going through a light buyer’s strike. Wednesday’s strong PMI print added fuel to the fire and helped drive the second worst 5y auction in fifteen years (Figure 4). The 7y auction was also weak, and we pointed out that a weak 2y and 5y auction, both tailing, portends a weak 7y auction on average (see US Rates Strategy - Tell-tail signs?). records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 September 2026 Citi Research 34 Global Equity Strategy nDespite swings in risk sentiment, global equities are just slightly below all-time highs and remain c15% higher YTD. While there are growing reasons for short- term caution around higher rates and ongoing geopolitical risks, we remain comfortable with our call for further earnings-driven upside for global equities to mid-27. nKey Theme—The Fed and the Long End: Risks from more restrictive monetary policy (from the Fed and other key global central banks) compound preexisting worries around higher long-end bond yields. So, will higher yields derail the current equity bull market? On the Fed, we find that global equities tend to wobble around the start of hikes, while still climbing 6/12m later. The US market tends to underperform after the first hike, while Japan and Europe typically outperform. Value tends to outperform Growth. On the long end, we find that underlying macro conditions remain key; equities can better digest higher bond yields when growth stays resilient, while falling inflation also helps. So, while the first Fed hike rarely ends equity bull markets, the stagflationary impact of geopolitics, and knock-ons for the broader rates complex, will remain key to watch going forward. We see scope for a more pronounced pickup in fresh food prices in countries most affected by this summer's heatwaves, notably France. Further out, we continue to see food inflation reaching an inflexion point by year-end and accelerating to above 3% in the second half of 2027, reflecting the combined effects of 1) energy pass-through; 2) the ripple effects of this summer's heatwaves (Figure 11), which have weighed on agricultural output; and 3) the effect of El Niño on a range of commodities. 25 September 2026 6 Barclays | Euro area inflation: Forecast update & September preview

Assets whose volatility is easier to forecast are easier to risk-manage, and all else equal should command less for warehousing that risk. Rates volatility remains more persistent across all horizons and correlation regimes, implying a higher degree of predictability and therefore a structurally lower volatility premium. records.text: The key market theme in recent weeks has been the accelerating selloff in n long-end rates. With 10-year UST yields surpassing the October 2023 peak, mortgage and structured product investors are increasingly drawing comparisons with the volatile market conditions of 2022-23. While current coupon MBS OAS has widened as Treasury yields have backed-up, n it remains well below the 55bp+ levels reached in 2023. For a number of reasons, MBS markets are in meaningfully better shape than during the October 2023 selloff. First, the macro and volatility backdrop is considerably less challenging. In 2023, n rates rose more rapidly from lower levels amid high inflation and aggressive Fed tightening. Rate volatility was also substantially higher, while sharp MBS price declines and forced portfolio liquidations added to market stress. Second, investor portfolios are better positioned for rising rates through n allocations to higher coupons, shorter duration, and/or floating rate cashflows - all of which should reduce extension and mark-to-market risks. Third, demand has been broad-based and relative value vs. tight IG corporate n spreads, the last two days notwithstanding, remains a key supporting technical. Our stochastic simulations—which consider the risk of recession and model the government’s historical behaviour—suggest that risks are skewed further to the upside, and point to a 12% probability that public debt in France surpasses that of Italy (which we forecast at 135% of GDP) by that time (Exhibit 3). The trajectory of public debt in France therefore looks concerning across several dimensions. At a simple level, our forecast and simulations just about meet the classic definition of fiscal sustainability, which requires the debt ratio to be sufficiently likely to stabilise in the medium-term. Moreover, countries in which public debt is high and expected to increase over the medium term usually face higher borrowing costs. We show this in Exhibit 4 by plotting the sovereign spreads of seven large Euro area countries against the change in their debt ratio—as projected by the IMF—for countries with lower (in blue) and higher (in red) levels of public debt. The implication is that higher debt can entail higher rates, lower growth, and ultimately, even higher debt. Additionally, the larger negative beta to energy requires a decline in oil and gas prices for a more constructive outlook. As we enter the eighth month of the US/Iran conflict, and, consequently, the eighth month of the disruption of normal traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, US diesel prices have reached record highs ($6.50+/gal national average since September 19th) and reopened conversations about a potential export ban to help boost US supply and cap prices. Similar policies have already been implemented in Russia (outright ban on diesel, gasoline and jet fuel exports) and China (significant export quota cuts on refined petroleum products). On paper, restricting US diesel exports looks attractive: the US consumes ~3.6 mbd but exports ~1.3–1.6 mbd; keeping some barrels in the US could quickly rebuild inventories and lower wholesale prices and crack spreads. The problem is logistics: exports are concentrated on the Gulf Coast (81% of total August 2026 exports), and pipeline capacity cannot move enough diesel to the import-dependent East Coast. records.text: Lee Ferridge 23 September 2026 1 Insights Classification: General, Complimentary Material DM FX Weekly : Peak hawkishness. Now what? Last week’s Fed hike and subsequent hawkish message has seemingly given the green light for markets to price aggressive tightening across the G10. Total hikes of a little more than 800bp are now priced for the next 12 months. Given the ongoing Iran conflict and subsequent oil price increase this, on the surface, seems understandable. However, the market seems to be ignoring the fact that elevated oil prices also act as a tax on consumers . A slowdown in ex-fuel consumer spending is a growing risk. This leads us to the conclusion that we are now at peak hawkishness. This week we take a look at which countries are most vulnerable to any consumer led slowdown and, hence, may be unable to deliver on elevated tightening expectations. This analysis leads us to shift our portfolio around this week adding short NZDJPY and long EURAUD to sit alongside our existing short USDNOK trade. Long EURGBP, short CHFJPY and long CADSEK are all closed this week. Our models suggest an unexpected +75bp Fed Funds shock would lower real consumption by about 30bps after a year. With markets expecting hikes and much of consumer debt fixed rate, the effects could be smaller, but higher borrowing costs likely dampen spending on large-ticket items. For housing, higher rates deepen the affordability divide. With sales volumes near 40-year lows, we see little room for further declines, and prices remain supported. Existing homeowners are insulated, but prospective buyers face worsening affordability and are likely stuck renting for longer, potentially pressuring rents. The K-shape dynamic is evolving, but we believe it persists. Nominal wage growth has converged across cohorts and inflation differentials have narrowed, but real wage growth has still deteriorated across groups. Differences among cohorts are increasingly balance sheet driven; low-income consumers benefit less from wealth and are more exposed to higher rates, so we do not expect broadening out near- term. We expect a modest deceleration in spending growth, as those most insulated account for an outsized share of spending, with real consumption growth slowing to 1.8% (4Q/4Q) in '27 from 2.2% in '26. Our estimates show that the elasticity of PPI and CPI to import prices has risen substantially since around 2021-22 (Figure 11). Here, elasticity refers to the percentage change in each price index in response to a 1% change in the import price index. This suggests a major structural change in Japanese firms’ price-setting behavior with global inflation in the wake of COVID (see Import price pass-through to CPI strengthens and lengthens, 10 June). All of these speeches are avail- able on the website of the Joint Member Agencies, and we choose to focus on some of the key themes and remarks. While in the past this conference has been a forum to introduce new policy initiatives, this year’s conference attempted to advance the ball on current policy initiatives. The morning panel brought together a wide array of market participants to discuss the recent TBAC charge, which investigated whether Treasury should invest some of its excess cash beyond and above the buffer it holds in the repo market. We discussed this charge in depth here, and will not rehash all those points. The panel members largely agreed that this idea has merit, but is only truly scalable in an environment in which TGCR trades above IORB, closer to a scarce reserve regime. To the extent the Fed remains committed to an ample reserve regime, this will limit the scale of the program unless the operating framework for monetary policy shifts from its current floor system back to a corridor. The panelists highlighted that volatility in the TGA can create undue volatility in reserve balances and therefore contribute to volatility in money markets. Overall, we would view divided government as modestly supportive for duration on the margin, largely as the tail risk of substantial fiscal easing is priced out. Away from fiscal policy, bank deregulation has become an important source of Treasury demand. Wider swap spreads despite a deteriorating fiscal backdrop suggest markets have assigned meaningful value to greater bank participation in Treasury markets. Some investors may worry that a Democratic sweep could impede further deregulation. Our base case, however, is that the overall regulatory trajectory remains broadly intact, limiting the implications for rates. Debt limit: Oh no, not again A divided government outcome would also bring renewed attention to the debt limit. Last year, Congress raised the debt ceiling as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, providing roughly $5trn of additional borrowing capacity. In our estimates, that capacity is likely to be exhausted sometime during Q1 of next year. One possibility is that Congress addresses the issue during the lame-duck session, removing it from markets for another year or two. If not, investors will once again need to focus on extraordinary measures, Treasury cash balances, and ultimately the projected X- date. US refiners take abundant domestic and imported crude, process it through some of the world’s largest and most sophisticated refineries, and sell diesel, gasoline, jet fuel and other products wherever they are most valuable. During the current crisis, that flexibility has been especially important: as Middle Eastern and Russian refining supply was disrupted, international buyers turned increasingly toward the United States, pushing US refinery margins, production, and exports higher. Exports, then, are not simply excess barrels leaving America. They are central to the economic rationale for maintaining such a large US refining system in the first place. A one-off, 30-day emergency intervention would not dismantle that model. But it could change how refiners think about it. The question for the industry would be simple: if diesel (or gasoline) becomes politically expensive again, will Washington once more restrict our ability to export it? That matters because refining investments are made over decades, not months. If access to international markets becomes conditional on whether domestic prices spike, the expected return on export-oriented refining capacity falls. The asymmetry is important. Refiners still bear the downside when margins collapse, but their upside during periods of global scarcity could effectively become capped by the risk of government intervention. The household saving ratio remains almost 2pp above its pre-pandemic level, However, the level of the saving ratio is probably not the best way to assess the potential level of excess savings. A more informative approach is to compare the level of savings with the trend prevailing before Covid. Under this methodology, excess savings are measured as the cumulative deviation of household savings from their pre- pandemic trend. On this basis, excess savings still amount to around 4% of gross disposable income in cumulative terms (Figure 6).3 The existence of excess savings should normally be supportive of consumption. However, the distribution also matters. Figure 7 presents our estimate of how excess savings are allocated across household asset classes. By combining data on household asset holdings from the ECB's Household Finance and Consumption Survey with information on each group's share of aggregate financial wealth, we infer the distribution of excess savings across income and wealth cohorts. Our results suggest that excess savings, which is largely concentrated in debt securities, less liquid assets than deposits, remain heavily concentrated among wealthier households (Figure 6 and Figure 7). That said, it’s not clear to us that the underlying path of economic activity or the trajectory of inflation will mandate such aggressive action. The hike by the Bank of Japan was broadly expected, but markets were disappointed that Governor Ueda continued to sound restrained about the future path of policy. In his tenure to date, Governor Ueda has pursued a strategy of being systematically behind the curve in hiking rates. The rationale is that Japan’s economy has endured decades of sub-target inflation. As such, he has sought to avoid hiking too quickly and inadvertently jeopardizing the economy’s ongoing reflation.4 Until recently, we supported his approach. However, two developments strike us as now justifying a more aggressive approach. First, the reflation of Japan’s economy looks to be entrenched. Growth and inflation appear to be on a solid trajectory. Second, pressures in the JGB and foreign exchange markets have become more intense. Both of these developments justify a somewhat tighter stance from the BoJ. records.text: 25 September 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Ireland strongly boosted euro area growth in Q2 and we assume a reversal in Q3, which could result in a downside GDP surprise this quarter. This is reflected in our euro area GDP forecast of 0.8% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027. Excluding Ireland, we expect euro area GDP to grow 0.9% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027. Using Irish Modified Domestic Demand (MDD) instead of volatile GDP, we expect the euro area to grow 1.0% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027. European resilience is not a new phenomenon. The recession that was feared in 2022 after the Nordstream pipeline was cut never materialised. Fiscal easing, labour hoarding and pent-up demand helped. The US tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty in 2025 did not weigh as heavily on growth as expected, thanks to a robust labour market, the benefit of ECB rate cuts and NGEU disbursements. In this note we look beneath the surface of the current episode of economic resilience to understand its durability. We seek to understand whether the energy supply shock is merely lagged or whether an underestimated positive demand shock is outweighing the negative supply shock. We also think about the structural features of the economy that may be supporting economic resilience relative to previous cycles. Ultimately, the question we grapple with is whether the growth resilience we have observed in 2026 will prove to be transitory or persistent. Investment of TGA cash n balances in repo has gained more traction as a potential way of reducing funding volatility since the May Quarterly Refunding. TGA swings are the largest source of volatility in reserves and consequently responsible for much of the volatility in funding costs. Investing excess TGA balances in repo could help neutralize the impact of TGA swings on funding, but as we noted in May, details around implementation will matter. Panelists at this week’s US Treasury Market Conference highlighted a few possibilities, noting that an excess cash position is available through most of the month, and Treasury could deploy more funding during tax season, or specifically when TGCR exceeds IORB. We think Treasury could also set a minimum threshold for cash on hand, above which it would readily deploy up to an announced amount when there is an economic incentive, i.e. TGCR > IORB. The direct economic benefits of this policy more broadly are likely small—TGCR has rarely exceeded IORB this year, meaning that any returns to lending are likely to be marginal. That said, ample reserve conditions have mitigated funding volatility, and the supply/demand backdrop could change, especially if coupon issuance begins to climb. While Washington will naturally command most of the attention, state-level elections may ultimately prove more consequential for municipal investors. With 36 state governorships (evenly split between the two parties) and the vast majority of state legislative chambers on the ballot, changes in state trifectas could have a more direct impact on taxation, Medicaid policy, education funding, and infrastructure spending than the federal election outcome itself. Currently, there are 23 state government trifectas, including 13 Republican and 10 Democratic trifectas. There are also three gubernatorial elections in U.S. territories: Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and the Northern Mariana Islands. There are 145 statewide measures scheduled for November 3, according to Ballotpedia. For municipal investors, the most important initiatives relate to property taxes and income/wealth taxes. These concerns (and the lack of blowups) led us to dig deeper into how CRE CLO managers were managing this rate and valuation shock (see here, here, and here). In a nutshell, managers utilized PIK mods and borrowed bank and non-bank balance sheets to warehouse troubled loans through par loan buyouts. And in the last 2 years or so, bank and non-bank warehouse lines have facilitated whole deal calls. By our count, since the start of 2025 to now, 68 CRE CLO deals totaling $34.5bn have been whole deal called, most of which are the troubled 2021-2023 vintages. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 September 2026 Citi Research 23 China China’s economic momentum stayed soft in August with a deepening K-shape. Exports and the AI-centric new economy remain the key support for China. The supply side beat expectations with industrial production picking up to 5.2%YoY in August. Export growth accelerated to 25.0%YoY in August from 23.9%YoY in July, supported by the AI cycle, robust Asian supply-chain demand, and US-bound export recovery, as well as higher prices. Yet domestic demand missed expectations again. Retail sales retreated to 0.4%YoY. Contraction in fixed asset investment deepened to -7.2%YoY in Jan-Aug from -6.7%YoY in Jan-Jul, and its monthly rate stabilized at a low rate of -10.6%YoY per our estimate vs. -12.8%YoY in July despite improving base effect. Both markets and policymakers could look through this set of data, in our view. The August numbers haven’t really changed the policy calculation. For 26Q3 so far, the supply side has strengthened marginally, while the demand side hasn’t turned materially worse. Our quarterly forecasts of 4.5%YoY for 26Q3E still apply. September indicators are key to deciding whether the Chinese economy can find a bottom within the year. So far, trade activities have held up, and fiscal policy deployment has picked up with the RMB800bn policy-financing tool. records.text: • Rice was one of the drivers of the renewed rise in inflation through 2025. However, reflecting weaker supply-demand conditions and lower prices for the 2025 rice crop, its contribution to core-core CPI inflation has already turned negative. We estimate that rice will contribute about -0.3pp in October-December 2026. This downward pressure is likely to remain strong in early 2027, with the drag during October-February widening by around 0.1pp relative to August. • We believe the key to whether the BoJ falls behind the curve is the extent to which wage growth is passed through to prices. Inflationary pressure from external factors is susceptible to y/y base effects. Therefore, for CPI inflation to remain elevated, a stronger and more sustained pass-through of stickier wage growth to prices – that is, “second-round effects” – is essential. • A comparison of scheduled cash earnings with CPI inflation in high labor cost services shows a marked decoupling: although the former has accelerated notably since 2026, the latter has been on a downward trend since peaking in May 2025. • Our analysis shows that the response of scheduled cash earnings growth to core-core CPI inflation has strengthened markedly in recent years, with no sign of weakening since the start of the year. The first is immaculate disinflation—a belief that inflation will gradually return to central bank targets without a need for a period of weak demand. The second belief is that policymakers remain New Testament deities, forgiving of our inflation sins. While adjusting policy rates to reflect a higher neutral rate of inter- est (r*), policymakers are expected to tolerate a further period of sticky inflation without actively hiking to promote weak- ness. From our perspective, the greatest risk to the expansion is that these views are shaken and rate hikes become more “Old Testament” in pushing rates high enough to smite growth and strike down high inflation. As we move along this path of synchronized strong growth, we see rising risks of a return to this “old time religion” com- ing from two sources. • The return of the common. The interaction of strong global growth, buoyant commodity prices and supply- chain pressures is reviving a common global inflation impulse. Pressure on goods prices is most significant: we project a sharp acceleration to a 2.5%ar rise in global core goods prices over the coming six months. Core service price inflation is unwinding an acceleration in the early months of this year and benefits from moderating wage gains. This transaction introduces a new form of AI development risk into a universe dominated by asset-heavy data centers, raising the question of what “AI risk” means for HY investors. In this report, we discuss implications for portfolio performance and volatility going forward. Record Issuance Reshapes the AI Universe — SoftBank's $10 billion deal, the largest in HY history, cuts data center concentration in the HY AI universe from 82% to 69% and drives AI outstanding to roughly $64 billion. Capacity to Absorb More Supply — Even after this deal, AI-related debt accounts for only 4.3% of the HY index, a fraction of IG’s 13% Tech weighting. The figure can still climb to 7%-10% within a year if issuance continues at pace. Equity Sentiment Hasn't Reached HY Yet — AI equities have rallied 16% since August, while HY AI bonds gained just 1% over the same stretch, with data center bonds themselves diverging sharply between construction-stage and still-in- development names. records.text: M Update 2 New Home Sales: Reversal and revision of last month's weakness New home sales rose 6.4% m/m to a 684k annual rate in August, above consensus' 616k estimate and even our stronger 660k estimate. Last month's softness was also revised away, with July sales revised up from 607k to 643k. Sales rose m/m in the South and Midwest in August and fell in the Northeast and West. We are now tracking 2Q residential investment at -1.4% (q/q saar) versus -1.6% before the print. New home sales are somewhat soft versus last year, with the year-to-date average at 643k pace versus last year's 679k. Our housing strategists expect home sales to end the year little changed, with new home sales down 1% y/y and existing sales flat. In August, new home sales made up 15.8% of all single-family sales, a bounceback after the lower share in July. Months of supply of new homes, volatile from month to month, fell from 9.0 in July to 8.5 in August. The median price, equally volatile, was down 5.8% y/ y in August after averaging -1.4% y/y the prior 6 months. At least part of this price weakness is likely due to the regional composition of sales in August. The percent of new home sales that are already completed units remains elevated. During the pandemic, homes under construction and not yet started made up a larger shares of sales, as households scrambled for new housing. That trend reversed over the past three years, with homes not started now making up nearly the lowest share of sales in decades

records.text: M Idea 8 Financial conditions: The Fed Awakens Following the 25bp rate hike in September and the shift into an "oil risk premium" baseline, we reset our financial conditions index to September 15 2026, the day prior to the September FOMC meeting, to track our FRB/US-based measure of financial conditions in this new hiking cycle. As of the September 24 market close, financial conditions were about one hike tighter than they were before the September FOMC meeting. The index aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. It includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate using the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since the day before the September FOMC meeting, the easing in financial conditions has been equivalent to about a 27bp hike in the federal funds rate, driven primarily by a higher 10-year Treasury yield and USD appreciation. Equity returns and BBB credit spreads have offset some of the tightening. records.text: g ). In terms of inflation-specific catalysts, the risk of a US diesel export ban added some intra-week volatility to the inflation market. Such a ban would be in line with actions taken by two of the largest exporters of refined petroleum products, Russia and China, which our commodity strategists find, in combination with a Jones Act waiver, could be effective for 30 days in rebuilding US inventories (see Oil Markets Weekly: Day 31 and beyond, Natasha Kaneva, 9/24/26). Such a temporary restriction would resemble one of the two bills introduced by Tim Burchett on September 17: one would prohibit diesel exports through January 2027, while the other would impose controls conditional on the national diesel price. Regardless of the length or likelihood of such a ban, the political incentives ahead of the midterm elections argue for early implementation. Inflation markets initially priced roughly 5bp of probability-weighted downside, concentrated in the October-December fixings. Using the approximately 35% prediction-market probability at the time, this implied a conditional impact of around -14bp on the 1-year CPI rate if a ban were enacted (see US Treasury Market Daily, 09/23/26). We find this pricing has largely unwound post the media reports suggesting White House officials dismissed the idea, and given the real rate volatility on Wednesday and Thursday.

Meanwhile, the Fed has primarily supplied reserves through asset purchases, and although repo operations are offered, the Fed’s Standing Repo Program (SRP) works differently. It lends at the top of the target range, above IORB, so it functions principally as a ceiling backstop. It also is available to a smaller set of counterparties against a more limited set of collateral. A more repo-led framework could allow the Fed to supply fewer reserves through outright securities holdings while meeting additional demand elastically through repo operations. Lorie Logan has said that the Fed could rely more heavily on ceiling facilities and hold fewer securities if it were confident that market participants were willing and able to use those facilities. Roberto Perli in his speech this week spent considerable time comparing securities-led and repo-led approaches. He noted that a repo-led approach could help to achieve a shorter portfolio duration, if that is desired, as well as a smaller overall balance sheet size. He concluded that neither of the operational approaches is inherently superior to the other, but he acknowledged that local realities matter and that there are trade-offs to consider with both approaches. Overall, we see scope for the Fed to make its framework somewhat more demand- driven, but little support for moving fully back to scarce reserves, and further improvements to the SRP design will likely be necessary.

records.text: M Idea 8 Can the Consumer and Housing Handle Higher Rates? Effects of Higher Rates on Consumer Spending Comparing inflation versus income growth is one way to measure affordability, but this does not tell the whole story. Recent moves in rates will also worsen affordability for consumers who borrow to fuel their spending. This is especially relevant for purchases of large-ticket items, such as cars and other durable goods, and of course, for housing. Following the Fed meeting last week, we updated our outlook to include two additional 25bp hikes in December and March, to a terminal target range of 4.25%-4.5%. The market is pricing in an even more hawkish outcome, with 1-2 more hikes priced into 2027 than we expect ( Exhibit 12 ). In our note last year, we discussed how rate cuts could affect consumer spending. To do so, we used a vector autoregression (VAR) model. Given that this is a linear model, we can scale the results to similarly estimate the effects of rate hikes on consumption. The model shows that an immediate +75bp shock to the Fed Funds rate would result in a drag of 30bps on the level of real consumption after a year, while a +150bp shock would result in a drag of 60bps ( Exhibit 13 ). We find these results a useful guide, but we take the exact estimates with a grain of salt; the model assumes the hikes come immediately and unexpectedly and does not take into account the current level of policy. That is an uncomfortable historical reference, but Europe today is not Europe of 2011. The euro area has stronger institutional backstops and southern European economies are less reliant on external borrowing. The region, however, remains energy-dependent and exposed to geopolitical shocks. That distinction matters because we think inflation risk has been critical in pushing OAT-Bund spreads beyond 90 bps (Figure 3R e s p o n s e o f 1 0 y F r e n c h y i e l d s t o 1 p p t i n f l a t i o n a r y s h o c k , Figure 4R e s p o n s e o f 1 0 y G e r m a n y i e l d s t o 1 p p t i n f l a t i o n a r y s h o c k ). This is a different regime from the largely political spread widening of 2024-25. Higher inflation risk, higher term premia, political and fiscal uncertainty are now reinforcing one another. Stay in 2s10s ESTR flattener - close ECB Oct'26 at 15bps (opened: 17bps) We stay in our 2s10s €STR flattener, targeting an inversion towards -10bp, from an 18bp entry. records.text: US Economic Perspectives23 September 2026 ab 4 Optimism around the manufacturing sector in the US is on the upswing. After the sector's contraction into mid-2025, output has been rising modestly and employment gains have resumed. At the same time, inventory rebuilding has also helped. Going the other way, auto production was a tailwind through July with rising assemblies, which also has upstream tentacles into chemicals, glass and other inputs. Auto assemblies are now pulling back. Autos, light trucks, and parts represents more than 10% of all manufacturing shipments in the US. With different sectors experiencing both ups and downs, where is the growth in production? The growth in manufacturing output has been highly concentrated in high tech equipment. The Federal Reserve's production data shows high-tech production rising 12.5% over the year ending in August. That includes computers and peripheral equipment, communications equipment and semiconductors and related electronic components. What is the rest doing? Excluding energy production, the rest of manufacturing output is up only 0.3% over the 12 months ending in August. Overall ex- energy manufacturing production has risen 0.6% over the 12 months. In other words, over the most recent 12 months, half of the growth in manufacturing output excluding energy comes from a small share of overall production: ~2-1/2%. records.text: e policy rate path in the near term, as did the exchange rate. However, neutral interest rates, output gap and foreign interest rates were behind the revision to the upside. Our forecast: Based on our current forecasts, we see the Norges Bank remaining at 4.5% until June 2027. Yet, we note a risk of further tightening mainly on the back of the external environment. Still, with the policy rate at 4.5%, the domestic picture would need to align too. We would look to three avenues: wages, currency and economic activity. First, we could see the Norges Bank considering another rate hike if we start to see wage pressures rising in 2027 (the Regional Network report so far presented unchanged expectations for 2027, while the Expectations survey even saw wage expectations being revised down in 2027). Second, the currency has been supportive of goods inflation in recent prints, but a significant weakening could adjust the inflation outlook to the upside and hence the willingness of Norges Bank to tighten further. Third, the Norges is concerned about "restraining the economy too much", and in order to see hikes beyond 4.5%, we would need to see a much stronger re-acceleration in the growth momentum than Norges Bank expects. At this point, we do not see the constellation of these three factors materializing and hence expect Norges Bank on hold.

The Fed released FAQs in 2024, which clarified that banks can point to their capacity to borrow at the Fed’s discount window, SRP , or a FHLB as a means of monetizing HLA. However, as Bill Nelson at BPI explains, the ILST rule still only recognizes lines of credit (including those facilities) beyond the 90-day horizon. Thus, bank treasurers have indicated that formally recognizing discount window capacity in ILSTs would significantly reduce their required reserve balances. While these changes would only require action by the Fed, it’s unclear if there is sufficient support for such a revision among the Fed. Even if the Fed moves in this direction, it would likely need to go through the notice of proposed rulemaking and public-comment process, likely making that a mid-2027 event at the earliest. In the scenario in which both of these changes are made to the liquidity regulatory framework, Miran estimates an implied roughly $100bn-$400bn reduction in reserve demand. What happens next? On the margin, such changes would arguably reduce demand for HQLA altogether, suggesting potentially lower bank demand for Treasuries and narrower swap spreads on the margin. If Republicans lose either the House or the Senate, we think they may prioritize passing a reconciliation bill during the lame duck session of Congress in December to increase the debt limit and add defense spending. In July, House Republicans passed a budget resolution for $95bn in additional reconciliation spending, which we see as a starting point for a defense spending increase. The Trump administration has proposed a defense spending baseline of $1.15trn in FY27, which would be a $311bn increase over FY26 defense baseline, and Congress is working on a FY27 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) presuming a $1.15trn defense topline. In 2017 and 2024, President Trump previously criticized congressional Republicans for failing to resolve the debt limit themselves, leaving him to negotiate directly with Democratic leaders.2 We could see him pressing congressional Republicans to address the debt limit before Democrats take control of Congress. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 September 2026 Citi Research 6 Even more worrisome, markets for refined products—gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel—are tighter than the market for crude (Figure 6). Global refining capacity is in very short supply. Accordingly, gasoline prices have outpaced oil prices by roughly 20%, while diesel prices have run nearly 50% ahead. President Trump’s threat of a ban on US diesel exports poses further risks to these markets. As such, energy prices are an outsized threat to inflation and growth even beyond the high level of oil prices. In line with this discussion, global headline inflation is projected to move up to 3.5% this year (Figure 7), nearly a full percentage point higher than we anticipated when the year began. This rise mainly reflects the upsurge in the broad complex of energy prices that we have described (Figure 8). Food prices, in contrast, have stayed subdued. We remain concerned about pressures associated with El Niño, which are likely to hit hardest later this year and early next year, but the muted performance of food prices to date is encouraging. Notably, we see headline inflation moderating to 3% in 2027, but the recent pressures in energy markets and potential disruptions from El Niño pose risks to the forecast. Global core inflation has also risen but by less than headline. Policy rates were probably tighter than in the US and inflation tolerance remains greater. We pencil in two rather reluctant hikes from the BoE now (Nov/Feb) to 4.25%, but as soon as inflation is back on a firm downward trend, we expect the central bank to start cutting to 3.50% terminal in 2028. How much more can they hike before they have to stop? We are frequently asked how much more the ECB could hike, or what level of energy prices would break the economic resilience. We have embedded the ECB signal of a December hike in our base case – that now makes 75bp of hikes for this cycle. We see the risk of a fourth hike, but more likely in Mar-27 than Oct-26. To be clear, four hikes is not our base case. But given the ECB is implying that 3-4 hike range in their base case and adverse scenario from September, we have to take that range seriously. The market seems sceptical, pricing close to 150bp for the whole cycle again (ie almost 100bp from here by next summer). Our impression from Lagarde and Lane is that a gentle pushback against pace and quantum of hikes priced has begun – arguing against October and in favour of a measured rather than a forceful response. Unified government: Fiscal expansion back in focus A Republican sweep would likely have the largest implications for rates markets pushing yields higher across the curve. Unlike divided government, unified government would preserve the possibility of further fiscal expansion. Investors would likely assume a greater probability of additional reconciliation packages, extensions of provisions currently scheduled to expire, and potentially additional tax or spending measures. As a result, investors would likely become less confident that fiscal policy turns restrictive. Growth expectations would move higher, inflation risks would remain elevated, and markets would be willing to price a hiking cycle rather than a modest adjustment. In addition, the fiscal outlook would be seen as deteriorating. Our rule of thumb is that if budget deficits were expected to be permanently higher by 1pp of GDP , long-term Treasury yields could rise by roughly 25-40bp. records.text: the 30y cheapens Into mid-Nov: 60% retraced Source : Ministry of Finance, Deutsche Securities The early-October steepening is not simply a generic turn-of-the-month effect. Across all 12 months, the five-business-day change in 10s30s is largest in early October: the curve steepened by an average of 2.6bp, widening in 22 years and flattening in only four (t-statistic: 4.6). The next-largest move is a 1.8bp steepening in early July, while early February produces an average 1.2bp flattening. Even after adjusting for multiple testing, both the early-October move in 10s30s and the rise in the 30-year yield remain significant at the 5% level. Plausible drivers include renewed dealer balance-sheet capacity at the start of the new half-year, concession building ahead of the 10- and 30-year auctions, and a lag before real-money investors deploy second-half allocations. Any resulting supply-demand imbalance is therefore likely to be most pronounced in the less liquid super long sector. The pattern is present across the 2000–12, 2013–21 and 2022–25 policy regimes, suggesting that it is robust to changes in the monetary-policy framework. Late October: The Seasonal Cheapening Reverses The year-by-year results reinforce the signal. The 30-year yield declined over the 10 business days following September month-end in only four years—2008, 2009, 2013 and 2015. Philip Jefferson’s speech at this week’s annual Treasury market structure conference described several concrete improvements that directly address operational and standardization criticisms of the discount window. These improvements have resulted in more usage of the discount window amid periods associated with temporary upward pressure on money market rates, such as those observed around quarter ends (Figure 5O p e r a t i o n a l i m p r o v e m e n t s h a v e a l l o w e d f o r s l i g h t l y g r e a t e r d i s c o u n t w i n d o w b o r r o w i n g a r o u n d q u a r t e r e n d s ). However, these improvements do not address the full incentive problem. Pricing and disclosure concerns remain, and banks still have limited regulatory reasons to conduct routine borrowing tests or maximize prepositioned collateral. More modernization may therefore be required before discount-window capacity can substitute materially for permanently held liquidity.

R-star appears undefined, almost like dividing by zero, or with either multiple solutions, or in a range, perhaps depending on the time frame involved, but overall lacking any one, singular solution. As a result, not only is r-star not a useful concept, as Chairman Warsh said, the solution to the problem may yield no one point estimate at any point in time. That offers little guidance for financial market participants casting about for what to think about the FOMC. However, the actual answer is that even without any concept of neutral in theory, we are all still learning about Chairman Warsh and his FOMC in practice. He has downplayed the real economy trade-offs from raising rates, another unanchoring of the reaction function. We are also learning about the data. Next week we get important inflation data that could rewrite recent history. The following week we get another CPI. In our forecast, the current level of the funds rate is sufficient to return inflation to target over time. But how quickly the Chairman wants to do so remains an open question. records.text: ABS ABS Issuance: Taking Stock of 2026, Setting the Table for 2027 With nearly three quarters of 2026 in the books, we take stock of issuance trends across the ABS landscape and lay out our 2027 forecasts. In aggregate, we expect 2026 gross issuance to reach $278 billion (largely including only the consumer-focused ABS sectors discussed below and digital infrastructure ABS), roughly in line with 2025 issuance (Exhibit 8). Gross issuance year to date has translated into net issuance of $37.2 billion, and we look for full-year net issuance across our tracked ABS categories to reach $60 billion (Exhibit 9). For 2027, our gross issuance forecasts total $287 billion, which we expect to translate into $73 billion of net issuance (again, Exhibit 8). Our central message is one of continuity: most of the trends that have defined 2026 should persist into 2027. This is largely consistent with GDP growth rates trending sideways and as consumer spending could soften because of slow nominal wage growth, higher gas prices, and the waning tax refund boost. Given the large share of spending this cohort makes up, we could see much larger consumption effects. The second channel is inflation remaining stickier than we expect or reaccelerating, which is very dependent on oil prices. If we do not get the deceleration in inflation, there could be more consecutive quarters of negative real income growth. In this scenario, the Fed may also have to hike rates further. While we think the consumer could handle the 75bps of hikes we expect, a more significant hiking cycle would have larger effects and may also be accompanied by asset market declines. In terms of upside risks, as we describe in the Fiscal Policy Unlikely to Help Affordability Near-Term section, we do not see near-term fiscal support, such as stimulus checks, as likely. If midterm elections result in a Democratic sweep with a robust majority, it is possible SNAP and Medicaid cuts could be delayed or rolled back. This would be better relative to our forecasts, potentially adding a couple tenths to consumption next year, but in terms of consumer affordability, it is more so removing another headwind rather than adding support. In order to get more upside, we would likely need a faster resolution to the conflict in the Middle East, and thus a more significant reduction in oil prices.

records.text: 25 September 2026 UK Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 Initial conditions looking mixed So far, there is mixed evidence of unfavourable starting-point conditions. But we think tough decisions on additional defence spending. social care and welfare are likely to be delayed. BoE to hike in Nov and Feb, with balanced risks We change our BoE call- we now expect the BoE to hike twice in Nov ‘26 and Feb ‘27 to 4.25% to guard against the risks of second round effects, assuming high energy prices are sustained into early next year and barring big downside surprises in data. We then expect three quarterly cuts starting in Q1 ‘28 (Feb, Apr and July) to our terminal of 3.5% (vs. our previous call of no hikes and a cut in Nov. ‘27 to 3.5%). Our terminal remains the same, but we expect to reach it later. Risks to our view are balanced. A meaningful drop in energy prices due to a lasting deescalation or big downside data surprises can weaken the case for tightening and allow for one or no hike. At the same time, a meaningful worsening of the energy shock, upside data surprises or strong evidence of second round effects materializing can open the door to a third hike. Beyond that, risks are tilted to earlier cuts if disinflation late next year moves faster than we expect. Diesel has a broader inflation footprint than gasoline because of its importance in producer prices, as a result, the supply chian exposure is greater and hence a higher risk to core goods. Gasoline primarily affects headline inflation and household fuel costs, while lowering real disposable income. Diesel is embedded in road freight, agriculture, mining, construction and industrial distribution. Its direct CPI weight therefore understates its economic importance: higher diesel prices raise the cost of moving raw materials and intermediate goods as well as the final cost of distribution. Our input-output work shows this propagation accumulating through successive rounds of the production network, particularly through land transport.

records.text: Copper , Silver , PGMs: Tariff Uncertainty Likely to Persist; Tariff Risk Builds Inventories On September 10, a Reuters report suggested1 that the White House had not yet decided whether to impose tariffs on refined copper, noting that policymakers were weighing the goal of encouraging domestic critical minerals production against the risk of higher manufacturing costs. The resulting perception that US tariffs on critical minerals may not be imminent triggered a selloff across copper, silver, platinum, and palladium — all on the critical minerals list and subject to the S232 investigation. Yet, subsequent White House comments reported2 by Barron’s reiterated that reshoring critical manufacturing remains a policy priority and left the door open to future tariff measures. Taken together, this sequence fits into our ongoing view that uncertainty around critical minerals tariffs will likely persist, as the ambiguity itself may be serving the policy objective of supply security through domestic stockbuilding. records.text: f energy-related indirect effects. • We project euro area headline and core inflation to average 3.1% and 2.4% y/y in 2026, and 2.8% and 2.6% y/y in 2027. This forecast is conditioned on the latest futures curves for oil, gas and electricity, which point to energy inflation running close to 20% y/y in the coming months before easing gradually through next year and turning negative in 2027 H2. • Our projections assume a stronger pass-through from energy prices to food and core inflation than pre-pandemic patterns would imply, but a more limited transmission than observed during the 2021-24 inflation episode. We see core inflation peaking at 2.8% y/y in March 2027 and remaining sticky thereafter, driven by firmer core goods prices — which we expect to approach 2% by early 2027 — while services inflation continues to trend range-bound around 3%. Food inflation is set to become a key driver of 2027 inflation, drifting north to 3% from Q2 27 onwards. • We explore the mechanical implications of alternative energy price paths for the trajectory of headline inflation (see Sensitivity analysis — alternative energy paths). Under a constant energy price assumption, we would see headline inflation still running at 2.3% y/y in December 2027, c.0.3pp above our baseline projection. In the morning session, Vice Chair Philip Jefferson discussed the Fed’s efforts to modernize the discount window, arguing that the facility needs to better reflect today’s faster-moving banking and funding environment. He emphasized the importance of ensuring that banks can access the discount window on a “no questions asked” basis. A notable theme was tight- er Fed–FHLB coordination to improve collateral interoperability—so collateral can be repositioned more quickly as liquidity needs shift—strengthening relationships, putting operational and documentation frameworks in place, and refining joint processes to improve day-to-day coordination and preparedness. For context, banks have historically been reluctant to use the discount window given the perceived stigma, often preferring alter- native liquidity sources such as the FHLBs—an approach that was evident during the 2023 regional banking episode. Since then, regulators and Fed officials have stepped up efforts to encourage banks to treat the discount window as a viable liquidity source and, important- ly, to be operationally ready to access it when needed (see Short-Term Fixed Income , 1/19/24). Supply-demand: the dimension history cannot measure The most important driver may be the one sixty years of returns cannot settle. Tail risk, jump risk, spot/vol correlation and volatility persistence are properties of the underlying asset, observable long before options traded on it. Structural demand for protection is not. It is also not orthogonal to the other four, e.g. investors pay more to hedge assets that gap, that are hard to forecast and whose vol spikes alongside portfolio losses. The part that the framework cannot capture is what sits on top: positioning, leverage and behaviour, which are far more time- varying and can push demand well beyond what the risk characteristics alone would suggest. Qualitatively, when bonds stop hedging, investors need something that does. A portfolio that relied on duration to absorb equity drawdowns must replace that hedge when the correlation flips, and explicit equity protection is the natural substitute. records.text: Under Section 14(b) of the Federal Reserve Act, the Fed can acquire securities directly from Treasury only in exchange for maturing holdings, so a rollover must go into securities that settle on the maturity date. For this reason, maturing bill holdings are reinvested as add-ons across all bill auctions that settle on a given day (Tuesday or Thursday), while maturing coupon Treasury holdings are reinvested as add- ons at coupon Treasury auctions (settling mid-month or end-of-month). Thus, the easiest way to accelerate the shortening of the SOMA portfolio would be to reinvest coupon Treasuries only into the shortest security settling that day – i.e., reinvest end-of- month maturities into 2-year notes and reinvest mid-month maturities into 3-year notes. Would it be possible to reinvest maturing coupon Treasuries into T-bills? If the Fed pursued this option, theoretically the Fed could allow coupon securities to mature, and then subsequently buy an equal amount of bills in the secondary market. The bill purchase operation could be made prior to the coupon maturity date, such that the operation and redemption would settle together. However, coupon maturities can be quite sizable relative to secondary bill market liquidity, particularly during refunding months, and thus secondary market purchases of this size could drive significant market moves around those dates. records.text: US Outlook The kettle reassembles Fed communications reinforced September's hawkish message, with several policymakers embracing Chairman Warsh's doubts about policy restrictiveness. Limited incoming data pointed to resilient growth, placing next week's employment report, GDP revision, and the NIPA annual revision in focus. • Fed officials broadly reinforced Chairman Warsh's post-meeting message, emphasizing• elevated inflation, full-employment labor markets, and doubts about policy restrictiveness. Despite recent tightening from higher yields and a stronger dollar, the Fed's FCI-g measure reinforces growing doubts within the FOMC about whether financial conditions are restrictive overall. • Robust PMI readings and business-investment data supported growth expectations, but we• remain cautious about reading too much into either signal. Historically, S&P Global PMIs have proven most useful for identifying major cyclical turning points, with little evidence that modest month-to-month fluctuations provide a reliable signal about underlying GDP momentum. • Next week's employment report, GDP revision, personal income and spending release, and• the NIPA annual revision should provide a much clearer read on momentum. records.text: 10 US Economic Weekly | 25 September 2026 Core views Growth: Resilient economy with solid growth outlook • Relative to our mid-year forecasts, we have lowered 4Q/4Q 2026 growth by 20bp to 2.1%. Oil prices have risen recently, and we see shrinking prospects of a deal to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Hence, we have penciled in more energy-related inflation, which should reduce real consumer spending and capex on the margin. More generally, we continue to see AI-related investment and consumer spending as the key drivers of demand. Bottom line, growth in the US economy is expected to remain solid through our forecast horizon. Inflation: Underlying inflation stuck above target • Our inflation outlook is largely unchanged. We continue to forecast 4Q/4Q core PCE inflation at 3.3% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027, while raising headline inflation in both years, reflecting higher energy and food prices from the Iran war. We still see underlying inflation running near 2.5% with little progress over the past year and view risks as skewed to the upside, including strong AI-related investment, labor supply constraints from lower migration and aging demographics, trade policy uncertainty, the Iran war, and weather-related supply shocks. Labor market: Remains roughly in balance • We have made mark-to-market changes to our labor outlook. The indicator is calculated by combining measures of inflation expectations among firms, households and professional forecasters using principal component analysis. As we do not have access to some of the data used by the BoJ, we track composite inflation expectations using the three long- term inflation expectation measures shown in Figure 7 (see Composite inflation expectations (our estimate) finally exceed 2%, 21 July). According to this measure, composite inflation expectations reached 2% for the first time in the latest data (Q2 26; Figure 8). However, Japan’s long-term inflation expectations are highly susceptible to actual inflation outcomes over the previous several years, particularly energy and food prices. In the tables below, we illustrate how Classic FICO buckets would be redistributed using both Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's scoring systems for 2021 and 2023 vintage CAS and STACR collateral. Given that the scoring systems use different ranges, the share of collateral migrating to different credit score buckets should be expected to vary by GSE. Energy prices and financing conditions limit growth We update our Euro area forecasts to incorporate higher energy prices through the winter, tighter financing conditions and a more hawkish ECB. Our commodities colleagues now expect TTF at EUR 90-100 and Brent at USD 90-100 in 4Q26 and 1Q27, before correcting towards EUR 40 and USD 74 again by end-27. That lifts our inflation forecasts to 3.0% for 2026 (+10bp) and 2.5% for 2027 (+30bp). We keep core inflation at 2.3% this year, but raise it to 2.3% in 2027 (+20bp), driven by indirect energy price effects and German healthcare reform. We see headline and core at or below 2% by end- 27 again, with headline and core inflation averaging 1.8% in 2028 (unch). Our growth forecasts move to 1% in 2026 (+20bp due to Irish growth revisions in 2Q). But higher energy prices and even tighter financial conditions constrain growth

We established in the section Mapping Global Diesel Flows that the US is increasingly a key marginal producer of diesel (Exhibit 7 ). records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 23 September 2026 1 Oil: Take profit on long Oct-Dec26 ICE gasoil spread Tidfa We have reached the extended target for our long Oct-Dec26 ICE gasoil spread and take profit given our believe the market has overreacted to the prospects of an imminent US gasoil export ban. Gasoil has bucked the trend across the energy complex by opening significantly stronger today – presumably driven by concerns around a US export ban. While we think such a ban is more likely than some people think, we do not believe it is imminent, as there are still a few potential leve rs to arrest the diesel upside left: a return (or increase) in Russian diesel exports ; more product SPR releases from Europe; and more product exports from the Middle East. Only after these options have been explored and Middle Eastern flows don’t improve do we think there is a choice to be made between the US domestic market and exports. As we believe the domestic market will be chosen in that case, an export ban is likely to be implemented (in a gradual manner). Given that, we take a USD558k profit on our long Oct-Dec26 ICE gasoil spread (opened on 20 August and extended on 16 September) and are minded to put on a similar position if/when the current (overblown, in our view) reaction in spreads settles down a bit , as we continue to expect tightening gasoil balances until November. Following another move higher in US rates overnight, markets are now pricing more than 32bp in total for the December and January FOMC meetings. Jump risk: rates catch up when inflation dominates For option sellers, the pain is jumps, not volatility itself. Return and volatility distributions describe overall risk, but jumps capture a more damaging source of uncontrollability: large discontinuous moves that cannot be effectively hedged through conventional delta management, and therefore directly feed into hedging and replication error. Because sigma moves are scaled by prevailing vol, they measure how often the market moves by more than recent volatility would suggest, which is precisely the risk a short-volatility position warehouses. Equity jump risk is remarkably persistent across regimes, and skewed to down moves. Notably, the most extreme standardised moves in the entire sample are equity drawdowns (e.g. 1987, 2008, 2020, etc.). While one might have expected the positive-correlation decades to coincide with lower equity jump risk, the data offer little support for that view. Specifically we estimate that raising defense spending by $311bn over the FY26 baseline, and spreading it over three years, would boost the real GDP level by about 0.2% in 2027 and 2028 before returning toward the original path in 2029 and 2030. If a Republican sweep In the event of a Republican sweep, Congress could contemplate a larger fiscal package. The president proposed a $5,000 per adult check, which would amount to a transfer of roughly $1.3trn, or 3.8% of 2027 nominal GDP . We think that such a check would be difficult to pass even through a Republican-controlled Congress. However, in the spirit of this proposal, it is feasible that Republicans do a reconciliation bill involving tax cuts and some of it offset by spending cuts. We think that such a bill might lower taxes by $1.3trn, with some portion, say 40%, offset by spending cuts. This would raise the total deficit by about $780bn. Unsurprisingly, the year-on-year increase was largely driven by higher defense and investment spending, which accounted for about EUR 47 bn, or more than 80% of the total rise. Eight months into the year, the government has now reached more than 60% of its full-year deficit target. While the core budget has already met nearly 70% of its deficit target, SV BW and SV IK lag significantly behind, with current execution rates of only 48% and 54%, respectively ( see Figure 16 in the appendix). Assuming an even distribution throughout the year, nearly two-thirds of the deficit targets should have been reached by August. Although the monthly federal budget data are inherently volatile and thus require careful interpretation, the current YTD developments collectively signal that the government could miss its total deficit target once again this year. records.text: given the negative reaction to the previous buyback announcement. With 30y yields now at their highest levels since 2004, the obvious question is: where to from here? We remain cautious and do not suggest buying at these levels, just because yields are high. We have already discussed US fiscal concerns, as Treasury’s ballooning expenses may only worsen with the Fed hiking rates and a high T-bill share front-loading the interest burden (see The Debt Knight Rises, dated 22 September). But there are also technical factors in the market that could see higher yields beget higher yields. Indeed, if back-end yields rise by another ~15-20bp from here, there is likely to be a large, cheapest- to-deliver (CTD) switch in the market (see The Continuing To De -anchor (CTD) problem, dated 19 May). Put simply, a selloff could force bond futures to start tracking longer duration bonds as their CTD, creating a negative convexity profile for those owning bond futures (primarily in the US contract). We estimate t his switch would give the market an additional ~6mn/01 of duration, or a ~10% extension in asset manager exposure in the US contract. Consequently, as this switch occurs, fewer market participants are then able to use the market sell-off to buy the dip as their risk exposure rises. And for some who actively hedge, this could result in negative convexity -type selling flows , exacerbating the rise in yields. Stable wage growth on a six-month annualized basis (Exhibit 5) is consistent with a stable labor market and a negative labor supply shock but is not inflationary. This may not last if labor slack diminishes given limited labor supply. Breakeven: Likely slightly higher than 20k/month Labor supply constraints tied to a tighter immigration policy remain an important part of the labor market story. Immigration enforcement appears to have softened somewhat at the margin earlier this year. In addition, some immigrants who lost humanitarian protections last year are likely regaining work authorization through asylum-based channels. Even so, recent policy developments suggest immigration will continue to restrain labor supply, albeit to a slightly lesser degree than initially projected. As a result, the labor market's breakeven pace of job growth may be somewhat higher than our current estimate of 20k per month. But any increase in breakeven would be modest. Therefore, even our below consensus jobs forecast should allow payrolls to still continue to average ( 3-month average at 80k) comfortably above the breakeven pace.

Further increases in inflation are also a key risk for investors, particularly if inflation expectations were to become disanchored. In our view, carry strategies in FX, commodities, and rates (short volatility), complemented by Equity Multi-Factor, should perform well in this environment. We also like diversifying equity factors through Equity Reversal. This can serve as an effective hedge against Momentum – which is showing signs of slowing – and as a strong complement to other traditional equity factors, while also offering a defensive profile in the event of a market slowdown. records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 From Crude to Diesel Trade Flows Crude trade is comparatively legible. Production is concentrated in identifiable exporters, which sell into a finite set of refining centres. The first leg of the supply chain can therefore be mapped reasonably cleanly from producer to refiner. Once crude flows are defined, the network becomes much less linear. Large refiners simultaneously produce gasoline, diesel, jet and other products; refining hubs import and export products at the same time; trading centres redistribute cargoes to surrounding markets; and destinations change as relative prices and freight costs move. A country with little direct exposure to the original supplier can therefore still face a substantial shock through the refinery or trading hub that normally supplies it. Exhibit 5: Oil supply chains become harder to trace once crude is refined Source: UN Comtrade, Morgan Stanley Research. Note: 2024 trade data is used. This data is not exhaustive, and should only be interpreted directionality Bilateral trade data tell us where barrels normally move, but in a tightening product market they do not tell us who ultimately loses supply. Physical exposure becomes endogenous to price. If one market bids more aggressively for a cargo, the relevant loss of supply may occur somewhere entirely different from the initial bilateral trade relationship. The problem can also become logistical before the world is literally short of aggregate refining

records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 25 Sep 2026 14:03:35 ET │ 23 pages US Economics Weekly A more hawkish reaction function CITI'S TAKE We were neither expecting the sharp rise in energy prices nor the Fed’s increased willingness to react to them with higher interest rates. A reaction function that includes energy prices means risks skew hawkish in the near- term and make it hard for the market to price-out aggressive rate hikes until data convincingly show either slowing inflation or softening activity. That dynamic took Treasury yields meaningfully higher this week. But fundamentally, we see underlying inflation cooling. Higher long-term interest rates should slow growth and loosen labor markets. In our base case, the Fed will pursue significantly less hawkish policy than what is currently priced by the market. records.text: • Despite elevated market volatility—spanning themes from interest rates and inflation to AI—we do not see evidence of broad CLO de-risking. Instead, vehicles have contin- ued to buy across the quality spectrum, adding B-rated loans to support equity returns while also purchasing BB-rated loans to maintain portfolio quality. • As a thought experiment on whether manager size drives positioning, we see little rela- tionship in this between managers who overweighted lower-risk/BB loans. While many BB overweights are lower-AUM managers, we believe it is too large a leap to generalize that “smaller managers took less risk” based on this alone—the devil will be in the details. Separately, to support broader discussions around execution, positioning, and potential par-build strategies, we provide the top 20 US CLO managers ranked by the largest positive gap between their overall (or weighted-average) sale price and purchase price. • We try to measure “outperformance”—i.e., CLO managers selling assets at above-index prices—but also “sacrifice”—i.e., de-risking below index levels, acknowledging mea- surement challenges. Consistent with broader loan market trading (see here), the majori- ty of CLO sales are in Technology, Services, and Healthcare—three of the largest-held and among the areas most impacted by AI. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 25 September 2026 3 odd, but there is reduced patience to continue disentangling signal from the noise. That’s a type of “optimism” that makes us particularly nervous. We now worry at least as much about persistence as about energy price peaks. This energy shock has arrived in successive waves. From March to mid-June, the shock was mainly reflected in oil prices. Peace deal hopes then delivered significant relief until mid- August, remember markets started to question if the ECB would hike more than once. Now the shock is broadening and lengthening – oil prices are back close to USD 100 and our colleagues expect them to stay there for most of the winter. Gas prices are close to EUR 70 and our colleagues expect them to rise to EUR 90-100 over the winter, before moving closer to USD 70 and EUR 40 by end-27. That has led us to reduce our sequential growth forecasts to 0.2% for the winter (-10bp). The widening in Gasoil crack spreads (ie rise in Diesel prices) amid US export ban concerns, is not part of our base case. If current energy prices stay at these levels for longer, we doubt the economy would look as resilient. Hence, we still struggle to see a natural path for the ECB to hike in March, or deliver more than 100bp in total. It’s always hard to predict (or stop) non-linearities We still worry about non-linearities in growth, but also in market dynamics in the Euro area. France is arguably (and to a certain extent understandably) the weak spot here.

Inflation Call Delta Replication: Our Inflation Call Delta Replication strategies (US: BNPXU1C1, EU: BNPXE1C1) have exhibited the highest correlation to inflation in our universe. We see them providing robust protection against inflation increases while offering positive convexity (Figure 1). The average sensitivity is 70bp per 10bp increase in 10y inflation across both the US and the eurozone. Long rate volatility strategies: In our view, long rate volatility strategies should continue to benefit from rising rates. Our economists expect that as the US economy remains resilient and inflation continues to climb, the Fed will make two more 25bp hikes, at its December and January meetings, followed by an extended pause. In the eurozone, an additional hike is expected in December. Given the high-inflation environment and the upward trend in rates, we believe conditions remain favourable for the Notional Weighted with Trend version in both the US and Europe (US: BNPXLWNU, EU: BNPXLWNE; see Figure 2).
