SNB Head Schlegel perhaps summed up the current prognosis for the CHF: widening rate differentials have been the main driver of CHF underperformance. For the softening of the statement to have had any impact, one must believe that SNB rhetoric was a strong deterrent to CHF appreciation. The market simply moved on to focus on the substance of the forecasts. The SNB, like other central banks, faces the challenge of trying to out-hawk the market. The SNB did not even try to make a stand and this has been the main catalyst for further CHF weakness. OIS pricing has taken out some tightening, but not much. We continue to believe that that the SNB is in a prolonged holding period and that the adjustment in rates has some way to go. With the current environment remaining conducive for vol-adjusted carry trade and more symmetry around the JPY, the CHF stands out as the G10 funder of choice. Higher USD/CHF remains the natural conduit, despite some noise from quarter-end rebalancing flows. For those looking to hedge some of their underlying bearishness towards the CHF, lower EUR/CHF makes sense to us, with the skew increasingly moving towards CHF calls. We interpret this as investors hedging against CHF appreciation driven by localized European political and budgetary risks.

records.text: portfolio that relied on duration to absorb equity drawdowns must replace that hedge when the correlation flips, and explicit equity protection is the natural substitute. Greater demand for equity options supports richer implied volatility, and therefore a richer premium for those willing to supply it. Interestingly, this may be the same force behind the muted spot/vol beta highlighted in the previous section. Investors who own protection ahead of a selloff have less need to chase volatility as it unfolds, which dampens the vol reaction on the way down: the dynamic behind the 2022 grind lower that we have discussed at length previously. The equivalent argument for rates is weaker. Rates volatility buyers are arguably more heterogeneous, as they tend to hedge mortgage convexity, issuance risk and balance-sheet duration. Their demand is driven more by rate levels and policy uncertainty than by the correlation regime, so the regime shift is less likely to lift rates protection demand in the same way. Verdict: Qualified support for equity VRP , and the one dimension where the regime shift works clearly in equity's favour. We cannot measure it over the sixty-year sample, so we flag it as a directional judgment rather than a finding, though one that the 2022-24 experience supports. 23 September 2026 8 Barclays | Derivatives Research

records.text: USD: Passengers. We see recent Dollar strength as a function of Fed follow-through, n pressure from commodity prices, and the associated move higher in yields. But we are frequently asked why FX moves have been relatively contained compared to the moves in other asset classes, and particularly rates and commodities. We have found that FX volatility tends to increase when markets are worried about downside risks to activity or more divergent growth and policy prospects. For the most part, recent market moves have the opposite flavor; growth has been surprisingly firm in much of the world and that has helped catalyze markets to reprice policy expectations almost everywhere in the same direction. It makes sense for FX returns to be more contained in this environment, and our baseline forecasts reflect more of this to a certain extent. We expect relatively low total returns outside of carry, and more mixed Dollar performance from spot levels given our relatively dovish Fed call but solid capital return prospects in the US. We therefore tend to emphasize what we think could allow the Dollar to break out of this environment in either direction. On the one hand, downside risks to the Dollar stem mostly from policy risks in the US and beyond (see our Yen forecast change in the JPY bullet), which have been the catalyst for most Dollar downturns over the last 18 months. records.text: mplied volatility minus subsequent realised volatility, for equities and rates since 1998, when reliable options data became available, shaded by prevailing equity/rates correlation regime (red for negative, green for positive). Equity volatility has paid a remarkably steady premium (hit rate: 84%), punctuated by rare and violent drawdowns. Rates volatility has paid a noisier, genuinely two-sided premium (hit rate: 69%) with no comparable crashes, and a distribution close to symmetric where equity's is severely fat-tailed (kurtosis: 28 vs. 3). This aligns with our previous conclusion that equities, alongside credit, should command among the richest cross-asset volatility premia (see To carry the cross-asset vol premia) owing to their structurally greater tail risk, jump risk and volatility uncertainty. 2022 is the case study: bonds stopped hedging, and VRP still worked. The 2022-24 period is the most sustained negative-correlation block of the post-1998 era, and macro risk unambiguously migrated towards rates: inflation uncertainty, policy surprises and a bond market that stopped absorbing equity shocks. Yet both equity and rates vol premia remained robust. Equity VRP held its steady positive range, a feature we highlighted in our 2023 Volatility Outlook, and the rates volatility premium sat inside the range it occupied in the surrounding green stretches. Risk moved, and the premium followed. 23 September 2026 2 Barclays | Derivatives Research

The note below traces energy flows across the economy to help frame economic consequences. The US has become an important source of marginal diesel supply, particularly given reduced flow from Russia and the Middle East. Our commodity strategists believe an export restriction would likely lower US diesel prices initially but with potentially adverse reactions downstream. Not only would diesel prices be higher globally, but there could be a feedback loop to US gasoline prices as refinery runs adjust. There is only a smaller pool of flexible supply, which increases the risk of a volume adjustment. How higher diesel prices and volume shifts are absorbed in the economy will depend on each economy’s energy balance, refining capacity, and domestic pricing regime. Countries with larger refining buffers or access to alternative product supply are more likely to absorb the shock through higher prices; those that are structurally short of diesel and have less flexibility to replace lost barrels face a greater risk that the adjustment ultimately shifts into volumes and activity. Policy then determines where the price shock lands. records.text: 25 September 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 15 Shock amplifiers/absorbers 1/. Labour market Takeaway: Job losses have acted as a shock amplifier in previous cycles. An examination of the labour market today suggests that it is more likely to act like a shock absorber than amplifier, which should be helping support domestic resilience, at least in the near term. The labour market can amplify a downturn when firms cut employment or hiring, reducing household income and spending and reinforcing the initial shock. However, during the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2022 energy shock government support for workers and firms helped preserve employment. This interrupted the usual feedback loop and allowed the labour market to act as a shock absorber rather than an amplifier. Our replication of the ECB’s Labour Market Conditions Indicator (LMCI) confirms the exceptional strength of the labour market in 2022 (Figure 23). Its first principal component, which is most closely associated with the level of labour-market activity, stood around 1.5 standard deviations above its long-term average. The second principal component, which captures labour-market momentum, was also very strong. Both the level and direction of labour-market conditions therefore helped cushion the energy shock. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 15 low-, middle-, and high-income consumers, real wage growth was positive in 2024 and 2025, though it was weaker for the low-income group. Earlier this year as inflation accelerated, real wage growth fell sharply across all groups and was negative as of the most recent May data. If we measure each cohort's change in affordability by their real wage growth, then there is less of a gap between the groups now, but all groups are worse off. For high-income consumers, wealth has provided an important offset to these real wage declines. The recent gains in wealth were driven largely by equities, and equity holdings are very concentrated amongst high-income consumers. The top 20% income cohort accounted for over 80% of the increase in household net worth in Q2; this group's net worth rose 8.3% q/q, while the net worth of the bottom 40% income group rose just 3.3% ( Exhibit 28 ). Meanwhile, tighter financial conditions likely affect low- and middle-income consumers more, as these consumers have higher shares of floating rate and short- term debt. Lower-income consumers are also less likely to be homeowners; as of 2024, only 43% of the bottom income quintile were homeowners, compared to 88% of the top income quintile. As a result, a much larger share of high-income consumers will be insulated from the renewed housing affordability pressures described above, while lower- income consumers who are renters or first-time homebuyers will be most affected. Doing so, the regression coefficients have a useful interpretation: they capture how much an increase in a given category's contribution—holding all other sectors constant—is expected to spill over to growth next period. And since next period's growth is itself the sum of sectoral contributions, we can track how much of a given sector's dynamics spill over to other sectors. In this case, how much is the investment in AI spilling over into investment and capex in segments seemingly unrelated to tech cap ex directly. Two important points to keep in mind. First, this is a predictive regression set-up: if for generic variables Y and Z we run the regression Y(t) = bZ(t-1) + e, then EY(t+1)=bZ(t) is the expected/predicted value of Y tomorrow conditional on Z today. It will most likely not be the actual value of Y tomorrow, unless the regression is a perfect fit (the error term e is everywhere zero). What we show below is a decomposition of expected NRBFI growth, not actual growth (which is by definition the sum of actual contributions of its constituents). Second, the regression is run not on growth rates but on contributions to GDP growth, which are growth rates scaled by GDP shares. So a category that has a small share but a high growth rate can contribute just as much to overall growth as a subcategory with a large share but lower growth. But the recent increase in implied vol has been different from the typical repricing dynamics in a couple of ways. Firstly, the spike in rates vol has not been accompanied by a meaningful pullback in risky assets, which is the inverse relationship typically observed (Figure 30). This suggests that the higher implied rates vol is likely not due to a structural increase in macro uncertainties, but rather it could be due to factors specific to the rates market, such as a temporary buyer strike and/or forced stops. If so, it is more likely that the higher implied vols could be short-lived and eventually reverse rather than be sustained. records.text: US Rates Weekly 25 September 2026 Citi Research 10 The amount of excess cash available is quite volatile due to fiscal outflows, as we show in Figure 19 the size of TGA outflows and their volatility have been increasing in recent years. On the flip side, Treasury debt issuance tends to be predictable and slow-moving. Since coupon auction sizes are generally only changed every few years, Treasury’s only short-term lever is T-bill auction sizes. These also tend to move within a range and while Treasury tends to shift sizes at the front end of the T-bill curve (4-week through 8-week), other sizes tend to be more constant (Figure 20). Lastly, when Treasury increases T-bill auctions sizes, there is a delay between the announcement and the actual settlements of the T-bills which means they need to anticipate changes in their funding needs. This mismatch between fiscal outflows and Treasury’s inflows result in excess TGA balances. Since Treasury may not have a perfect measure of their outflows ahead of time, we think in practice only a fraction of the “excess” would be invested in repo. Figure 18. Excess cash in the TGA tends to be very volatile; we think in practice only a fraction would be invested into repo markets. Figure 19. Data center and EV investments have generated limited spillovers given Thailand's lack of integration across the full value chain. This has contributed to a USD18bn decline in the current account balance over the past six months, marking the sharpest deterioration since 2006 (Figure 3). At the same time, a backdrop of higher US real yields and renewed USD strength is likely to cap upside in gold prices, an important driver of the THB given its close relationship with gold imports. Valuation and positioning metrics further support our bearish view. Outside of Singapore, most South Asian economies have str uggled to deliver strong growth, a dynamic that has already been reflected in weaker currency performance. Real effective exchange rate valuations for IDR, INR, and PHP have adjusted materially lower, leaving the THB as the second-most expensive currency in Asia (Figure 4). The message from the FOMC was both more hawkish and more united than we had expected. Not only did the committee hike 25bp without dissents, but 16 out of 18 participants—Chairman Warsh again didn’t submit a dot—signaled at least one more hike by yearend. We expect that hike to come at the October 27-28 meeting. Although this is the week before the midterm election, the second hike is probably less problematic from a political perspective than the first one. And there is little precedent in modern FOMC history for skipping meetings before elections; most strikingly, the committee hiked by 75bp six days before the 2022 midterms. Beyond October, we see a stable funds rate as core PCE inflation comes down faster than the committee projects, and we still expect rate cuts to our neutral rate estimate of 3.25-3.5% starting in late 2027. Whether markets price these risks conditionally on the prevailing regime or through the longer-run characteristics of the asset is harder to establish. What is clear, however, is that rates VRP has remained robust through a period marked by rising fiscal concerns, sticky inflation, hawkish policy shifts and political uncertainty, suggesting that the heightened risk was sufficiently reflected in implied volatility for rates carry to continue working. Equity VRP remains the stronger core source of carry. Consistent with our earlier findings, its premium remains robust across equity/rates correlation regimes, and the framework provides no clear case for timing equity volatility carry on that basis alone. Its structural supports change across regimes, but they do not disappear. Rates volatility can be a useful complement. Rates carry can perform even during persistent inflation and negative equity/rates correlation, provided the associated uncertainty is reflected in implied volatility, particularly in short-dated gamma. Cross-asset VRP does tend to suffer together in sudden shocks, so the role for rates VRP is not to replace equity VRP or to offer a richer standalone premium, but to diversify the sources of carry across a different macro risk. records.text: Sensitivity analysis — alternative energy paths Similar to the ECB's projection exercises, our forecasts are anchored in the energy price paths implied by futures curves for oil, gas, and electricity. Given the central role that developments in energy markets are likely to play for the euro area inflation outlook over the coming quarters, we also examine the implications of alternative energy price configurations. Specifically, in this iteration, we consider one alternative scenario assuming flat energy curves, effectively stripping out the backwardation currently embedded in futures markets. The projected path for headline inflation reflects only the mechanical impact of the alternative wholesale energy price assumptions on energy HICP . All other components are left unchanged relative to our baseline. In other words, these scenarios do not incorporate any change in the assumed pass-through from energy prices to food or core inflation; only the energy component is adjusted to reflect the different wholesale price paths (Figure 26). Should the backwardation currently embedded in energy futures curves fail to materialise, headline inflation could peak at 4.3% in January 2027, c.0.2pp above our current projections. End-2027, headline would still trend at 2.3% y/y, c.0.3pp above our forecast. FIGURE 26. Could regulatory reforms lower the level of reserves banks want to hold? The more plausible route to a smaller balance sheet is to lower the amount of reserves banks demand while preserving the ample-reserves framework. Stephen Miran’s March 2026 paper reviews the literature on this subject and offers a number of options for achieving this outcome. Recent central bank QT decisions and potential reviews of the investment frameworks of major institutional investors have brought renewed attention to shifts in the price -insensitive investor base and their potential impact on global term premia (TP). Over 2004Q1 -2025Q4, the relationship implies that a 1bp increase in the composite term premium is associated with around a 0.23ppt increase in free float. records.text: Markets, Bloomberg High concentration, so what? Reliance on a small group of large stocks may feel uncomfortable, but it is neither unusual nor necessarily detrimental for future returns. Indeed, a State Street Associates paper, (The Fallacy of Concentration) analysed previous periods of elevated market concentration and found that concentrated index weights have not been a reliable indicator of either higher risk or weaker future performance. We reached a similar conclusion today. Technology's outperformance reflects not only its own strong earnings growth, but also the lack of compelling earnings opportunities elsewhere. Figure 2 illustrates this dynamic well. Over the past year, Technology and, somewha t surprisingly, commodity sectors have expanded margins, while much of the rest of the market has struggled to pass rising input costs on to customers. Figure 2 Margins are under pressure Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg Still, could higher interest rates prove to be the final straw that derails the rally? Higher rates can hurt equity markets in two ways. First, they can compress valuation multiples by increasing discount rates. To some extent, this has already happened. Multiples have declined across most equity markets this year, forcing equities to rely o n stronger earnings growth to generate returns. Breakeven: Likely slightly higher than 20k/month Labor supply constraints tied to a tighter immigration policy remain an important part of the labor market story. Immigration enforcement appears to have softened somewhat at the margin earlier this year. In addition, some immigrants who lost humanitarian protections last year are likely regaining work authorization through asylum-based channels. Even so, recent policy developments suggest immigration will continue to restrain labor supply, albeit to a slightly lesser degree than initially projected. As a result, the labor market's breakeven pace of job growth may be somewhat higher than our current estimate of 20k per month. But any increase in breakeven would be modest. records.text: ergy prices and even tighter financial conditions constrain growth through the winter – we cut sequential growth to c 0.2% qoq (-10bp). We expect 1.0% growth in 2027 (-10bp) and 1.1% in 2028 (unch). We are not oblivious to 1H26 growth surprises, but we find noise in the data almost everywhere. That makes us very reluctant to extrapolate; we prefer to remain cautious. ECB guided to a Dec-26 hike, Mar-27 not so obvious We change our ECB call and embed a Dec hike in the base case. We still think the ECB is unlikely to go further. An Oct-hike is not impossible, but would require central bank panic and big surprises – not our base case. Relatively speaking, the risk of a fourth hike is greater in Mar-27, but that would not be easy either. Wholesale energy prices should be lower after the end of the heating season, while headline inflation would be about to drop on base effects, and we think core would be below the ECB’s expectations then. Inflation stays above 3% until mid-2027 in our forecasts and undershoots target in early 2028 temporarily due to energy driven base effects. There are risks that the return to target sustainably is delayed. We expect the passthrough of the energy shock to domestic inflation and second round effects to remain somewhat contained, but risks are on the upside given the high inflation peak. Core inflation is likely to hover around 3% for the next few months and reach closer to target in early ‘28. Growth to slow after being firmer than expected Growth moves higher in 2026 to 1.3% (+10bps) as the economy is weathering the energy shock better than expected so far, driven by household consumption and business investment. We increase our estimate of Q3 growth to 0.4%, given the upside surprise in July GDP, some of which seems to be potentially driven by AI related investment. At the same time, household savings are potentially helping to buffer the shock, boosted further by the warm weather and the World Cup But we expect higher inflation, tightening of financial conditions, policy uncertainty ahead of the Autumn Budget along with our expectation of BoE hikes to lower growth in 2027 to 1.0% (-20bps) and in 2028 to 1.4% (-10bps). records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 25 September 2026 15 yen-based import prices for general, production and business machinery rose around 42%, versus 18% on a contract-currency basis. In other words, yen depreciation since 2022 nearly doubled the price increase that Japanese machinery purchasers faced. Given machinery's high import content, imported cost inflation, amplified by the weaker yen, was likely a meaningful driver of the ~19% rise in the machinery deflator. Construction faces a domestic cost & capacity constraint The story is somewhat different in non-residential construction. With no direct import channel, foreign costs explain less of the increase in construction prices than they do for machinery. Instead, the pressure has come from domestic costs. Construction costs for steel-frame buildings in Tokyo are up 24-28% since 1Q CY22. Labor shortages are a significant constraint: the job openings-to-applicants ratio for structural construction workers rose to 7.94x in July 2026, compared to 1.18x for all industries. Construction order backlogs have risen from around 14 months of work pre-pandemic to 20 months today. As with machinery, the weakness in real construction investment is not a demand problem. Projects are being commissioned. But they are taking longer and becoming ever more costly to complete. We expect issuance to remain subdued within the sector at $3 billion in 2026, and another $3 billion in 2027. Credit Card: Financing Costs Bite Credit card ABS issuance has declined in 2026 relative to 2025, and we expect that trajectory to continue into 2027. The key headwind, in our view, is the current high-rate environment, which has pushed the cost of ABS financing into inefficient territory for a sector dominated by bank issuers. The availability of alternative sources of cheaper funding (e.g., deposits) and with potential relaxation in the BASEL III endgame capital rules, the calculus for card issuers continues to favor balance sheet retention over the new issue market. Auto ABS: The Balance Sheet Wins Prime auto ABS suffers from the same pressures as credit card ABS. This year, the sector is on track to see a decrease in issuance relative to 2025, and we expect a further decline in 2027. Issuers in the prime auto space—predominantly banks and auto manufacturers—are increasingly likely to retain loans rather than distribute them. records.text: on. Maintaining physical supply after any reduction in US availability would therefore require the region to attract replacement cargoes from elsewhere. Diesel demand has been weak enough since the start of the conflict that the region has materially closed its diesel trade deficit. LatAm — the largest direct trade exposure to the US though, economically, market support mechanisms dampen consumer exposure. The Americas absorb a large share of US diesel exports, making the region the most exposed to US supply. Domestic fuel-price transmission has so far been comparatively muted across much of the region, with Chile the more visible exception. Policy and pricing regimes are important in understanding the domestic impact: subsidies, administered prices, taxes and quasi-fiscal mechanisms usually dampen the immediate household-price response. Asia — stronger refining buffers, lower pass through on average, but an important source and buyer of the marginal barrel. Several of the major Asian refining economies generate substantial product surpluses, leaving the region as a whole better positioned on diesel than Europe. The direct macro shock is therefore smaller than the potential role Asia plays in clearing the global market. If prices elsewhere rise, surplus cargoes can be redirected. The relevant risk is less a generalized regional shortage than the cost and availability of the marginal export barrel.

records.text: al-bank response depend on a range of factors. The core focus of this note is to trace flows to think through inflation and growth implications. Then a separate analysis needs to be considered to think about central bank reactions, as they will not be uniform. First, the mandate of the central bank matters. Specifically whether they target inflation and employment or just inflation and how their inflation mandate is interpreted vis-à-vis headline versus core inflation. These nuances are important because it determines how sensitive a central bank may be to a growth-inflation trade off. In terms of the importance of oil to inflation, that is a function of oil in consumption baskets and economic linkages between energy prices and wages, for example. In the US, energy prices are usually transitory and do not leave a persistent impact on core inflation, the exception being when the disruption lasts multiple quarters and begins to disrupt supply chains for goods. In the Euro area, the focus is more direct and the link between non-core and core inflation is stronger, so the sensitivity to energy is higher. These nuances mean that while central banks are all leaning more hawkish in the current junction, the reaction function is not symmetric.

records.text: Jan Hatzius +1(212)902-0394 | jan.hatzius@gs.com Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC Global Views: Lower Inflation, Limited Hikes 22 September 2026 | 6:27AM EDT 1. We see three fundamental reasons for the Fed’s hawkish turn, which has upended our prior forecast of no hikes this year. First, renewed escalation risks in the Middle East have driven up the prices of crude oil and especially refined products, with diesel and jet fuel back to the 2022 highs. Second, the activity news has beaten expectations, with real GDP growth tracking 3.3% in Q3 and nonfarm payrolls rising 162k in August. Third, the August CPI and PPI data suggest that core PCE rose 0.27% last month, somewhat above pre-CPI expectations. 2. The news should turn less hawkish over the next several months. Our commodity strategists point out that overall oil exports from the Middle East have recovered to nearly 80% of prewar volumes despite the partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz and disruptions in the Red Sea. Moreover, China has again curtailed its imports since early August given higher prices, helping stabilize the demand-supply balance in the global oil market. Thus, our strategists project a gradual decline in Brent prices to $85/barrel by December. But product prices are likely to remain elevated given the shortage of refining capacity, and we still worry about renewed escalation that destroys more energy infrastructure. JGB: This Week in Review, The Week Ahead Ahead of the fiscal half-year-end, investors often look for yields to decline on quarter-end short covering and month-end index extensions. Yet our analysis of Ministry of Finance closing yields over the 26 years since 2000 finds little support for that view. The 10-year JGB yield moved by an average of just -0.05bp over the final 10 business days of September, rising in 14 years and falling in 11—hardly a meaningful directional bias. The same holds for the 20- and 30-year sectors and for 5s20s. The exception is the 2-year sector, where yields rose by an average of 1.3bp into the half-year-end before largely reversing over the first four business days of the new half-year. In short, September month-end seasonality offers little justification for a bullish super long stance. The more compelling signal appears in early October. Over the first five business days, 10s30s steepened in 22 of 26 years by an average of 2.6bp (t-statistic: 4.6)—the strongest start-of-month move of the year. From September month-end, the 30-year yield rose by an average of 5.1bp over 10 business days and was higher by day 12 in 24 of 26 years. The cheapening was concentrated in super long JGBs, with limited spillover into the 10-year sector and shorter maturities. Crucially, however, the move proved temporary: after peaking around day 15, the 30-year yield retraced roughly 60%

Not all studies have equity wealth MPCs as low as those in Beach et al. Maki and Palumbo (2001) had found MPCs out of total wealth of roughly 3.5-5.0% in 1992-2000, a period when equities were contributing the most to wealth gains. records.text: M Idea 2 Riksbank: En Route to a Hike Policy rate on hold: In line with our expectations, the Riksbank remained on hold today. The motivation for a hold remained the same as at the last few meetings. Spot inflation remains below target and there is spare capacity in the economy. The Riksbank therefore still has time to wait before making policy rate adjustments. However, higher energy prices, weaker krona and stronger growth were noted as an upside risk to the inflation outlook. Indicators point to inflationary pressures remaining above normal. The decision today was unanimous, but the time to hike has moved closer, and the new policy rate path reconfirms that. Full hike in 4Q26 and chance of another one in 1H27: As we expected, the policy rate path was revised to the upside as the balance of risks has moved to the upside for the inflation outlook. Our main focus was the expectation for 4Q26: the Riksbank now prices in 27bp worth of a rate hike by the end of the year on our calculations. We think the split is 16bp attached to November and 11bp to December. Another 18bp is priced in 1Q27, and 17bp in 2Q27 on our calculations. The intention was also confirmed in the statement which said that "the increases in the policy rate will begin this year". Our call: As we flagged in the Preview, we noted the risk that if the Riksbank includes a 100% chance of a rate hike in 4Q26, we could see the Riksbank going already in November. BoE to hike in Nov and Feb, with balanced risks We change our BoE call- we now expect the BoE to hike twice in Nov ‘26 and Feb ‘27 to 4.25% to guard against the risks of second round effects, assuming high energy prices are sustained into early next year and barring big downside surprises in data. We then expect three quarterly cuts starting in Q1 ‘28 (Feb, Apr and July) to our terminal of 3.5% (vs. our previous call of no hikes and a cut in Nov. ‘27 to 3.5%). Our terminal remains the same, but we expect to reach it later. Risks to our view are balanced. A meaningful drop in energy prices due to a lasting deescalation or big downside data surprises can weaken the case for tightening and allow for one or no hike. At the same time, a meaningful worsening of the energy shock, upside data surprises or strong evidence of second round effects materializing can open the door to a third hike. Beyond that, risks are tilted to earlier cuts if disinflation late next year moves faster than we expect. The change in our BoE call is driven by the move higher in our inflation forecasts showing a higher peak and greater persistence which can increase risks of second round effects, stronger than expected growth so far along with the hawkish shift in the BoE’s communication.

records.text: 25 September 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 10 The global fiscal drift Francis Yared | Strategist | +44-20-754-54017 We argued in our 2026 outlook (1) that most of the post -GFC decline in the equilibrium rate was likely to be unwound and (2) that the US labour market was likely to bottom as the policy setting switched from tight fiscal and monetary policy in 2025 (fed funds above 4% and tariff reven ues) to easy fiscal and monetary policy in 2026 (fed funds below 4% and BBB spending). Since then, the Fed has pivoted, the market is pricing equilibrium rates above 4%, and the labour market has stabilised. Our view was predicated, among other things, on structurally easier fiscal policy, not only in the US but globally . To assess how fiscal policy has evolved since our outlook, we compare DB economists’ current estimates of the global fiscal impulse for 2026 and 2027 with their forecasts from January 2026. The fiscal impulse is calculated as the annual change in deficits, and the global measure is the GDP-weighted aggregate for the US, eurozone, UK, Canada, Japan and China. Fiscal policy is now set to be slightly easier than expected in both 2026 and 2027. This reinforces our view that the repricing towards higher equilibrium rates is likely to be structural for now. records.text: ndix Let each firm i choose investment xᵢ at unit cost to compete for a fixed prize V. Its probability of winning depends on how much it invests relative to its peers. That is: pᵢ = xᵢʳ / (x₁ʳ + x₂ʳ) where r measures the strength of the “winner takes most” effect. When r = 1, winning probabilities are proportional to investment shares; when r > 1, an investment advantage produces a more than proportional increase in the probability of winning. Private Consumption Takeaway: Despite its remarkable resilience to the inflation shock so far, there are reasons to be cautious about both the strength and the sustainability of private consumption going forward. The inflation shock is larger and more persistent, labour income growth is slowing, non-labour income growth may be less beneficial, and excess savings are not available to shield all consumers. Private consumption has proven remarkably resilient in recent quarters, (Figure 5) particularly in Q2, when higher inflation would normally have pointed to weaker household spending. Instead, private consumption growth accelerated to 0.4% qoq, following broadly stagnant growth in Q1. This resilience is somewhat surprising. The increase in annual inflation is estimated to have reduced households' purchasing power by more than 1pp. Based on standard elasticities, this shock would, all else equal, be expected to reduce consumption by around 0.6% over a one-year horizon or slightly more. The key question, therefore, is whether the strength recorded in Q2 merely reflects the usual lag between inflation and consumer spending, or whether there are factors suggesting that household consumption can remain resilient. records.text: uity jump risk, the data offer little support for that view. In our view, structural changes in market microstructure have likely offset any reduction in macro uncertainty. Indeed, the growth of passive investing, volatility-targeting strategies, systematic flows, options-related feedback loops, retail participation, and the prevalence of "buy-the-dip" behaviour have likely contributed to a market that remains prone to discontinuous repricing. Largest rate jumps appear concentrated in the inflationary 1960-1980 period. The likely explanation is that persistent inflation and heightened policy uncertainty make bonds increasingly vulnerable to large, abrupt moves. In such environments, markets are forced to second-guess which side of the central bank's mandate policymakers are prioritising, increasing the likelihood of abrupt narrative shifts and policy surprises. The September 2026 FOMC meeting, which delivered the least anticipated rate hike of the past decade despite limited changes in the macro backdrop, is a recent example of this dynamic. Verdict: Jump risk also offers qualified support for a richer rates volatility premium in persistent negative-correlation regimes. The support rests on the severity of the largest rate moves rather than necessarily on their frequency, and the claim is further confounded by market structure. 23 September 2026 6 Barclays | Derivatives Research

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 27 HMDA 2025 Takeaways The average cost associated with obtaining a mortgage remained high, at $7,819 per agency-eligible mortgage in 2025, or 2.6% of the loan size. That's an improvement since borrowers paid 3.3% in 2023, but it remains well above 2020-2021's ~2.0% levels. Discount point usage declined while expanded credit features increased in balance. Purchase loans drove 69% of agency-eligible volume. With the slight dip in mortgage rates, the share of refinance loans increased 6pp to 17% of total origination. Florida, Colorado, Virginia, and Washington saw higher purchase volume share vs. their population share. Bank-originated mortgage borrowers saw a slight advantage in terms of mortgage costs. As a percentage of loan size, non-banks charged 2.8% in closing costs, on average, compared to banks at 2.0%. UWM and Rocket remained the top two lenders in 2025, with $162bn and $107bn of closed first-lien single-family mortgages. Banks and homebuilders increased their mortgage lending. Mortgage denial rates declined across loan purposes, from 13.5% to 12.9%. Refinance loans saw a larger reduction in denial rate compared to purchase loans. The Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data offers data on over 13 million mortgage applications, reported by nearly 5,000 institutions each year. records.text: Our thoughts on JPY, USD, MXN, CHF, BRL & Diesel and FX JPY: A shift in tide. We argued back in July that, without a shift in domestic n policy or a deterioration in the global growth outlook, the Yen’s cheap valuation would be insufficient to relieve the depreciation pressure on the currency. The Yen subsequently reached new 40-year lows until Japan conducted its largest FX intervention in 15 years, forcing a sharp reduction in tactical JPY carry positions. In the weeks that followed, the BoJ shifted to a faster pace of rate hikes (stabilizing the persistent rise in Japan term premium seen over the past year as shown in Exhibit 1), and the likelihood of a Japanese investor rotation back towards domestic assets increased—both developments we had flagged in July as conditions that could shift the Yen’s trajectory without an emergence of growth concerns. For years, domestic policies and the global backdrop justified the Yen’s undervaluation. Now, domestic policies seem to be turning more constructive, with scope for more to come. Faster rate hikes have reduced the inflationary impact of expansionary fiscal policy, taking pressure off the currency. A shift in portfolio flows remains mostly speculation so far, but the higher probability of it occurring increases the downside asymmetry in USD/JPY on top of the Yen’s valuation signal, strengthening its attractiveness as a portfolio hedge. BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Norges Bank: a 25bp hike, with a higher-for-longer rate outlook Norges Bank surprised us with a 25bp rate hike, with market expectations broadly split ahead of the meeting. At 4.5%, the policy rate is now at its highest level since the post- pandemic years. Following the hike delivered in May, Norges’s decision in September effectively reverses the rate cuts implemented in 2025. The policy rate path has been revised higher over 2027-29, reinforcing a “higher-for-longer” outlook. The projected peak in the policy rate has been raised to 4.60% (from 4.55% in June), preserving a modest tightening bias consistent with inflation risks remaining skewed to the upside. That said, we believe rates have probably peaked and do not expect further tightening from Norges Bank. However, persistently high energy prices and the prospect of a more hawkish global central bank backdrop in the short term could still create conditions for one additional hike by 1Q27. RMBS Non-QM spreads have remained relatively resilient amid the recent increase in front-end rate volatility Despite elevated front-end rate volatility and the market pricing in a 100+bp Fed hiking cycle, new issue non-QM spreads have shown remarkable resilience. This is all the more impressive considering the greater exposure of non-QM tranches to the front-end of the yield curve. When front-end yields sold-off sharply in 2022, non-QM AAA spreads widened out to as high as 250bp. A combination of a smaller front-end rate move (vs. 2022) and broader investor sponsorship for the sector has contributed to the resilience. A few large/repeat issuers and some smaller issuers priced new deals this week. The pricing color suggests that the trends we highlighted last week have largely held and that spreads have remained contained across ratings buckets. The spread between non-QM AAAs and agency MBS basis remains in line to marginally tighter vs. its longer-term average (Exhibit 7). The sharp rate sell-off has resulted in more questions being asked around the incentives for issuers to let deals extend rather than call them as assumed at pricing, however optimism largely prevails. records.text: arranted. She appeared to tie her support to the September inflation data. " By September, it was clear that inflation risks were growing … That's why I supported raising the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at last week's meeting. This recalibration brings policy closer to what I believe is needed to return inflation to 2 percent at a pace that appropriately balances inflation risks with risks to the labor market. Looking ahead, if conditions evolve as I expect, some modest further tightening may be warranted," she noted. Hammack notes persistent shocks raise risk of "inflationary mindset" FRB of Cleveland President Hammack made brief remarks this morning opening the FRB of Cleveland's Inflation Drivers and Dynamics 2026 Conference. She noted that while central banks typically "look through" supply shocks because they tend to cause only temporary price-level increases, that approach becomes riskier when shocks are frequent and inflation has remained elevated for several years. In such an environment, inflation expectations can become entrenched, making it more difficult and costly for policymakers to return inflation sustainably to target. "When the environment is more prone to shocks or the shocks arrive one after another in a period when inflation has been elevated for years, there's a greater risk that an inflationary mindset could take hold," she said. "The longer that high inflation persists, the more challenging and costly it can be to bring it back down ." Hammac

We expect 1.0% growth in 2027 (-10bp) and 1.1% in 2028 (unch). We are not oblivious to 1H26 growth surprises, but we find noise in the data almost everywhere. That makes us very reluctant to extrapolate; we prefer to remain cautious. ECB guided to a Dec-26 hike, Mar-27 not so obvious We change our ECB call and embed a Dec hike in the base case. We still think the ECB is unlikely to go further. An Oct-hike is not impossible, but would require central bank panic and big surprises – not our base case. Relatively speaking, the risk of a fourth hike is greater in Mar-27, but that would not be easy either. Wholesale energy prices should be lower after the end of the heating season, while headline inflation would be about to drop on base effects, and we think core would be below the ECB’s expectations then. Growth could still look ok, but it would likely be less robust than today, and we doubt meaningful second-round effects would have emerged. We still see ECB cuts in 2H27 We stick to our call that quarterly cuts will follow in 2H27 (Sep, Dec). We still see the depo rate dipping below 2% in 2028 again. The rate increase, revised inflation forecasts and greater emphasis on inflation persistence were broadly consistent with our pre-meeting assessment. SARB’s focus has consequently moved from evaluating alternative oil-price outcomes to assessing the implications of higher global interest rates, elevated inflation expectations and stronger wage growth. Morgan Despite rates moves and the largest move in real yields since ‘Liberation Day’, breakevens have remained steady moving under a basis point across the curve. Notably, the move in breakevens has continued to track the historical average around the initial hikes in a tightening cycle, which points to a narrowing in breakevens over the coming two weeks. While we have not seen a deterioration in market functioning with the rise in real and nominal rates, we have seen a liquidity premium being built into inflation markets. Additionally, TIPS fund inflows had the lowest 4-week period of inflows since the conflict began, and flows could further weaken as the 12-month total return for the TIPS index turned negative in September and the past month was the weakest period of total return for the index since 2024. This backdrop supports our narrowing bias in inflation markets; therefore,we maintain 2Yx3Y zero-coupon inflation swap shorts. Repo market conditions continue to be relatively calm as we head into quarter-end next week. We think this is evidence that reserves are lightly abundant, and we struggle to see significant catalysts for repo stress into year-end. Within goods-producing sectors, construction should post a seventh consecutive monthly gain. Manufacturing employment could also continue to show momentum. Both survey indicators and hard activity data suggest that activity in the sector has picked up this year, likely supported by firm demand, defense spending, reduced tariff uncertainty, and robust AI-related investment. Professional & business services is also showing signs of a more durable recovery. The sector has now added jobs for eight consecutive months after contracting in ten of twelve months during 2025. While part of the improvement reflects gains in temporary help employment, hiring has also strengthened across more technical industries. While the details have yet to be finalised, the package is expected to include a fuel tax discount and a €0.20/L subsidy on diesel for households, as well as for professional and agricultural users. These measures would help offset some of the pressure from gas prices, which are expected to rise sharply in October, with regulated prices potentially increasing by as much as 54%M (see here). Its final impact on headline is still unclear given the government is also reportedly considering introducing gas price caps to limit the pass-through to final consumer prices (see here). Diesel crack spreads and HICP fuel inflation Historically, changes in crude oil prices have strongly predicted fuel inflation. However, since the start of the Hormuz crisis, refined products have often captured more of the price strength than crude (see more here). Models built on crude alone lost accuracy as a result. We test this with two distributed-lag models for the euro area HICP subcategory fuels and lubricants for personal transportation. The first uses Brent alone, while the second adds the diesel crack spread to Brent. Both models have four lags, are estimated on month-over-month euro-denominated data to February 2026 and are then used to forecast the crisis months out of sample. Over the pre-crisis years the crack-augmented model was a slightly better fit, with a root mean squared error of 1.39%M against 1.71%M for Brent alone

The real time model produces the adjustments to employment from January through December as each new month of data is released. This is the data we forecast each month. At the annual revision, another model, the post-benchmark model generates new estimates that replace the real-time or "preliminary" RNBD for the non-benchmarked months of April through December. The benchmarks align the prior March to source data so the RNBD is no longer needed for January, February and March. This year, the methodological change added matched sample data (so-called weighted link method) to the models, so that the monthly sample receipts could inform the estimate (and thus the imputation added to NFP each month would also reflect some real-time information). We now have eight months of the real time experiment underway. We show the preliminary or real-time model estimates in the table. However, note those are not estimated from the model that produced the adjustment in the data for April 2025 through December 2025. Those post-benchmark estimates are shown in the other table, above, to show how much the post-benchmark model revised the preliminary model estimates at the annual revision. We estimate that 80% of the $5.3tr public fund universe is benchmarked to the US Agg, meaning any index change would have meaningful implications for both investors and issuers. Our view is that 144A-for-life securities should be included in any benchmark seeking to accu- rately represent broad USD IG credit risk. There isn’t a single fund that tracks just 144As despite it being a larger segment than HY and newer ETFs have used 144 inclusive benchmarks to a larger extent, two indications that the market already believes 144As to be a core part of IG credit. The case for inclusion has strengthened since Bloomberg’s prior consultation in 2023 as 144As have grown to 16.7% of the market, an 11 year high. They account for 23% of issuance since the last review, the highest share since 2012. Datacenter issuance has been an incremental driver of this and this issuance is likely to remain elevated, which in turn raises the question of a broad syndication requirement which we also address inside. Presumably the Director could introduce the GSEs models into the marketplace and price those scores at cost (or close to it), providing access to better risk classifiers at a more compelling price. LLPA grid gaming incentivizes multiple pulls—increasing total score costs to reduce LLPAs, which costs the GSEs. As we've written many times before, cherry picking the best score from multiple models allows borrowers in aggregate to reduce their rates, but only at the expense of the GSEs. Assuming that the GSEs need to collect a certain amount of reve- nue to generate an appropriate ROE on their guarantees, in a gamed LLPA world they need to charge a higher base g-fee. The net effect is that borrowers could spend more on total credit score costs, while on average not saving any money on rate (though there will be odd cross subsidization between borrowers, depending on their treatment across models). The GSEs opted against only allowing originators to pull a single credit score, perhaps antic- ipating that it would be too hard to ensure that score gaming wasn't being done behind the scenes. If they're going to stick with this approach, introducing multiple GSE scores to flood the box with cheap scoring options might be one approach to try to reduce the frequency of FICO or VS4 pulls. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 September 2026 Citi Research 14 North America United States Resilient activity, stable unemployment, and sticky core PCE inflation led the Fed to raise policy rates 25bp in September and markets to price in more hikes to come. But underlying fundamentals do not suggest sticky inflation despite higher energy prices. We expect no further rate hikes from the Fed, with 25bp of rate cuts in each of June, September, and December next year. GDP rose 2.1% in Q1 as consumer spending growth slowed but AI-related investment remained strong. Q2 consumption growth is tracking stronger with overall GDP likely growing around 2%. We continue to expect solid growth in 2026, driven by strength in AI-related business investment and resilient consumption. Core PCE inflation has been sticky above 3%YoY while core CPI has slowed meaningfully, an abnormal divergence as CPI typically runs stronger than PCE. There has not been much passthrough from energy prices to core inflation so far. Soft real income growth with less support from larger tax refunds compared to earlier in the year could limit the ability of businesses to raise selling prices despite higher input costs. Core PCE inflation is sticky in part due to rising prices for AI- related goods like computer software and accessories that get a much larger weight than in CPI. Across components, the acceleration in headline inflation will, in our view, again be driven by energy (+3.7, to 18.0% y/y), mostly on account of rising pump prices. Among non-energy components, we expect food inflation to remain broadly subdued (+0.1pp, to 1.2% y/y). Within core, we expect a further incremental uptick in core goods prices (+0.2pp, to 1.4% y/y) and a rebound in services inflation (+0.2pp, to 3.2% y/y), though we think evidence of indirect energy effects on energy-sensitive items in the basket will have remained contained in September. Our forecast sees headline inflation moving close to 4% by year-end, before easing gradually over 2027 and reaching target-consistent levels in H2. On an annual average basis, we project euro area headline and core inflation to average 3.1% and 2.4% y/y in 2026 and 2.8% and 2.6% y/y in 2027. Our forecast is conditioned on the latest futures curves for oil, gas and electricity and takes into account the latest fiscal support measures, including the 17c/L rebate adopted this week in Germany, running from early October through year-end. Source: Citi Research, National Statistical Offices Japan We had expected that, as inflation (primarily food) eased this year, real wages would turn positive and support private consumption and, by extension, the broader Japanese economy. However, the deterioration of the Middle East situation has significantly altered the macro environment. Inflation has continued to track below 2%, supported by the deceleration in food inflation and the impact of government energy subsidies, among other factors, and real wages have remained in positive territory as expected, but consumption has been less buoyant than anticipated. It is also worth noting that while net exports have made a positive contribution to GDP — owing to the decline in energy imports stemming from the Middle East conflict — capital expenditure has been weak despite AI-related demand. In the second half of the year, as the rise in energy prices since the spring is expected to fully feed through to consumer prices with a lag (see: August CPI review), the extent to which private consumption can hold up will be a key factor in determining the trajectory of the Japanese economy for the remainder of the year. We don’t think so, as we discuss in more detail here. First, these were regional elections with little direct repercussions for Federal policy making. The fiscal expansion rests on two pillars, defence and infrastructure. As such, spending commitments are tied either to Germany’s geopolitical position, and the need to react to a concrete threat, while also meeting NATO commitments (defence), or a far-reaching investment agenda, executed mainly at the regional level (the infrastructure package). These types of spending are very likely to continue at present speed. As for policies, key elements of the German reform agenda are either already decided or are close to a vote in Bundestag. Higher inflation and higher yields are associated with a more negative equity/rates correlation Source: Bloomberg, Barclays Derivatives Research Source: Bloomberg, Barclays Derivatives Research The option era is largely a single macro regime in disguise. The shading in Figure 1 and Figure 2 makes the constraint plain: negative correlation episodes are scarce in the option era. In twenty-eight years of option data there are only three meaningful negative-correlation episodes, one of which is still unfolding. Figure 3 puts that in perspective: across sixty years, inflation-dominated regimes are not rare at all. The option era simply happens to sit inside a long disinflationary stretch in which bonds were close to the perfect hedge. Any answer drawn purely from the option sample is really an answer about one regime. So the option era answers an important question but not the one that matters now, in our view. It tells us both equity volatility and rates volatility carry a steady premium, with equities the larger and more consistent of the two. It cannot tell us how a genuine inflationary regime reshapes either, because it barely contains one. For that we need to go behind the premium to the characteristics that generate it, i.e. quantities that can be measured over sixty years rather than twenty-eight. 23 September 2026 3 Barclays | Derivatives Research

Therefore, as the ECB delivers more hikes beyond neutral, we think the pricing of rate cuts will gain momentum, and the curve will flatten more. The risk to this trade, aside from a meaningful drop in energy prices, is a strong economy, potentially benefiting from the AI revolution more than we think, and as a result a ‘higher for longer’ policy stance remaining firmly in place. The curve is currently stuck between cyclical forces (the Middle East and ensuing central bank actions), which favour a flattening bias, and structural forces (fiscal concerns, heavy bond supply and the Dutch PF transition), which favour a steepening bias. records.text: Unlike most commodities, precious metals supply is relatively unresponsive to higher prices. Stronger demand must therefore be balanced primarily through demand destruction. During 2025-26, palladium inventories were increasingly pulled into the US and China, leaving less metal available to the rest of the world. Palladium holdings also increased in London and (especially) Switzerland, where physically backed ETF demand is typically stored. Investment demand is generally less price-sensitive than industrial demand and can even accelerate as prices rise. As inventories tightened, the required demand destruction increasingly fell on industrial consumers, including automotive manufacturers, that became less willing or able to buy metal at higher prices (Exhibit 8).8 8 Palladium prices more than doubled from the start of 2025 to the late-January 2026 peak. Its members bring meaningfully different perspectives. Raghuram Rajan has been a prominent advocate of shrinking the balance sheet, while Jeremy Stein has defended a large balance sheet as a potentially useful financial-stability tool (see here and here). Karen Dynan's research has focused on fiscal and monetary policy, and she has not taken a definitive position in the debate. After conclusions are delivered, likely by the end of the year, any decision to change balance sheet policy would be made by the full FOMC and the Board of Governors. The debate inside the Fed is likely to be similarly wide-ranging. Lorie Logan has offered one of the strongest defenses of the ample-reserves framework, while NY Fed President Williams this week noted that the framework of holding "ample" reserves has proven "highly effective at delivering interest rate control and supporting the smooth functioning of core financial markets." Warsh’s own messaging has evolved. He has long favored a smaller balance sheet and has repeatedly questioned whether SOMA holds too much duration. In the past, he has argued that a smaller balance sheet creates room for lower short-term rates without excess inflation – an argument he made while campaigning for the job as Fed chair in 2025 (see here and here). records.text: ) BCI, US At times, midterm elections can have a substantial effect on our market, but we view the 2026 midterms as less consequential for municipals than prior election cycles. That said, investors will be closely watching several policy issues in November that could ultimately prove meaningful for the asset class at both the federal and state levels. Focusing first on the federal elections, there are effectively two broad scenarios. The less likely outcome is that Republicans retain control of both chambers, while the more likely outcome is that Democrats gain control of at least the House and potentially the Senate as well. For municipal investors, we do not believe the distinction between these scenarios is significant. If Republicans retain control of both chambers, attention will likely shift toward extending and potentially expanding provisions of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act beyond their current sunset dates. We place little weight on a serious challenge to the municipal tax exemption, although certain subsectors could become more vulnerable. More importantly, lower marginal tax rates would modestly reduce the value of the municipal tax exemption and could limit retail demand at a time when net issuance remains elevated at $200-250bn annually and strong demand is needed to absorb supply. records.text: M Idea 14 Affordability Across Income Cohorts Despite the overall deterioration in affordability this year, there has been debate around if the "K" (the divergence between low- and high-income consumers) is widening or narrowing. Some measures of spending using transaction data have pointed to convergence between the groups, while comments from companies point to continued low-end pressure. Overall, despite some improvement in wage and inflation differentials, we think the income, wealth, and rates dynamics point to a continued K- shape dynamic, with little room for that to change in the near-term. Wage growth and inflation rates vary by income cohort, and at the start of this year, both of these were worse for low-income consumers. Low-income consumers experienced the strongest nominal wage growth in the immediate post-pandemic period, but that trend reversed in mid-to-late 2024, leaving them with the weakest wage growth throughout last year. On the inflation side, low-income consumers have historically experienced higher inflation rates than high-income consumers on average, which was especially true over the past few years. This year, both of those gaps have narrowed. Nominal wage growth for the lowest- income tercile is now running about in line with that of the middle- and high-income groups, due to both acceleration at the low end and deceleration at the high end. Historically for floorplan ABS, EFA of greater than 30% over three/six consecutive months would have resulted in early amortization of notes. The EFA thresholds were amended due to the pandemic to as high as 70% with a longer lookback. While sellers/servicers are not obligated to support ABS transactions, in the past, ABS issuers have amended deal docu- ments and added credit support to mitigate against rating downgrades as well as early amor- tization risks. For example, during the COVID lockdowns with no inventory to sell amid supply chain disruptions, issuers amended EFA triggers and/or added credit enhancement to support their floorplan ABS programs. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 September 2026 Citi Research 25 South Korea & Indonesia South Korea We expect South Korea's chip-led economic expansion to persist, underpinned by a prolonged memory upcycle. We see chip strength adding 3.2ppt to real GDP and 15.6ppt to nominal GDP in 2026E. We assume our 2026E nominal GDP growth at 25.0%, the strongest since 1981, with real GDP growth at 3.7% in 2026E, 3.1% in 2027E and 3.0% in 2028E. In our view, Long-Term Agreements (LTAs) should lift sustainability of exports and the current-account surplus, raising BoK's estimates for potential economic growth and neutral rates for 2026-28. LTAs sustain investment via advance payments and preserve elevated operating margins, likely boosting capital stock accumulation and productivity growth. records.text: We continue to expect uncertainty around critical minerals tariffs to persist, as n the ambiguity itself may be serving the policy objective of supply security through domestic stockbuilding. We therefore expect much of the metal already in the US to remain trapped, while periodic increases in tariff risk could encourage further stockbuilding. Implementing tariffs is unlikely to create new critical mineral supply because n mines and smelters take far longer to build than tariffs take to change. But the risk of tariffs still achieves a national-security objective by pulling metal inventories into the US without requiring large-scale government purchases or immediately raising costs for downstream consumers. The result is lower liquidity outside the US, even if global inventories remain comfortable on paper. The tightening in available ex-US inventories came as investor interest broadened n beyond gold into silver, platinum, palladium, and even copper. In a less liquid market, the same investor inflow can have a disproportionate impact on prices. While investor demand has softened as the market now prices a Fed hiking cycle, we expect much of the metal pulled into the US to remain trapped there, leaving available ex-US inventories tight and creating scope for a repeat of the 2025H2/2026H1 volatility should investor demand recover. records.text: ab 23 September 2026 Global Research European Economic Comment Germany: Elevated political risks - implications After the regional elections, where do we stand? We have written about the elevated political risks in Germany - and more specifically the uncertainty about the position of Chancellor Merz - in the context of the regional elections in Berlin and two east German states over the past weeks (see here). The parties of the national government coalition - and in particular the CDU/CSU - have seen substantial losses in these regional elections, with the far-right AfD being the main vote winner. Historically, the direct relevance of regional elections for policymaking at the federal level has been limited. That has changed though: In all of the recent elections, the AfD has been very successful and has put significant pressure onto the ruling coalition in Berlin. The AfD is now also leading the polls at the national level (with currently 29%, Figure 1O p i n i o n p o l l s - f e d e r a l l e v e l , % ), ahead of the CDU (20%), the SPD (12%), Greens (15%), and the Left party (11%). This outlook is broadly in line with the latest CBO budget outlook, published February 2026, but accounts for lower-than-expected tariff revenues, as well as higher-than-expected interest rates and inflation. records.text: at without the AI impulse, the declines in non-tech investment the last two years would be even worse. The level of real investment in the economy at these interest rates might otherwise be falling without the support from the AI impulse. We estimated that for every 1 pp the AI-related component of business fixed investment (BFI) contributes to real GDP growth, that impetus creates sufficient demand that the remaining components of BFI contribute another 0.5 pp to real GDP growth. Indeed, from a domestic activity point of view the spillovers may be as important as AI itself given how much of the AI-related investment we import. To build on this, in the chart below we make an assumption for the wealth effect from equity market valuations and the AI/tech impulse and the spillover effect, and subtract off the net exports offset. We assume that the growth in real consumption exceeding the growth in real disposable income is the contribution of the wealth effect to real GDP growth (and which in turn is a result of AI/tech investment and expected future profitability). These contributions are shown in the chart. The remaining contributions to growth, "other", include all the rest: government, spending from income, and non-tech investment. So we divide real GDP growth into the contributions of the AI impulse and ex-AI growth. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 September 2026 Citi Research 28 Turkey The authorities’ new Medium-Term Program (MTP) adopts a more gradual disinflation path than its predecessor, with single-digit inflation now envisaged in 2029 rather than 2027. The authorities’ projections for inflation, growth and the external balance remain more favorable than both market consensus and our own forecasts. The program envisages a gradual decline in inflation alongside a strengthening in economic activity and an improvement in the current account position. In our view, achieving this combination of outcomes may require meaningful progress in productivity, expectations formation and structural adjustment, particularly as growth remains demand-led. From a policy perspective, the projected macroeconomic adjustment appears to rest on several supportive assumptions. The envisaged fiscal trajectory suggests only limited additional support for disinflation. Similarly, the projected improvement in the external balance assumes lower energy prices and a moderation in import intensity despite stronger economic growth. The program’s increased emphasis on economic security, manufacturing and industrial policy is a welcome development. However, in our view, further progress in structural reforms, institutional quality, labor- market efficiency and product-market competition would help strengthen the credibility and internal consistency of the medium-term growth and disinflation objectives. Funding is soft: Short USDZAR positioning from CTAs (Figure 5) has pushed term funding lower, leaving front-end SAGB carry attractive on a term-funded basis. Paying term funding also provides a hedge: if funding pressure re-emerges, the pay-implied leg should cushion the position, in our view, even as the bond itself likely underperforms. From a valuation perspective, local-currency ASW levels look stretched for SAGBs, but we think the tightening has been largely funding-driven, with the cross-currency basis moving lower through the year – the USD ASW on R2030 has tightened by only around 10bp (Figure 6). Front-end steepening, as the curve prices in two further policy-rate hikes from the South African Reserve Bank against our view of an on-hold policy stance after today’s hike, combined with 1y funding at around 7.2%, has pushed carry/roll to 4.2bp/month. Fiscal performance remains strong: South Africa's fiscal performance continues to run ahead of the National Treasury's targets (Figure 2), supported by healthy tax buoyancy from commodity-price windfalls. The NT has already delivered two issuance cuts over the past year – in the 2025 MTBPS and this year's budget – and with the 2026 medium-term budget statement approaching, we see a reasonable chance of a further cut (alongside the formalisation of a fiscal anchor), which should be supportive for bonds. records.text: CHF: More underperformance ahead. The SNB kept rates on hold at this week’s n September meeting but reverted to a neutral bias on FX intervention for the first time since December, in line with our expectations and previous work showing that the SNB tends to take a more hands-off approach to intervention when inflation is in this range. That said, we noted ahead of the meeting that this incremental shift would be insufficient on its own to reverse the Franc’s recent trend of underperformance, particularly against a backdrop of resilient global growth, large carry interest, and widening rate differentials. Consistent with that view, EUR/CHF gained on the statement, which otherwise continued to express comfort with both the inflation outlook, noting that medium-term inflation pressures having “increased only slightly”, and the current policy setting. Ultimately, a firmly on-hold SNB, in contrast to other central banks that have moved toward more aggressive policy tightening, has been a key driver of CHF underperformance this year. Without a more meaningful policy shift from the SNB—against our economists’ expectation for a continued on hold stance—we think this underperformance can continue and now expect EUR/CHF at 0.95, 0.96, and 0.97 in the 3, 6, and 12 months (vs 0.92, 0.92, 0.92 previously). The main point is to highlight that, if decision -makers and investors believe AI to be a “winner takes most” set -up, then it becomes plausible to expect aggregate overinvestment. Crucially, such overinvestment is not reflective of a bubble or a lack of eco nomic benefits from AI. Rather, it is driven by the disproportionate advantage of being the dominant market leader. Rate market implications The “traditional” textbook impact of a new technology is to raise the equilibrium rate. Initially, higher capex shifts the savings/investment balance and pushes equilibrium rates higher. Subsequently, increased productivity results in higher growth and higher wages, which ultimately leads to higher consumption. So far, we have sided with the traditional textbook view, arguing that equilibrium rates were likely to reverse most of their post -GFC decline. We have highlighted both tails of AI (a bubble or a significant impact on the labour market) as risks to this view. This note highlights a third risk: rational overinvestment. If the AI race is genuinely a “winner takes most” set -up, one could expect a reassessment of the profitability of aggregate capex without denying the significant economic benefits of AI. If that occurs, the ensuing capex slowdown could result in lower rates. Appendix Let each firm i choose investment xᵢ at unit cost to compete for a fixed prize V. records.text: M Idea 4 RMB: Modest appreciation, but not a regime change The same domestic weakness that argues for incremental policy support also limits the case for a large RMB appreciation cycle. The market continues to debate whether RMB can strengthen further, and by how much. We now expect USD/CNY to reach 6.65 by year- end and 6.60 by end-2027, reflecting mark-to-market adjustments, tighter controls on capital outflows, and robust exporter FX conversion amid inertia in appreciation expectations. But we still see the move as gradual rather than the start of an aggressive appreciation cycle, with a stronger broad dollar, as well as negative rate differentials, likely to cap the trajectory in our forecast horizon. RMB "fair" valuation – macro context is broader than just the current account A weak RMB has not been the policy tool behind China’s export strength. The recent policy record is difficult to reconcile with the view that Beijing has deliberately suppressed the currency to support exports. When depreciation pressure intensified from 2022 onward, the PBoC repeatedly leaned against the move through the fixing, macroprudential tools and other forms of FX management. A record current-account surplus does not have to produce a commensurately stronger currency. Strong demand for foreign assets—reinforced by domestic deflation and deeply negative China-US rate differentials—can absorb FX generated by the current account. records.text: Jan-24 Jan-25 Jan-26 New Car Loans rate: 48 Month Duration( %) 30-Year Fixed Mortgage Rate (%) Source: WSJ, Haver Analytics, Morgan Stanley Research Higher Rates Keep Housing on Hold James Egan While the large portion of fixed rate debt and fixed rate mortgages will keep many consumers insulated from recent rate moves, renewed affordability challenges in the housing market will only drive greater divergences between previous homeowners, first-time homebuyers, and renters. The US Housing market is unaffordable. It does not feel like too long ago - late February of this year - we were celebrating mortgage rates falling below 6% for the first time since 2022. Today, mortgage rates are back above 7%. At that level, the monthly payment on the median priced home would be up over $230 from local lows in the first quarter, an 11% increase. When combined with home prices continuing to set record highs, our affordability calculation, defined as that monthly payment as a percentage of income, is at its most challenged levels of the year. The unfortunate reality, in our view, is that affordability is likely to be challenged for quite some time. The severity of the housing cycles over the past few decades has made it difficult to define what exactly a "normal" or "equilibrium" housing market is. In Exhibit 16 below, we show what it would take in both mortgage rate terms and home price terms to bring affordability back to different longer-run averages.

records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 September 2026 Citi Research 19 The budget is, again, looming. The fiscal landscape is difficult. Relative to the last budget, borrowing costs are very high and the OIS implied path for the Bank Rate is now upwards sloping rather than downward. This noticeably dents the ‘buffer’ that the Treasury had against their primary fiscal before you incorporate additional spending pressures. Whether or not the OBR will forecast a deficit or a surplus in 2029/30 remains unclear as of yet. It is clear, however, that if a surplus remains it will be significantly smaller than it was in March. The challenge is as political as it is economic. Levers for tax raises that are both politically viable and economically ‘sound’ (in the sense that they raise sufficient revenue) are few and far between and, for the most part, inhibited by the Labour manifesto. Similarly, spending cuts are not yet a serious topic on conversation. The question now, in our view, is whether or not the Chancellor opts to restore the ~£24bn headroom or whether we see a return to a smaller buffer. A smaller buffer will undoubtedly bring back memories of Labour’s first budget in Autumn 2024 and risk unsettling an already volatile gilt market. We now expect the BoE to start hiking. Despite what we consider to be a clear aversion to hiking from a majority on the committee, we now think that the chance of a hike is greater than not.
