Rather than selling a vanilla USD/JPY call, we prefer selling a reverse knock-in (RKI) call. The RKI creates a useful buffer between the strike and the barrier while giving up very little premium relative to the vanilla. In other words, the structure retains most of the premium from selling the 160 call but requires spot to extend further before the short option becomes active, which is attractive precisely when our view is that intervention risk should increasingly constrain the top- side. To identify the most efficient second leg, we compare spot FX betas and feed those betas through the option pricer, adjusting the hedge strike accordingly. On this basis, CHF, EUR, GBP and then AUD provide the best substitutes for JPY . CAD and CNH also screen favorably on option price, but we are less comfortable with their ability to provide suffi- cient protection in a forceful USD rally. EUR therefore offers a good combination of option value and USD-beta hedge. At 0.5x notional, the EUR/USD leg allows us to retain roughly half of the premium collected on USD/JPY , while the beta-ad- justed strike distances imply that EUR/USD should be approaching its hedge strike if USD/JPY reaches 160. US MBS: Don't fret the midterms, watch GSEs Michael Khankin, CFA(i) BCI, US | Pratham Saxena, CFA(i) BCI, US We expect little immediate impact from the midterms on MBS and Securitized Products in general. At this point, there is a strong consensus that midterms produce a divided government, with polling averages7 showing Democrats holding a considerable lead of 8% on the generic ballot and prediction markets expecting the house to flip Democratic by a margin exceeding 4:1. Realization of such an outcome should therefore be a non-event for rates, volatility, and spreads. However, pricing assumptions are liable to change if the Republicans manage to surprise markets and hold on to both legislative branches. Under that scenario the administration would avoid legislative gridlock and gain considerable leeway to boost defense spending, cut taxes, and pursue other policies that further the Republican agenda. Looser fiscal policy, coupled with a wider range of potential legislative outcomes would bias rates and volatility higher until 2029, a negative for mortgages that have traded directionally to rates this year and are explicitly short vol (Figure 5, Figure 6).

The July Monetary Policy Report set out a useful framework for monitoring second-round effects. Essentially, the Bank set out three different channels through which second-round effects emerge: 1. Initial conditions – These starting-point conditions can amplify second- round effects. If the labour market and the economy are overheated, it becomes easier for firms and workers to set higher prices and wages. 2. Price-setting – Firms may increase prices by more than the size of th e shock, simply to pre-empt future price increases or because they expect their competitors to move. 3. Wage-setting – Workers facing a real income squeeze may push for a higher pay rise if they expect inflation to stay high. All these channels interact with each other which could lead to an amplification of second-round effects. Morgan Credit score competition—what would reduce costs without increasing risk? A few weeks ago, as part of the FHFA Director’s latest salvo against credit score costs, the GSEs released a historical set (similar to the releases of historical data for VS4 and FICO 10T) of their own mortgage credit scores. Moreover, the Director indicated that he was look- ing at pulling back from requiring a tri-merge from the three bureaus, potentially as a way to further reduce costs. Our resi credit colleagues have crunched the numbers of the relative effectiveness of the GSE scores and compared the relative predictive power of tri-merge, bi-merge and single scores. Please see their report this week for the details, but in summary it appears that the GSEs’ scores are better credit risk classifiers than 10T or VS4 (which in turn appear to be superior to FICO), and that a bi-merge could be just as effective as a tri- merge at predicting defaults (though a single score would lose some predictive power).

These results provide no evidence that month-end index-extension demand materially supports super long JGBs. Indeed, over the final five business days, the 30-year yield rose by an average of 1.3bp and 10s30s steepened by 0.8bp, if anything pointing to modest cheapening and bear steepening. September month-end therefore offers no statistically significant directional edge. The 2-year sector is the sole exception. Between T-10 and T0, the 2-year yield rose by an average of 1.3bp and increased in 20 of 26 years (t-statistic: 2.6). It then fell by an average of 1.1bp from T0 to T+4, almost fully reversing the premium accumulated into the half-year-end. A similar pattern is visible around the March fiscal year-end, likely reflecting a combination of balance-sheet constraints and positioning ahead of the month-end 2-year auction. In 2026, that auction falls on 30 September itself, leaving the sector particularly exposed to seasonal upward pressure on yields. Even so, as of 24 September, calendar effects alone provide no reliable guide to the direction of yields over the final five business days. On the other hand, the PBoC also rejects a mechanical current-account/RMB link. In its 1Q26 Monetary Policy Implementation Report, the PBoC noted that China’s US$735bn current-account surplus in 2025 was accompanied by an US$820bn non-reserve financial- account deficit, with “the fund inflows formed by the current-account surplus transformed into outward investment uses under the financial account.” The implication is that a large current-account surplus does not translate mechanically into RMB appreciation: the FX inflows generated by trade can be offset by residents’ demand for foreign assets and other capital outflows. Latest guidance allows market-driven RMB moves, while sharpening its guardrails against one-way expectations. Compared with the 2Q26 Monetary Policy Committee meeting, which focused on “enhancing the resilience of the FX market, stabilizing market expectations, and keeping the RMB exchange rate basically stable at a reasonable and balanced level,” the 3Q26 statement adds that the PBoC will “uphold the decisive role of the market in exchange-rate formation” while “guarding against herd behavior and the self- reinforcement of irrational expectations.” The shift suggests tolerance for orderly, market- driven RMB moves—including appreciation. As we discussed previously, the disruption of the East-West pipeline and heightened risks to Red Sea shipping routes have underscored vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s export network. Despite stepped-up diplomatic efforts to contain regional spillovers, preserve maritime security and advance de-escalation, Saudi Arabia faces an increasingly complex environment in which energy security, export reliability and regional stability have become inextricably linked. The Kingdom's detailed 2Q GDP data, crude production data through August and other growth indicators suggest to us that the economy is likely to contract 2.4% this year, following growth of 4.6% in 2025. This forecast envisions a 16.7% contraction in oil GDP in 2026, following 5.7% growth in 2025, alongside a slowdown in private non-oil GDP growth to 1.9% from 5.1%. We believe the Kingdom’s growth outlook, fiscal position and external balance depend critically on the pace of the recovery in crude oil production and, following this month’s attacks on the East-West Pipeline, the security of this key export corridor. Reducing its dependence on foreign critical mineral supply and rebuilding domestic capacity appear to be increasingly important US policy objectives. Long Lead Times and Geology May Limit the Effectiveness of Tariffs to Create New Domestic Supply In theory, tariffs are a way to achieve this policy objective: make imported minerals more expensive, protect domestic producers and ultimately incentivize investment in US mines, smelters and refineries. records.text: . Interest on reserve balances (IORB) establishes the return banks can earn on funds held at the Fed. The overnight reverse repo rate (ON RRP) provides a Fed investment option for eligible money-market participants that cannot earn IORB directly. When reserves are ample, the federal funds rate is only modestly sensitive to changes in their supply. In late 2025, money-market conditions tightened as QT reduced reserves toward the lower end of the ample range and closer to scarcity. The FOMC therefore ended QT effective December 1 and, on December 10, directed the New York Fed to begin RMPs to maintain ample conditions. The purchases were concentrated in Treasury bills and sized to accommodate both trend growth and seasonal changes in demand for Fed liabilities. The key assumption is the presence of sufficiently strong “winner takes most” dynamics. This assumption is not purely theoretical. Public statements from policymakers and industry participants frequently frame AI as a race for leadership with disproportionate benefits for the market leader. For example, President Trump recently argued that “whoever wins AI, wins”. It is beyond the scope of this paper to argue whether AI is indeed a “winner takes most” set -up. There are some arguments in favour of this view, such as self - reinforcing leadership through economies of scale and data accumulation. There are also counterar guments, including the ease of switching from one model provider to another (literally a drop -down menu), the fact that most tasks do not require the most advanced frontier models, and a plausible focus on sovereign AI and data control, even at the expense of model performance. It is also beyond the scope of this paper to opine on the aggregate expected profitability of current and prospective capex plans. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Oil Tracker: Running Out of Buffers Our baseline outlook for the US economy assumes a permanent oil risk premium. The renewed pressure on energy prices has dragged the world into the seventh month of this prolonged energy price shock. Historically, episodes of acute geopolitical or physical supply disruption have mostly lasted 3–6 months, with the notable exception of the 1978–79 oil shock and its aftermath. As buffers such as higher U.S. exports, weaker Chinese imports, and ample inventories begin to fade, we update our oil tracker to highlight developments and trends that matter for U.S. economic growth. The latest data suggest that crude oil inventories in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) have fallen further, while both U.S. crude oil imports and exports have remained on an upward trend. Our X-asset vol premia framework: built on decades, not one cycle This is where our cross-asset vol premia framework becomes useful. In To carry the cross- asset vol premia, we argued that volatility risk premia compensate investors for warehousing risks that are difficult to model and hedge: how severely an asset can surprise you (fat tails, jumps), how closely volatility shocks coincide with broader portfolio losses (spot/vol correlation), how hard volatility is to forecast, and the structural demand for protection that follows. Viewed through this lens, credit and equities should command structurally larger vol premia than rates, with FX1 at the bottom of the ranking, a conclusion broadly validated by empirical vol premium (VRP) data. Page 5 Early October: Super Long-Led Bear Steepening Figure 4 plots the 26-year average change in yields by maturity from September month-end. After remaining broadly stable through T0, the 30-year yield cheapens in October, reaching +2.5bp at T+5, +5.1bp at T+10 and +5.9bp at T+15. By T+12, it stood above its September month-end level in 24 of 26 years. The 10-year yield, by contrast, was only 1.2bp higher at T+10 (t-statistic: 1.2), while the 2-year yield was essentially unchanged—clear evidence that the seasonal effect is concentrated in super long JGBs. Earlier in the week, Europe's strong September flash PMI further conveyed a message of resilience in economic activity, with the composite index rising to 53.1, reflecting underlying momentum across services and manufacturing. The improvement in PMIs was concentrated across core economies, with Germany extending its momentum, the composite index rising 2.0pt to 53.8. France moved back into expansionary territory for the first time since November 2025. While the activity readings painted a promising picture for growth prospects, the inflation backdrop from the PMIs was less sanguine. Input measures for manufacturing and services accelerated, suggesting a second wave of input price increases is taking shape, rising 3.7pt to 66.5 in composite terms. The more muted uplift in output prices (+1.6pt to 56.3) relative to input prices (+3.7pt to 66.5) points to continued margin compression, which is dampening the broader pass-through of rising input costs. In contrast to the acceleration observed in Europe, the UK flash composite PMI moderated to 51.7, down from 52.5 recorded in August. The moderation was broad based, underpinned by softer readings across services and manufacturing. Consistent with the European price pressures, UK composite input prices re-accelerated following a period of moderation (+2.0pt to 68.8)

records.text: inferring the answer from a sample that contains only one. This report puts that question to sixty years of data. We classify history by equity/rates correlation regime. We split the sample into quintiles based on trailing one-year SPX/US 10-year yield correlation. Negative-correlation quintiles capture inflationary regimes in which bonds fail to diversify equity risk; positive-correlation quintiles capture conventional growth-driven environments in which they do. Each quintile is well populated over sixty years of underlying returns, even where the option sample is not. We then re-examine each component of the framework within these regimes to analyse how some of the structural drivers of volatility premium, i.e. tail risk, jump risk, spot/vol correlation and volatility persistence, evolve with the changing macro backdrop. A quick caveat: Throughout this report, we focus on the implied-realised volatility premium (gamma), using realised volatility as the benchmark against which premia are assessed. As such, the framework is most directly applicable to shorter-dated volatility strategies whose returns are predominantly driven by gamma carry. Longer-dated structures embed additional exposures to volatility term structure, forward volatility and vega dynamics, which may respond differently to the correlation regime. 23 September 2026 4 Barclays | Derivatives Research

The Shift in Central Bank Policies In response to this higher inflation, central banks have pivoted to tighter policies (Figure 9). Generically, the monetary policy implications of higher energy prices are unclear. Should central banks cut rates to support spending or hike rates to fight upward pressures on prices? As such, there is a good case for central banks to initially look through the shock to see which of these two effects dominates.3 In this instance, however, central banks have generally leaned toward tighter policy. As shown in Figure 10, our projections for policy rates are now higher than in February for 20 of the 27 major central banks that we track. In our view, DM central banks are seeking to incorporate the painful lessons they learned in the aftermath of the pandemic when they initially “looked through” rising inflation. While inflation pressures are more contained than a few years ago, they fear that making the same mistake again would be damaging to their credibility. With confidence building that an imbalanced China is receiving a significant fiscal impulse, and that other Asia tech exporters are still booming, the global expansion appears to have entered a phase of broad-based strength rarely seen over the past two decades. Amidst strong growth and firming perceptions of resilience to high energy prices, it is no surprise that interest rates are moving higher while equity prices remain close to record levels. Our G4 policy rate expectations through mid-2027 have moved up roughly 40bp over the past two months, but adjustments reflecting the synchronization of growth and inflation dynamics are evolving more slowly (Figure 1). This week we saw hikes from Norges Bank and SARB, and we expect a hike from the RBA next week. We also changed views this week to anticipate a hike from the Bank of Thailand. Markets expect larger and more synchronized hikes than our forecasts. But what is most notable about recent market moves is their extension of higher policy rates well beyond the coming year. Indeed, a proxy for DM terminal rates (one-year yields, three years ahead) has moved up roughly 50bp over the past month (Figure 2). While stressing upfront that we do not forecast political outcomes nor attach probabilities, we see at least three political scenarios going forward. First, the government coalition could remain in place under Chancellor Merz. In recent days, the CDU/CSU parliamentary group and CDU regional prime ministers have expressed their support for the chancellor. Second, notwithstanding the recent expressions of support, Chancellor Merz could be replaced with another person from the CDU/CSU. This would work via a constructive vote of no confidence (Article 67 of the constitution), implying that parliament on its own initiative (without new elections) would elect a new chancellor. If that were to happen, it would imply that the Social Democrats and the CDU/CSU would need to agree on a new chancellor. Third, Chancellor Merz could trigger a vote of confidence (Article 68 of the constitution), which could be followed by new national elections if he were to lose the vote. This is how the "traffic-light" coalition of Chancellor Scholz collapsed. Chancellor Merz dismissed this scenario in his speech after the last regional election. And given the strength of the AfD in the current polls, this would likely lead to a significant loss in votes for the current government parties - which arguably makes this third scenario unlikely. ...and implications for domestic economic policy... records.text: 24 September 2026 Focus Germany Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG A look at the MoF's September 2026 Monthly Report In this update, we take a look at the September 2026 Monthly Report from the Federal Ministry of Finance (MoF), which contains the financial statistics data on federal budget developments for the first eight months of the year. The analysis builds on our previous work regarding Germany's fiscal policy shift (see also here and here). It considers the latest dynamics of a) the federal government's core budget as well as b) the two major off-budgetary funds SV BW (Federal Armed Forces Fund) and SV IK (Infrastructure & Climate Neutrality Fund) for which the government provides monthly credit stock/flow data.1 The MoF's August 2026 budget print Monthly budgetary developments in a nutshell As Figure 1 illustrates, the total federal financing deficit (comprising the core budget, SV BW, and SV IK) widened to EUR 167 bn in August on a 12-month smoothed basis (approx. 3.6% of 2026F GDP; full-year target: EUR 182 bn or 4%), up from about EUR 159 bn in July. Consequently, the total deficit, based on the trailing twelve-month sum, has expanded by about EUR 107 bn since the 2025 federal budget effectively took effect in October last year. records.text: Alexandre Stott +33(1)4212-1108 | alexandre.stott@gs.com Goldman Sachs Bank Europe SE - Paris Branch European Daily: France—An Increasingly Challenging Debt Trajectory 24 September 2026 | 6:05PM CEST The trajectory of France’s public debt is looking increasingly challenging, given n the lack of progress in reducing the deficit and the recent increase in borrowing costs. We now estimate that France will eventually need to run a 1% primary surplus to stabilise its public debt-to-GDP ratio, a feat rarely achieved in recent history. As a result, we are revising our forecast for public debt to reach 125% of GDP by the start of the next decade (vs. 123% before). The longer public debt remains high and increasing, the more likely it is France n will face durably higher borrowing costs. This could lead to self-reinforcing pressures where higher debt entails higher rates, lower growth, and ultimately, even higher debt. At the same time, we have noticed some more encouraging signs in the French n fiscal debate. Recent polls suggest that economic and fiscal issues have risen to the top of voters’ concerns, with a large majority in favour of reducing public debt, the deficit and spending. Moreover, both Marine Le Pen and Edouard Philippe—whom polls see as the favourites to become President—have started making the case for reforming France’s fiscal framework. If the actual funds rate in one year is above the "Wicksellian" neutral rate, then inflation should be lower the following period. That would imply that the FOMC participants are trying to push inflation below 2.0% in 2030. Another interpretation is that the FOMC participants have no actual estimate of such a rate any longer, and instead are guessing what kind of nominal rate might be required to get inflation to 2.0%. Voila...at the time of the meeting the resounding answer to the guess was..."at least as high as the funds rate is now." The four-year ahead assumption for the appropriate funds rate is also 0.4 pp above the longer-run rate. Presumably at the end of 2029, we might be getting close to the longer- run. Yet the participants themselves seem unconvinced of the concept, its usefulness, or any ability to estimate the neutral rate of interest. Keynes would smile. One observer we spoke to looked at the range of longer-run dots, with the modal value at 3.0%, median at 3.2%, and an average of 3.4%, and said the FOMC's assessment was "clear as mud." That perception may have been enhanced by the Chairman and one other participant not supplying a dot. Our guess would be, if any changes are coming to the SEP , the longer run funds rate assumption is dropped. Across the G10 real retail sales growth remains positive in nine of the 10, with Norway the exception. However, this is likely only a matter of timing. As Figure 3 illustrates, spending tends to lag changes in real incomes by around six months. US real hourly earnings turned negative in April and have remained there ever since. The impact of this on ex-fuel spending is likely to become clear in the remaining months of 2026. However, we already see consumers shifting spending priorities. Over the last three months real consumer expenditures in the US have risen by 0.8% or, US$136bn. However, of that, spending on healthcare, housing/utilities and insurance account for 64% of the change. Real spending on gas (less journeys being taken) and recreation goods (discretionary spending) both fell in the last quarter. In the latest month (July) spending declined in six of the sixteen broad PCE categories. All six were goods sectors, including clothing, recreation goods and cars and parts (as well as gas). records.text: ab 24 September 2026 Global Research European Equity Strategy Bond yield effects in European equities Rising yields are a headwind to valuations but not an equal one across the market The US 10-year has moved from 3.94% at the end of February to 5.00% last week, with the real yield up from 1.68% to 2.67%. Equities have absorbed the level better than the velocity. Since 1 March, weeks in which the 10-year rose have averaged just 42% of MSCI Europe index weight rising, against 64% in weeks the yield fell - a 22pp gap and the widest in our sample. Controlling for the index return itself, every additional 10bp on the 10-year costs roughly 1pp of index weight participating. The market is not falling on higher yields so much as narrowing under them. It is the combination of level and speed that breaks breadth, not the level alone At a 10-year below 3%, even a greater-than-20bp weekly move left 57% of the index higher - rising yields were read as growth. In the 4.0–4.5% band, breadth falls from 61% on down-yield weeks to 30% when yields jump more than 20bp. Above 4.5% the level in isolation is benign; it is the sharp weekly increase that does the damage: as the discount rate rises, the growth hurdle required to hold investor attention rises with it, and fewer companies clear it. Each incremental move demands more powerful earnings momentum to offset what is being priced into valuation. While a repo-led approach is possible in theory, we view a near-term transition as unlikely: reserves remain comfortably ample, RMPs have been effective, and a repo- led framework would require additional operational and market-structure decisions to be worked through. That said, in the absence of clarity on the balance sheet task force’s longer-run direction, a more repo-reliant approach could be viewed as one of the implementation options that supports a smaller balance sheet at the margin—by supplying marginal reserves through market-based liquidity operations that distrib- ute liquidity more broadly and potentially reduce banks’ precautionary reserve buf- fers. Even so, if this were to be implemented, we would view this as a complementary rather than the primary lever for balance sheet reduction; a more durable downsizing would likely require broader changes that structurally reduce reserve demand, including potential adjustments to liquidity regulations that would shift the reserve demand curve inward. If the AI race is genuinely a “winner takes most” set-up and this ultimately leads to overinvestment, a subsequent slowdown in capex could result in lower rates. The theory: overinvestment in “winner takes most” set-ups Consider two firms that must decide how much to invest in a new technology to win a prize. Investment affects who wins the prize rather than the size of the prize itself. For each firm, the probability of winning depends on the size of its investment relative to that of its competitor. Finally, assume that the technology leads to a “winner takes most” environment. In that context, a small investment advantage translates into a disproportionately large increase in the probability of winning the prize. For instance, a firm investing 75% of total industry investment has a probability of winning that exceeds 75%. As shown in the Appendix, this simple framework can generate overinvestment relative to the level that would maximise the firms’ combined profits. The intuition for this result is as follows. Each firm invests not only because of the prize, but also becaus e investment improves its relative position. records.text: Agency MBS Recent uptick in interest rate volatility provides an enticing entry point for owning agency MBS On September 17th, we upgraded our MBS call to a modest overweight after current coupon Treasury OAS widened to 36bp following the hawkish September FOMC meeting, roughly 10bp over its long-term average. As long-end yields stabilized in subsequent sessions, MBS basis outperformed and current coupon OAS dropped to as tight as 29.5bp. However, the outperformance proved short-lived as interest rate volatility re-emerged this week. Although spreads held-up relatively well on Wednesday despite the 15bp sell-off in 10-year Treasuries, investors remained in a state of unease. The renewed rate volatility eventually flowed through to the mortgage market, diving spreads sharply wider on Thursday. MBS spreads have now essentially round-tripped and are back at their post-FOMC wides. In our view, the current dislocation in MBS, driven by the sharp rise in Treasury yields to multi-year highs, presents an attractive investment opportunity. We maintain a modest overweight on the MBS basis while retaining some dry powder to capitalize on further MBS underperformance and/or an additional selloff in Treasuries. records.text: put to the following Q1s, which we’ll be watching out for. Inflation remains the great unknown for monetary policy. The Bank of England, at its most recent policy decision, raised its inflation projections. Part of this was compensating for what looked like an underestimation at their last forecast round, but part reflects an underlying reality that the energy shock has been more sustained than most expected it to be. There is now a credible chance that inflation will sit above 4% in Q1 2027. However, this presents something of a conundrum for policy makers. For while inflation is more problematic, we still see limited evidence of second-round effects which has kept questions over whether to pre-emptively hike before they materialise (as the hawks would argue) or hold steady on the assumption that they won’t appear. This, in turn, requires a judgement that extends from the economics to the geopolitical. It remains true that a ‘swift’ resolution to Straits of Hormuz can materially alter the path of inflation, especially should energy contracts moderate before the Q1 2027 energy price guarantee is announced in November. As leases expire, today’s market rents influence the terms offered to new and renewing tenants. But that signal passes into CPI shelter only gradually because leases reset infrequently, land- lords tend to smooth renewal increases, and the BLS mea- sures rent changes over six-month intervals. That lag was evident during the recent inflation cycle. New- lease rents accelerated before CPI shelter took off and turned down well before the subsequent shelter disinflation. We track this signal using the Zillow Observed Rent Index (ZORI), which measures asking rents across single and multi- family properties. records.text: M Global Idea 2 Tracing Diesel Flows See views from our Commodity Strategists here: The Oil Manual: A US Diesel Export Ban...What If? (23 Sep 2026) The Trade Almanac This update leverages the database we built on global trade — the Trade Almanac — to run supply chain analysis on global trade shocks. These pressures are tied to the work we began over a year ago with Supply Chain Strain. In our client-facing database, users can explore monthly data on US trade (and tariffs) across products and economies, monthly exports by China and the EU, and map global trade flows across sectors, products, and geographies over time. The oil shock has moved downstream from crude availability into refining and diesel. Higher diesel prices will have knock on effects that are different to crude; discussions of a prospective US restriction on diesel exports add impetus to understanding diesel flows. Market focus often centers on oil prices, but the current juncture shows spreads and downstream capacity driving added complexity. With oil hovering near ~$100 for a couple weeks, the level is lower than in the first phase of the oil shock, but materially wider spreads have shifted focus downstream, particularly diesel. First, as widely expected, every Asian currency suffers from a stronger USD, but the magnitude varies substantially. KRW stands out as the most USD-sensitive currency, reflecting its high-beta nature and strong dependence on exporter and capital flows (Figure 2). The next tier comprises THB, MYR and IDR, while TWD, INR and PHP appear considerably less exposed. The latter group is driven primarily by equity flows, whereas both equity and bond flows play a larger role elsewhere in the region. As a result, higher US yields alongside a stronger USD could exert disproportionate pressure on THB, MYR and IDR. Second, both CNH and JPY matter positively for Asia FX, but China matters far more. While appreciation in both currencies tends to support regional FX, the relationship has been decisively skewed towards CNH over the past three years. Put differently, Asia has become more sensitive to developments in China than to those in Japan (Figure 3). Third, KRW is the clearest beneficiary of stronger CNH and JPY. If the AI race is genuinely a “winner takes most” set-up and this ultimately leads to overinvestment, a subsequent slowdown in capex could result in lower rates. The theory: overinvestment in “winner takes most” set-ups Consider two firms that must decide how much to invest in a new technology to win a prize. Investment affects who wins the prize rather than the size of the prize itself. For each firm, the probability of winning depends on the size of its investment relative to that of its competitor. Finally, assume that the technology leads to a “winner takes most” environment. In that context, a small investment advantage translates into a disproportionately large increase in the probability of winning the prize. For instance, a firm investing 75% of total industry investment has a probability of winning that exceeds 75%. As shown in the Appendix, this simple framework can generate overinvestment relative to the level that would maximise the firms’ combined profits. The intuition for this result is as follows. Each firm invests not only because of the prize, but also becaus e investment improves its relative position. FAQs We are frequently asked what level of energy prices would trigger a recession or when we should expect growth resilience to fade. A short lived spike might still be less difficult than a very long plateau at current prices, we think. So far, energy prices have been on a rollercoaster, with episodes of relief on hopes of a peace deal. If prices remain at current levels well beyond the winter, they may take their toll on sentiment and growth. That would put us closer to the ECB’s adverse scenario, and raise risks of a fourth hike (not more), but with weaker growth, we think. Outside Germany, public finances remain vulnerable to potential shocks, limiting governments' ability to maintain an accommodative fiscal stance. The euro area fiscal stance remains accommodative. We estimate the fiscal impulse, a measure of the extent to which government policies support aggregate demand, at around 0.3-0.4pp of GDP this year (Figure 16). However, this fiscal easing is concentrated in Germany (Figure 16). Most other euro area economies have either limited fiscal space or none at all. France and Italy, the second- and third-largest economies in the currency union, remain under the Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP) and therefore need to continue consolidating their public finances. Germany's role is particularly important given that it is both the largest economy in the euro area and the main trading partner of several member states, including France and Italy. We continue to believe that that the SNB is in a prolonged holding period and that the adjustment in rates has some way to go. With the current environment remaining conducive for vol-adjusted carry trade and more symmetry around the JPY, the CHF stands out as the G10 funder of choice. Higher USD/CHF remains the natural conduit, despite some noise from quarter-end rebalancing flows. For those looking to hedge some of their underlying bearishness towards the CHF, lower EUR/CHF makes sense to us, with the skew increasingly moving towards CHF calls. We interpret this as investors hedging against CHF appreciation driven by localized European political and budgetary risks.

Since monetary policy is not well-equipped to deal with supply shocks, this scenario assumes the committee accepts relatively slow convergence to the 2% target. A second scenario is a more hawkish Fed that desires a much quicker return to 2%. Instead of leaning against second round effects from higher energy prices, the Fed reacts to the direct effects of higher energy prices on inflation. Advocates of this view point to Chair Warsh's comments in the press conference which strongly linked geopolitics, inflation, and a need for restriction. Since the Fed cannot control oil prices, it would need to constrain domestic demand more forcefully to achieve faster convergence. In our view, the most likely transmission mechanism for monetary policy in this scenario would come through lower asset prices and softer consumption. This would likely require the Fed to take the target range for the federal funds rate back toward 2023 highs as the thinking goes, or about 150bp in total rate hikes.

That is, if a decent share of credit score gaming can be done between Fannie and Freddie score, then there would be less need to pull the others. Still, for some borrowers there could be a statistical advantage to pulling more scores until the LLPA cards broke their way. We can imagine scenarios where three out of four scores say that a borrower deserves a high LLPA, but the fourth generates a significant LLPA sav- ings. That seems a bit silly in the context of risk based pricing, but is unavoidable under the current grid optimization system. Of course, since the GSEs have demonstrated superior score models, an alternative would be to move towards a utility system where there's just one pull—a unified GSE score. That would produce the largest reduction in score spending, and the cleanest risk analytics. The Fannie and Freddie scores would likely need to be merged in some way in order to avoid originators diverting volumes to one GSE or the other in another form of score gaming. But while this approach might be the simplest and guarantee the largest reductions in borrower score spending, it also would hamper score competition going forward, and undoubtedly generate a lot of score industry pushback. THEME OF THE WEEK: CAN EM STILL RALLY? The chart highlights the three key external drivers of EM asset performance: the US dollar, US real yields, and oil prices. A weaker dollar has historically been the strongest tailwind, supporting EM FX, equities, and local bonds, and helps explain the resilience of EM assets year-to-date. In contrast, higher US real yields have typically weighed on EM performance, with local currency sovereign bonds the most vulnerable given tighter financial conditions and higher risk premium. Meanwhile, rising oil prices produce a more differentiated outcome. EM bonds generally struggle as rising energy costs feed through to inflation, prompting more hawkish central bank responses and wider local bond yields, while EM FX and equities tend to remain resilient given their positive exposure to commodity cycles. records.text: ons. The eventual unwinding of those positions makes equity selloffs more discontinuous and produces fatter return tails. Once bonds cease to behave as a reliable safe haven, risk is distributed more evenly across asset classes rather than concentrated in equities alone. Rates tails, on the other hand, fatten when bonds stop hedging. Rates kurtosis peaks in the most negative-correlation quintiles, perhaps owing to inflation and policy surprises that tend to cause equity/rates correlations to turn negative in the first place. Notably, the distribution of rates volatility tells a more consistent story across regimes. Equity vol remains more fat-tailed than rates vol in every correlation regime, including the most negative. Despite the nuances in returns distribution, the volatility process itself stays structurally more extreme for equities - one of the key supports for a richer equity vol premium that the regime shift leaves untouched. Verdict: On fat tails alone, a persistent negative-correlation regime marginally favours a richer rates volatility premium. But the support primarily comes from fatter tails in rate moves, not in rates volatility, which makes it a narrower foundation than it first appears. 23 September 2026 5 Barclays | Derivatives Research

Another is the health of private sector balance sheets, including banks. The credit cycle is not stretched. The new model incorporates VantageScore 4.0 by converting disclosed scores into estimated Classic FICO equivalents and combining the resulting averages and distributions with those of collateral reporting Classic FICO. For prior YB model versions, VS4 scores are ignored and cohort-average Classic FICO scores are used in cases when only VS4 scores were available. The conversion assumes a minimum 20-point downward adjustment, increasing to approximately 50 points for VS4 scores well above 800, with variations by loan purpose and occupancy type. The 20-point adjustment for lower-to-mid-range scores aligns with the shift in the GSE LLPA grids, while larger adjustments at higher scores often leave borrowers within the 780+ LLPA category. This move comes after the market has comfortably digested roughly $500bn of private-sector bill supply over July and August, which we attribute in large part to declining leveraged borrowing demand. As we show in today’s chart, repo pricing this year has been driven by private bill supply, money market fund AUMs, and repo volumes. Current repo pricing appears consistent with this framework. Using this model, we conduct a scenario analysis, incorporating our forecast of bill supply alongside a range of what we see as reasonable assumptions for money market inflows and leverage demand. As we’ve noted previously, MMF asset growth this year has been driven primarily by passive income accrual rather than meaningful inflows from the banking system. We don’t anticipate this changing as banks continue to look to compete for deposits to support loan growth. That said, we are entering into a seasonally stronger period of inflows, a trend that could be reinforced by the recent rate hike. records.text: ab 24 September 2026 Global Research Global Strategy The Fed's balance sheet debate We expect evolution, not regime change. The Fed is likely to retain its ample-reserves framework while exploring ways to reduce reserve demand and shrink its market footprint over time. A rapid return to QT remains unlikely. The more plausible path is to slow or halt reserve management purchases when conditions permit, allowing growth in currency and other non-reserve liabilities gradually to reduce reserves relative to GDP and banking assets. A more repo-led system is possible, but not our base case. Greater reliance on standing facilities could support a smaller securities portfolio, provided market participants are willing and able to use those facilities before funding stress becomes acute. Liquidity regulation could determine how small the balance sheet can become. Recognizing reliable discount-window capacity in the LCR or internal liquidity stress tests could lower reserve demand, but some hurdles remain. The Fed is likely to pursue a more aggressive shortening of SOMA duration. A shift toward shorter reinvestments could reduce the duration held by the Fed, with the effect on yields and swap spreads ultimately depending on Treasury’s issuance response. Balance-sheet task force likely to recommend evolution rather than revolution Chair Warsh’s balance sheet task force is examining the costs, benefits, and institutional implications of the Federal Reserve’s current balance sheet regime. records.text: 25 September 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 11 US CPI - 1y back to fair Markus Heider | Macro Strategist | +44-20-754-52167 Note: This note was originally published on 24 September 2026. Front-end US inflation has recently underperformed energy and, relative to our CPI forecasts, no longer appears to price significant upside risk. Against that backdrop and with energy price volatility re -emerging we take profit on our oil- hedged short 1y (April/May-27) CPI trade. The main rationale for initiating the trade in July was an unusually wide gap between 1y valuations and our CPI forecasts. That gap has since returned to more normal levels (Figure), as April/May -27 fixings have declined even as oil prices have risen further. From here, the risks appear more balanced. Economic activity remains robust, underlying inflation is sticky, pipeline price pressures are elevated, and new rent inflation appears to be picking up from low levels. records.text: The Speculative Grade Beat 24 September 2026 Citi Research 2 High yield primary market this week saw the largest issuance in HY history priced and completed, as SoftBank brought $10bn of new bonds tied to its AI-related capital commitments to market. The prior record high yield bond deal ($8.5bn) came in 2015 from healthcare and the previous largest AI-related deal was a $5.7bn from a data center issuer in April. With the SoftBank deal now priced, AI-related issuance in 3Q'26, together with three other $8bn worth of data center offerings, represents 31% of total quarterly HY issuance to date. Even so, as we discuss later, HY's overall exposure to AI remains a low single digit of the index (currently ~ 3.5% of the Bloomberg High Yield Index) and should be able to absorb more supply based on the IG credit market’s concentration. In addition, this marks the first time HY issuance has carried meaningful exposure to a frontier AI lab. T o be clear, bondholders do not have a direct or ring-fenced claim on OpenAI. Instead, they hold general unsecured obligations of SoftBank, the diversified holding company. That said, much of SoftBank's balance sheet, including Arm and its Vision Fund portfolio, is itself a leveraged bet on the AI cycle, given Arm's growing exposure to AI data-center chip architecture and Vision Fund's shift toward AI-focused startups, so the distinction may matter less in practice than it does on paper. More precisely, that coefficient maps the change in the ratio of net worth to disposable personal income into a change in the ratio of consumption to income. The $21tr increase in net worth over the last year raised the ratio of net worth to DPI by about 0.6, implying an increase in the consumption/DPI ratio of 3.5% * 0.6 = 0.021, and an equivalent 2.1%-pt drop in the savings rate. The actual savings rate has fallen 2.2% in the four quarters to 2Q26, almost the same amount. Per Fig- ure 1, the net worth/DPI ratio has also risen materially since the pre-COVID period, and the same calculation would imply a drop in the saving rate of 4.4% since the end of 2019, simi- lar to the realized drop of 4.0%. That MPC would imply a drop in the saving rate of 1.5% over the last year and 3.3% since 2019. This is despite its typical beta to broad Dollar performance, which would have argued for relative MXN resilience and likely reflects energy supply concerns stemming from the potential US diesel export ban. Mexico screens as relatively vulnerable to this ban if enacted (see FX risks from a potential US ban on diesel exports bullet), which contrasts with its otherwise more neutral terms-of-trade beta to energy prices year-to-date. Ahead of this shock, MXN implied volatility was near historical lows (Exhibit 3) and, more broadly, the Peso screens as overvalued relative to longer-run valuations. We think this starting point—where there is no premium for any negative news—largely helps explain the magnitude of the FX reaction this week. Tactically, the export ban (and whether Mexico could secure an exemption) remains the main risk to this view, and we think the bar for USD/MXN volatility to normalise higher is low. We continue to expect fine-tuning rather than a policy pivot. That said, some measures under discussion—notably mortgage subsidies—would be unusual in that they have not previously been rolled out on a nationwide basis. Even if their direct macro impact is modest, the novelty of such measures could generate a more visible improvement in market sentiment. Potential nationwide mortgage subsidies New homes only, with a modest fiscal footprint. A potential mortgage-subsidy program could run for 2-3 years, covering certain new-home purchases outside tier-1 cities and offering an effective subsidy of around 80-100bp of mortgage principal, subject to per- household caps. On our rough estimates, this could imply a fiscal cost of around RMB30bn per year, with central government subsidies supplemented by local-government top-ups. We think the measure would be aimed at supporting new-home sales and accelerating inventory destocking, rather than providing broad relief to the existing stock of mortgage borrowers. That is not something that pops out of the models of r-star. It’s difficult at the moment to think there is one single rate to address the dual mandate in any form of traditional model. The current rate looks restrictive for most of the US economy, which is not driving inflation. In contrast, the smaller share of GDP , but the share driving the growth, seems unrestrained. Part of this is Blanchard's point that one rate is not going to equilibrate two goals, stabilizing output and inflation. A second point is the current indeterminateness. If there is some range over which the policy rate continues to depress most of the economy, but within a reasonable range may not incrementally push back against AI investment and the related equity market wealth, then what is the unique neutral rate? Combine that problem, with the observation that the neutral rate may be changing period by period, perhaps as we flip from fiscal stimulus to fiscal drag, or over the horizon over which inflation returns to target. Combine both of those points with the observation that the economy is being shocked all the time by other shocks, and for some no interest rate gap prevents that shock's impact on inflation. records.text: Ben Luk, Macro Strategy Team* 25 September 2026 *Special thanks to Tony Tang for his substantial contributions to the research, analysis, and development of this report 1 Insights Information Classification: General Asia FX NOT Just a Dollar Story , Find Your RV Trade USD strength remains the dominant headwind for Asia FX. Rising US yields and higher oil prices only reinforce the challenge. Yet focusing solely on the dollar risks missing two increasingly important regional forces: China and Japan. This is particularly relevant across EM Asia given the sharp divergence between USD/CNH and USD/JPY over the past year (Figure 1). In this note, we attempt to isolate the independent sensitivity of Asian currencies to the USD, CNH and JPY by stripping out the overlapping influence of each factor. Using data since January 2023, we employ a three-step framework to decompose Asian FX returns into DXY ex-JPY, CNH and JPY factors. We first extract the components of CNH and JPY daily movements that are independent of broad dollar dynamics by regressing both currencies against DXY ex-JPY and retaining the residuals. We then estimate the standalone sensitivity of each Asian currency to DXY, CNH and JPY through a combination of residualized returns and partial correlations, controlling for the overlap among the three factors. Spot/vol beta: inflation dulls equity vol's response to selloffs Spot/vol correlation determines how badly short vol hurts. When volatility rises precisely as the underlying falls, option sellers face simultaneous losses from delta, gamma and vega, compounding the damage at the portfolio level. Equity spot/vol beta weakens as bonds stop hedging. Consistent with the earlier observation that equity return tails become materially thinner in negative-correlation regimes, equity spot/vol beta also weakens substantially as equity/rates correlation turns negative. While the 2022 grind-lower episode is a perfect example of this, we see this broadly across periods of negative correlations historically. Rates volatility remains inherently two-sided. While rates volatility reacts somewhat more strongly to rising yields in positive-correlation regimes, the overall spot/vol relationship remains small throughout the sample. The dominant effect is therefore not rates volatility becoming more asymmetric, but equity volatility becoming less so. Verdict: All else equal, negative equity/ rates correlation tends to dampen the volatility response and therefore weakens one of the supports for equity VRP richn

records.text: US Rates Strategy 24 September 2026 Citi Research 2 T oday’s 7y auction finds itself in the crosshairs of a hawkish Fed backdrop, with this week’s Fed speakers steadfastly hawkish, combined with the Treasury market challenging Bessent’s long-end “put” . More importantly, it follows one of the worst 5y auctions in recent memory yesterday, where we saw the second largest tail of 3.1bp over the past fifteen years (Figure 1). This follows the small 2y tail this past Tuesday. Historically, the weakest 7y auctions tend to occur after a poor 2y and 5y auction. The 7y auction tends to tail on average by 0.17bp (unconditioned back to 2009) but when the 2y and 5y note tail, the average 7y tail increases to 0.5bp. While the sample size is small, large 5y tails (3bp+) have been a predictor for a weak to neutral 7y auction (Figure 2). More specifically, the next 7y auction is skewed towards the tail side after a tailed 2y and 5y auction (Figure 3). It is also worth highlighting that the worst 7y auctions tend to occur after a 2y and 5y note tailing. In February, March, and April of this year, when the 2y and 5y both tailed, the 7y either stopped on the screws or tailed slightly. Figure 1. records.text: Interestingly, we did not encounter much disagreement with our view that ECB rates could peak at 2.75% in December. The current market pricing of almost four more rate hikes was widely seen as unrealistic. The ECB’s balance sheet and framework review often came up in the conversations. Aside from the questions on the timing of the operational framework review (which we think will still take place this fall) and whether the ECB would stop the QT in light of the recent bond yields increase (which we think is unlikely, at least for now), the primary focus was on the remuneration of excess liquidity. We argued (here) that the ECB is better served not addressing the increase in its interest rate expenditure through either increasing the MRR to 2% or the introduction of tiering. We therefore think we will not see any policy change on that front. Still, if the ECB were to act, we see an increase in MRRs as the more likely outcome. All investors we spoke to agreed with us. Tiering is widely seen as too complex and risky.

records.text: y in USD/JPY on top of the Yen’s valuation signal, strengthening its attractiveness as a portfolio hedge. The risk of additional interventions, particularly in the context of the US and Japan’s reported joint concern about the Yen’s undervaluation, should also keep the upside in USD/JPY more limited. Together, these developments raise the attractiveness of being long JPY, especially to protect against an onset of recession fears, and should make valuation a more meaningful driver of performance. As a result, we revised down our USD/JPY forecasts from 162, 163, 165 (in 3, 6, 12 months) to 158, 155, 150. The path reflects our cautious tactical bias but the stronger valuation anchor over the long-term. We see risks in both directions around the baseline. USD/JPY could defy our expectations and continue to rise if US growth runs ahead of the rest of the world, leading the Fed to pursue a bigger hiking cycle while BoJ hikes fall short of current pricing, and no shift in flows actually occurs. However, USD/JPY could fall even more than we expect if the data show signs of portfolio reallocation, the BoJ shifts to an even faster pace of hikes while the Fed disappoints current pricing, and the growth outlook deteriorates. Usually Wednesday’s third release for Q2 GDP (+1.5% vs. +2.1%) would not be particularly noteworthy. However, these data will incorporate the BEA’s annual benchmark revisions , which could recontextualize our views on recent growth trends going back to 2021. Assuming there are no major revisions, market participants will likely focus more on the August data on personal income (+0.5% vs. +0.4%) and consumption (+0.6% vs. +0.2%), released concurrently with the GDP report. The former should get a boost from the aforementioned strength in the August jobs report while the latter will likely also pick up given the 1.4% increase in August retail control. records.text: The abrupt halt to the relatively stable volatility backdrop that characterized most of the move higher in yields signaled a less fundamental quality to this week’s selloff. While the market likely needs a catalyst to reinvigorate duration risk appetite, US valuation and positioning measures are consistent with a building asymmetry towards lower yields. The initial window following the first Fed hike is typically consistent with front-end versus belly flattening. And although Fed pricing is stretched versus survey-based expectations, higher vol and hedge value considerations explain part of this gap, with the asymmetry towards hikes likely a near-term speed limit on front-end rallies. In a similar vein, we think that the recent underperformance of 5s on the European curve is overdone given the ECB’s comparatively low inflation tolerance. The idiosyncratic cheapening of OATs is not necessarily a harbinger of outperformance, but the extremity of the move combined with the distance to the elections tilt risks towards consolidation in the near-term. We expect the UK front-end to continue to trade largely as a function of energy prices, with upside likely to bring further flattening. Further out, uncertainty ahead of the Autumn Budget will likely limit scope for additional compression in Gilt risk premium until the fiscal picture becomes clearer. records.text: M Idea 6 Mark-to-market forecast revision We mark our USD/CNY forecast stronger, to 6.65 by end-2026 and 6.60 by end-2027, while still expecting modest trade-weighted RMB appreciation. records.text: o area credit impulse turned visibly positive despite the uncertainty stemming from the Iran shock. A key question is whether this virtuous credit cycle can continue. We see a couple of factors suggesting the strength may prove temporary. n The lag between changes in market rates and borrowing trends. Typically, there is short lag of around a month between changes in market rates and the interest rate charged on new bank loans. And it then takes some time for the higher cost of borrowing to drag on lending activity. This lag between the rise in rates and a slowing credit impulse was clearly visible in 2022, with a few factors potentially extending the delay (the post-Covid activity rebound, liquidity demand amid the energy shock and higher inflation expectations limiting the rise in real rates). So while credit flows have held up well, if the more recent rise in market rates persists, we should expect more of a drag on downstream credit conditions in the coming months. Indeed, the August data this week showed a degree of slowing. And while realised credit dynamics have outperformed the signal from the Bank Lending Survey of late, we will be watching whether the next BLS on October 27 shows signs of higher rates weighing on loan demand. records.text: Fiscal policy seems unlikely to shift the policy rate outlook Our latest thematic work on the upcoming US election ( US Midterms: Priced for Gridlock) argues that the principal macroeconomic significance of the midterms lies in fiscal policy rather than the election outcome itself. Divided government remains the clear base case and would likely leave the broad policy backdrop largely unchanged. Even so, we have revised up our medium-term deficit projections, reflecting lower tariff revenue, higher interest costs, and a less-favorable fiscal starting point than previously assumed. Under our baseline, the deficit edges up to roughly $2.1trn (6.2% of GDP) in FY2027 despite stronger tariff revenue, and remains on a gradually rising trajectory thereafter as growing interest costs increasingly dominate an otherwise flat path for discretionary spending. While divided government would likely constrain additional fiscal expansion, the risks around our baseline point toward less discipline rather than more. A Republican sweep would preserve the possibility of further fiscal stimulus, larger deficits, stronger growth, and higher interest rates. Regardless of the electoral outcome, fiscal policy appears unlikely to become materially restrictive for the foreseeable future, reinforcing our view that neutral interest rates and long- run financing needs will play an increasingly important role in shaping both Treasury yields and the broader macroeconomic outlook. 25 September 2026 16 Barclay

BOND WATCH Thailand Most Vulnerable, China Most Resilient Figure 6 Asia’s Dependency on Oil and Natural Gas Asia is one of the world's most energy -import dependent regions. However, vulnerability to oil prices is determined not only by import dependence but also by the composition of energy supply. Thailand appear s the most exposed economies in the region, with 80% of its energy consumption derived from oil and natural gas, leaving them particularly sensitive to elevated energy prices since the onset of the Middle East conflict. Taiwan, Korea, and Japan also rely heavily on imported hydrocarbons, but their energy mix is more diversified through greater use of nuclear power and renewables. Combined with their large current account surpluses, this helps cushion the impact of higher oil imports. In contrast, China and India appear relatively more insulated as coal remains the d ominant source of power generation, which reduces their oil sensitivity, but at the expense of longer-term environmental challenges. Conversely, if energy prices returned to pre-conflict levels, it would allow about half a percentage point increase in the savings rate without any off- setting reduction in other spending. One final point on the savings rate decline this year is around the BEA’s treatment of the OBBBA tax cuts. The BEA spreads the tax cut evenly across the year, but actual cash flows to households are more concentrated around the tax fil- ing season in March and April. Since households are likely to bunch their related spending around the time of the cash flows, this lowers the savings rate into the middle part of the year, and raises it later in the year. The accounting treatment should have contributed no more than a few tenths of a per- cent to the decline in the saving rate this year. But the yields are rising for the right reason This is not a term-premium accident or an inflation scare. Yields are rising because growth is strengthening and, more importantly, broadening. A genuine industrial capacity expansion cycle is emerging simultaneously across defence, AI equipment manufacturing, infrastructure and power - the first synchronised capex cycle of this type in a generation. That matters for rates because industrial activity carries a materially higher velocity of money than services. A euro committed to a fabrication plant, a grid upgrade or an ordnance line turns over through a supply chain in a way that a euro of services consumption does not. Rising velocity on a stable monetary base is a regime change we have not had to price in thirty years If velocity rises while the monetary base is stable or growing, nominal GDP accelerates and policy that looked neutral becomes loose. The arithmetic then requires more hikes, not fewer - and those hikes are explicitly designed to slow activity by restraining money growth, velocity, or both. Markets have spent three decades in the opposite regime and are not well practised at pricing this one. Mortgage rates are now about 7%, while risk assets have largely powered through the increase in yields thus far. With the market now pricing a nearly two-thirds chance for the FOMC to hike again in October, we are sensitive to what might get the Fed to move at the next meeting. Given that Chair Warsh and some other Fed speakers have argued the labor market is broadly in balance, it likely would take more than one hot jobs report — and specifically signs of an upward trend in wages — to convince the Committee that the labor market is overheating. But a strong labor report in con- junction with strong September inflation data that point to another high-side 0.2% monthly core PCE reading (after accounting for a possible reversal in last month’s spike in cell phone service prices) might be sufficient. That said, no one on the Committee has explicitly advocated for consecutive hikes, and we think a case may be made—as in July, per War- sh’s press conference remarks—for the Committee to wait and observe how the data evolve and how markets handle the first rate hike. • Incoming growth signals continue to strengthen • Fed officials continue to sound hawkish, but haven’t made a strong case for October so far • The upcoming annual GDP revisions should raise non- labor income and the saving rate; trim core PCE • Next week: 100k payrolls, 4.1% unemployment, 3.3%

records.text: FHFA proposal would move expected defaults, we build empiri- cal default curves for jumbo and non-QM separately, using 5-point FICO buckets. We then re-score every loan with a randomly chosen single bureau, look each loan up on the empiri- cal curve and aggregate to a pool-level predicted default rate. In both jumbo and non-QM, the pool-level predicted default under single-bureau scoring is only marginally lower than the actual realized default (Figure 9P r e d i c t e d d e f a u l t u n d e r s i n g l e - b u r e a u s c o r i n g i s o n l y m a r g i n a l l y l o w e r t h a n t h e a c t u a l r e a l i z e d d e f a u l t ). Two reasons drive this. First, the three bureau scores for the same borrower are tightly correlated, so swapping the composite for a random single bureau moves each loan only a short distance along the cali- bration curve. Second, on a pool of tens of thousands of loans, the loan-level shifts are rough- ly symmetric and mostly wash out in aggregate. Pulling it all together, every single-bureau score does a modestly worse job than the median of three at identifying which loans will default. However, the lower of 2-of-3 produces better risk segmentation while also introducing price competition between the bureaus. This could serve as a path towards compromise for balancing multiple objectives.

records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 September 2026 Citi Research 36 Developed Markets Rates Strategy US Rates Last week’s FOMC was decidedly hawkish, and since the Fed’s reaction function appears to be squarely year-over-year core PCE we have revised our forecasts taking into account the risk of future rate hikes (see US Rates Weekly - Only hawks outside the window). The challenge for markets, and the Fed, will be the upcoming January and February core PCE prints which tend to have strong residual seasonality. The market is likely to continue to price hikes into December and March due to uncertainty around this seasonality, even if Q4 inflation prints look more benign. Still, we think forwards are pricing too much Fed restriction as 1y1y RYs are now at post-Covid highs even though inflation is clearly falling on most metrics. If the FOMC decides to hike at a quarterly cadence, perhaps the modal outcome, then we think it will be hard to out-hawk forwards due to inflation base effects. We updated our yield forecasts, and we now assume Fed rate hike pricing will remain until YoY core PCE starts to normalize next year. We are inclined to trade the CAD from the short side (see FX: Long GBPCAD via 3m seagull , dated 27 August) . This view is predicated on two closely related factors: the US -Canada trade tensions introduce downside risks to the Canadian economy and as this plays a large part in the Bank of Canada ’s outlook , it leaves the CAD vulnerable as a low yielder. As such, the CAD’s largest driver has been front -end rate differentials. This is well reflected in our STEERTM model, which shows that rate differentials are the most important variable in the model (Figure 1). Our sense is that higher energy prices have supported Canada’s trade balance , but the extent to which the terms of trade pass through positively to FX may be more limited (see FX: CAD support to wane , dated 19 March). Rather, the stronger mechanism for FX so far seems to be oil driving front -end yields globally which then passes through to rate differentials (Figure 2) .

We expect issuance momentum to remain largely intact in 2027, forecasting $31 billion of gross issuance in datacenter ABS and $55 billion across digital infrastructure more broadly. The risks to our datacenter ABS issuance estimate is potentially skewed to the downside if the political backlash against datacenter construction results in greater construction moratoriums/delays. Page 8 The global fiscal drift Francis Yared | Strategist | +44-20-754-54017 We argued in our 2026 outlook (1) that most of the post -GFC decline in the equilibrium rate was likely to be unwound and (2) that the US labour market was likely to bottom as the policy setting switched from tight fiscal and monetary policy in 2025 (fed funds above 4% and tariff revenues) to easy fiscal and monetary policy in 2026 (fed funds below 4% and BBB spending). Since then, the Fed has pivoted, the market is pricing equilibrium rates above 4%, and the labour market has stabilised. Our view was predicated, among other things, on structurally easier fiscal policy, not only in the US but globally . To assess how fiscal policy has evolved since our outlook, we compare DB economists’ current estimates of the global fiscal impulse for 2026 and 2027 with their forecasts from January 2026. The fiscal impulse is calculated as the annual change in deficits, and the global measure is the GDP-weighted aggregate for the US, eurozone, UK, Canada, Japan and China. Fiscal policy is now set to be slightly easier than expected in both 2026 and 2027. This reinforces our view that the repricing towards higher equilibrium rates is likely to be structural for now. However, thanks to the robustness of their balance sheets, actual flows of bank lending have remained relatively strong despite BLS credit conditions continuing to weaken (Figure 27). As mentioned earlier, the resilient flow of lending probably won’t last as interest rates rise. We may have been the first sign of weakening in the latest credit data (August). Overall, the labour market and private-sector balance sheets are still more likely to dampen shocks than amplify them. Their cushioning capacity is weaker and less broad-based than in 2022: labour-market levels remain strong despite softer momentum, while balance-sheet resilience increasingly rests on structural strength amid less favourable financing conditions and weakening household positions. These buffers should continue to support activity in the near term, but their durability will depend on whether weaker labour demand and household balance sheets stabilise before they erode the still-robust headline indicators. records.text: 25 September 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 17 Our composite indicator suggests that private-sector balance sheets are weaker than in 2022 but remain strong by historical standards. Resilience is now concentrated in the structural component, which captures the size, composition and liquidity of balance sheets. By contrast, market conditions have deteriorated as debt-servicing costs and interest rates have risen relative to 2022. There is also a growing divergence between corporates and households. Corporate balance sheets have remained robust over the past year, whereas household balance sheets have become less resilient. This suggests that the private sector's capacity to absorb another shock is increasingly dependent on continued corporate strength. Bank balance sheets Banks’ balance sheets play an important role in the decision to lend to non-financial corporates and households. Thus, robust bank balance sheets help ensure the continue flow of credit during downturns which can help businesses and households smooth through shocks. According to the ECB’s Bank Lending Survey (BLS), the net share of banks reporting that financial factors (such as the bank’s balance sheet and liquidity) affected their credit lending standards did rise in 2022, but was significantly lower than during the global financial crisis or European debt crisis ( Figure 26). Separately, on the back of a recent Wall Street Journal article that highlighted CRE CLO distressed rates, we’ve received several questions from clients about whether the distressed rate is that high. While we understand that the spirit of the article was to point out that multifamily property bargains can be found as lenders foreclose and liquidate properties, we also think the public discourse on CRE CLOs and CMBS should be more balanced. We agree that a lot of aggressive underwriting happened during the ultra-low interest rate period following the pandemic. Multifamily transaction volumes spiked during this period, and according to MSCI Real Assets, $719bn of multifamily properties traded between November 2020 and January 2023, when average monthly multifamily transaction cap rates were sub-5%. However, when pointing out the severe “distressed rate” of older vintage CRE CLOs, they are in fact pointing to the most adversely selected sample of that admittedly aggressively underwritten population, but they’ve been almost completely factored down. The most sustained negative-correlation stretch of the option era brought inflation uncertainty, policy surprises, and a bond market that stopped absorbing equity shocks. Yet equity VRP remained firmly positive, while rates VRP stayed within its typical range. 28 years of options data is really one macro regime wearing different outfits. Only three negative-correlation episodes exist in that window, one still in progress: too thin a sample to settle the question. Our cross-asset vol premia framework can help test structural drivers over 60 years of underlying returns instead. The framework scorecard: higher rates risk but equity's structural edge holds. Our framework assumes that assets with undesirable downside risks, e.g. fat tails, jump risk, illiquidity and hard-to-predict volatility, should command higher premia. On that basis, rates appear riskier in inflationary regimes than they normally do. Equities retain the characteristics that argue for higher premia relative to rates. But risk only becomes premium if the market prices it. What matters is whether and how quickly implied volatility adjusts to the new regime rather than anchoring to historical norms. Rates volatility becomes genuinely riskier when equity/rates correlation turns negative, and the resilience of rates VRP through recent fiscal and inflation stress suggests much of that adjustment is reflected in pricing. LLC Michael T Gapen Chief US Economist Michael.Gapen@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-0571 Sam D Coffin Economist Sam.Coffin@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-4630 Diego Anzoategui Economist Diego.Anzoategui@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-8573 Heather Berger Economist Heather.Berger@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-2296 Arunima Sinha Global Economist Arunima.Sinha@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-4125 Lingdi Xu Economist Lingdi.Xu@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-2957 Exhibit 1: US new home sales 200 400 600 800 1000 1200 1400 80 82 84 86 88 90 92 94 96 98 00 02 04 06 08 10 12 14 16 18 20 22 24 26 New home sales (thous, saar) Source: Census Bureau, Haver Analytics, Morgan Stanley Research For important disclosures, refer to the Disclosure Section, located at the end of this report. Key Takeaways New home sales rose 6.4% m/m in August to 684k (MSe: 660k, Consensus: 616k). July sales were revised up from 607k to 643k, no longer showing as large a decline. Sales have slowed, averaging 643k year-to-date vs 679k in '25. That said, this print gives more confidence last month's reported decline was not a new trend. We now track 3Q real residential investment at -1.4% (q/q saar) versus -1.6% before the print. The housing market is still stuck, and recent rate moves do not help. That said, our housing strategists see little room for further downside in sales. September 24, 2026

Our GDP tracking is at 3.5% but with upside risks, and while the PMIs have a loose high-frequency relationship to growth, the very strong September reading pointed to around a 5% annualized pace. That is one reason to expect a solid job gain, independent of the more employment- specific leading indicators. Still, we wouldn’t lean too much on this: last year the economy averaged 4.1% growth in the middle half of the year, yet delivered private-sector job gains of just 31k over that stretch. In addition, the natural choppi- ness in payrolls could deliver a softer month after a 162k increase in August. In terms of the leading employment indicators, the four-week average gain in ADP private payrolls has accelerated to 80k in the week ending September 5 from 40k in the August pay- roll week. Weekly jobless claims also remain in excellent shape. Initial claims declined 9k between the August and Sep- tember payroll weeks—though the four-week average was flat—and continuing claims fell 52k. records.text: 21 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 US exports of crude oil and petroleum products US production of crude oil and petroleum Million barrels per day Source: EIA, Haver, UBS The active oil drilling rig count rose 2 rigs to 452 rigs in the week ending September 18. The active oil rig count has bounced sideways in recent weeks and now matches the level of rigs in late July. Still, it has hung on to much of the gains realized this spring and summer, which suggested some response to oil supply constraints. Active oil rigs are now up 34 rigs over the year (8.1%). Active gas rigs rose 2 rigs to 134 rigs in the week ending September 18, and are up 16 rigs over the year (+13.6%). MBA mortgage rates rise above 7% MBA mortgage applications for a home purchase fell -0.8% in the week ending September 19, remaining range-bound. The contract rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage jumped 15 bps to 7.12% in the week ending September 19, its first rise above 7% since January 2025. The Freddie Mac 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rose 8 bp to 7.03% in the week ending September 25. Since the beginning of August, mortgage rates had remained in a tight range around 6.8-6.9%, but now sit around 7% amidst ongoing movement in Treasury yields. Further or sustained increases in 10- year Treasury yields could be an upside risk to mortgage rates and risk further tightening housing affordability.

records.text: US Economics Weekly25 September 2026 ab 13 measures could mean that the more interesting thing this year is changes in the composition of growth or income rather than a significant change to the overall pace of real GDP or GDI. Production accounts: composition rather than levels Monday, September 28, the monthly retail sales report is benchmarked to the annual retail trade survey. That release should indicate how goods spending may shift when the NIPA revisions land two days later. Last year, the level of real consumer spending in Q2 2025 was revised up 0.6%, or $90.3 billion. Yet over half of that gain came from services: a $56.1 billion upward revision, rather than from the goods categories most directly affected by the retail sales data. The revisions to PCE prices will also matter for the pace of real consumer spending with the contour described above implying all else constant we would probably see upward revisions to the pace of real spending in 2026, but downward revisions in 2025. The BEA’s annual trade revision narrowed the goods and services deficit by about 3.2% on average from 1999 through 2024, but the recent contour moved in opposite directions: the 2025 deficit was revised 2.2% wider, while the Q1 2026 deficit was revised 4.1% narrower.
