Norges: a 25bp hike, with a higher-for-longer rate outlook Norges Bank surprised us with a 25bp rate hike, with market expectations broadly split ahead of the meeting. At 4.5%, the policy rate is now at its highest level since the post- pandemic years. Following the hike delivered in May, Norges’s decision in September effectively reverses the rate cuts implemented in 2025. The policy rate path has been revised higher over 2027-29, reinforcing a “higher-for-longer” outlook. The projected peak in the policy rate has been raised to 4.60% (from 4.55% in June), preserving a modest tightening bias consistent with inflation risks remaining skewed to the upside. That said, we believe rates have probably peaked and do not expect further tightening from Norges Bank. However, persistently high energy prices and the prospect of a more hawkish global central bank backdrop in the short term could still create conditions for one additional hike by 1Q27. records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 25 September 2026 Weekly view “Non-linearities” are back in active vocabulary Watching bond market screens is gripping at the moment. But when we talk with our colleagues in economics or rates strategy, we are still surprised by how a seemingly similar move across economies comes with such different narratives. Central banks have repriced since the summer, dragging longer-dated yields with them. But the difference in macro rationale seems stark: In the US, economic strength across growth and inflation and a reassessment of the new Fed Chair are the main drivers. In the Euro area, we are looking at energy-price effects on headline inflation and ECB concerns over second-round effects. The real economy matters only insofar as its current “resilience” doesn’t scream stop to the central bank’s singular inflation focus. That should eventually make for very different end-points. Our US colleagues expect two more hikes this year followed by a long hold from the Fed, while still forecasting core PCE at 2.3% in 2028. We have now pencilled in one more hike from the ECB in Dec, also taking the cycle total to three. records.text: US Economics Weekly25 September 2026 ab 22 S&P Global flash PMIs improve in September The S&P Global manufacturing PMI rose 3.1 points to 57.0 in the flash estimate for September, its highest reading since April 2022. Adjusted for ISM weights, the index rose 3.0 points to 56.8. Strength was broad among the composite's subcomponents, with the strongest improvements in the output and employment indexes. The output index rose 3.6 points to 56.7, and the new orders index rose 3.0 points to 57.3. The employment index made decent gains for the third straight month, up 3.4 points to 55.8, its highest reading since February 2021. Supplier delivery times, which are inverted in the S&P PMI, breached four-year lows, indicating longer delivery times. The input price index rose back to June levels after moderating for two months. The output price index was little changed, but remained elevated above pre-conflict levels. The S&P Global services PMI, which is a business activity index, rather than a composite, rose 2.2 points to 58.7 in the flash September estimate. The employment index rose 1.9 points to 55.4, and the new business index rose further into expansion for the fifth consecutive month. Expectations for future activity also edged up. Both price indexes rose, with the input price index at its highest since October 2022, while the output price index is below the pre-conflict level. See the tables below. records.text: US Economics Weekly25 September 2026 ab 3 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Economic Comment: is there an r-star? In a response to a paper by Ben Bernanke and Mark Gertler, among other papers, Olivier Blanchard made the point that a single interest rate poses problems for central banks, particularly for an economy facing sectoral imbalances. (1) Economic shocks affect sectors in different ways, and composition effects can pose a problem when only one tool affects different sectors differently. What if the policy rate needs to do two things, like stabilize employment and inflation? Not to mention the problem that the sector the central bank's interest rate might most affect may behave quite differently from other sectors the policy rate needs to support or constrain. We were asked this week about the neutral rate, described in the question as the overnight policy rate that should "calibrate the economy to a steady state." Looking at how extremely unbalanced the US economy is right now, such a rate may not exist. Chairman Warsh mentioned the "Wicksellian rate" in the September FOMC meeting press conference. The concept of the neutral rate of interest under Knut Wicksell was the interest rate in the economy that would prevent commodity prices from increasing or decreasing. (2) That concept probably already faced the problem that the interest rate that stabilizes copper might not stabilize gold, and tea, and whale oil, all at the same time. The conflicts in Iran and Ukraine remain unresolved, and—as the Trump Administration redefines the US role in the world—strains on the global order have intensified. In tandem, oil prices have recently traded near $100/barrel, central banks are pivoting to tighter policy, and long-term yields in a range of countries have rocketed up. Given the totality of these developments, it’s hardly surprising that measures of consumer and business confidence have shown sustained weakness (Figure 1). Nevertheless, the global economy continues to durably expand. Our forecast for global growth this year is now tracking at 2.6%, slightly stronger than last month (Figure 2). Notably, we’ve marked up our projections for the euro area by 40 bp, India by 60 bp, and Canada by 30 bp. records.text: 25 September 2026 US Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 5 Application to AI The example above is an obvious oversimplification. However, it does highlight the conditions that could lead to aggregate overinvestment even if every firm behaves rationally. The key assumption is the presence of sufficiently strong “winner takes most” dynamics. This assumption is not purely theoretical. Public statements from policymakers and industry participants frequently frame AI as a race for leadership with disproportionate benefits for the market leader. For example, President Trump recently argued that “whoever wins AI, wins”. It is beyond the scope of this paper to argue whether AI is indeed a “winner takes most” set -up. There are some arguments in favour of this view, such as self - reinforcing leadership through economies of scale and data accumulation. There are also counterarguments, including the ease of switching from one model provider to another (literally a drop -down menu), the fact that most tasks do not require the most advanced frontier models, and a plausible focus on sovereign AI and data control, even at the expense of model performance. It is also beyond the scope of this paper to opine on the aggregate expected profitability of current and prospective capex plans. The main point is to highlight that, if decision -makers and investors believe AI to be a “winner takes most” set -up, then it becomes plausible to expect aggregate overinvestment. Crucially

While lower coupon TBA OAS is near YTD wides, the sharp widening in DUS 10/9.5 TBA (i.e. Fannie Mae guaranteed CMBS with a 10-year maturity term and a 9.5-year yield maintenance period) to as wide as 45bp this week (or roughly 9-10bp wider week over week) makes this agency CMBS sector more attractive vs. low coupon MBS (such as FN 2.0s-2.5s), whose OAS widened only about 3-4bp week over week. CMO floater DMs have also widened: Shifting preference to 7% cap The Fed funds market is currently pricing nearly four additional hikes over the next 12 months, on top of the September hike. Based on SOFR forwards, lower-cap CMO floater structures are at risk of becoming capped. This has contributed to a sharp widening in CMO floater DMs across cap structures (Exhibit 6) and growing concerns among market participants about potential forced selling by levered holders. In contrast, our economists expect a considerably more dovish Fed policy path than what is currently priced by the market. As a result, investors willing to express a strong view on Fed policy rates may find the recent widening in lower cap CMO floaters to be extremely attractive. Investors with a more conservative risk appetite should favor owning 7.0% cap agency CMO floaters. One way to move higher in cap without losing out on the spread, albeit at the expense of liquidity, is to own the 7.0% cap floaters off Prime RMBS deals. records.text: 24 September 2026 Focus Germany Page 6 Deutsche Bank AG government's ambitious targets, YTD spending remains sluggish, signaling a clear under-spending risk for 2026. Although we previously flagged that this shortfall could range from EUR 10 to 15 bn (see here), the inherent volatility of intra-year budget dynamics makes the final outcome difficult to project precisely. This under-spending might, however, be partially counterbalanced by other deficit- increasing federal expenditures—specifically higher lending to the Federal Employment Agency (BA). Given the BA's sharply widening deficit , which by August already stood at a substantial EUR 6.2 bn (up from EUR 3.7 bn in the prior- year period), the nearly EUR 4 bn federal loan earmarked in the 2026 budget is highly likely to prove insufficient. In fact, according to federal government estimates, the BA's total borrowing requirement could ultimately reach EUR 8.4 bn this year. Thus, even with some federal under-spending, the broader fiscal deficit is poised for a sharp increase. We continue to project that the general government deficit (national accounts), which integrates all levels of government and social security funds and is based on a accrual-based recording of revenues and expenses, will expand to about 4.1% of GDP in 2026.3 While potential federal under-spending exerts some downward pressure on our deficit forecast, this is likely to be partially offset by the widening BA deficit. e markets. Each power-plant operator bids into the market, stating how much electricity it is willing to supply at different prices for each hour of the following day. Bid prices are typically based on short-run marginal cost (SRMC)—the cost of producing one additional unit of electricity. Generation sources include renewables (wind and solar), nuclear, coal and gas. The market operator compiles the bids and ranks them from the lowest to the highest marginal cost, creating the supply curve. The market-clearing price (or “system price” in some markets) for a given hour is set by the marginal plant—the most expensive plant needed to meet total demand. Gas has the highest marginal cost and therefore largely determines the electricity price. Because gas prices did not rise significantly, the gas component made only a limited contribution to HICP so far. With gas price rising, things can change. BoE to hike in Nov and Feb, with balanced risks We change our BoE call- we now expect the BoE to hike twice in Nov ‘26 and Feb ‘27 to 4.25% to guard against the risks of second round effects, assuming high energy prices are sustained into early next year and barring big downside surprises in data. We then expect three quarterly cuts starting in Q1 ‘28 (Feb, Apr and July) to our terminal of 3.5% (vs. our previous call of no hikes and a cut in Nov. ‘27 to 3.5%). Our terminal remains the same, but we expect to reach it later. Risks to our view are balanced. A meaningful drop in energy prices due to a lasting deescalation or big downside data surprises can weaken the case for tightening and allow for one or no hike. At the same time, a meaningful worsening of the energy shock, upside data surprises or strong evidence of second round effects materializing can open the door to a third hike. Beyond that, risks are tilted to earlier cuts if disinflation late next year moves faster than we expect. The change in our BoE call is driven by the move higher in our inflation forecasts showing a higher peak and greater persistence which can increase risks of second round effects, stronger than expected growth so far along with the hawkish shift in the BoE’s communication.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 17 More Credit Score Models (GSEs' Version) • This section is a reprint of our note, More Credit Score Models (GSEs' Version). • The GSEs have released historical data for their internal credit risk models, Fannie Score and Freddie Score. These will be disclosed on a loan-level moving forward. • Similar to VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T, Fannie Score and Freddie Score are trended credit models. Borrowers appear to be distributed more evenly across the full credit score spectrum compared to Classic FICO, and lower- scoring borrowers receive an uplift in scores, on average. • We find that Fannie Score and Freddie Score are better indicators of prepayment risk than Classic FICO, which could be valuable to investors, especially as existing borrowers gain loan pricing optionality with VantageScore 4.0 implementation. • From the credit perspective, we highlight overall borrower scores tend to be higher, but a healthy percentage of each Classic FICO bucket migrates to a lower credit score as well. • The GSEs scores provide for significant differentiation of default probabilities within Classic FICO buckets – borrowers that fall within the same Classic FICO bucket experience materially different default probabilities based on their GSE credit score. Inflation of non-tourism related items was only slightly lower, at 3.1%Y from 3.2%Y on our estimates, a broadly unchanged rate since Jan- 26. The set of measures of "underlying inflation" that we track (Exhibit 17 ) gives mixed signals, with "wage-sensitive" inflation slightly up, "domestic inflation" stable and "energy- intensive core" down (this includes weak airfares). Our take remains that underlying services disinflation has stalled, but also that there are no signs yet of a transmission from higher energy costs to services inflation. A slight push upward from tourism-related items: We think September will bring more of the same, with services excluding tourism-related items stable but some volatility from airfares, accommodation and package holidays. We suspect that the softness of those items in August compared with last year (Exhibit 18 to Exhibit 20 ) could be due to temporary factors (for instance the impact of wildfires in many European regions) and will correct this month when prices adjust after the summer season. With that, services inflation could edge up a touch, at 3.1%Y from 3.0%Y.

records.text: Platinum and palladium frequently appear on critical minerals lists globally due to their essential role in catalytic converters and, by extension, the automotive sector. Yet, platinum and palladium supply is highly concentrated in just two regions—Southern Africa (82%/46%) and Russia (11%/39%)—creating significant disruption risk. But options to reduce US import dependence appear limited (Exhibit 5): US domestic mine production is limited and scaling output is technically and n geologically challenging. Mining is confined to two deposits in Montana operated by one single company, with ore skewed toward palladium.6 A US government study estimates US platinum and palladium mining operates at roughly 50% of theoretical capacity. Even if full capacity were achieved—an uncertain scenario given price insensitivity—annual net imports for consumption would decline moderately to 58 tonnes for platinum and 22 tonnes for palladium (vs. 60/30 tonnes currently)(Exhibit 7). Secondary supply depends on vehicle retirements, the main source of scrap n catalytic converters. US recycling favor palladium—used predominantly in the gasoline-dominated American fleet, over platinum, which is more common in diesel vehicles. So far, energy prices have been on a rollercoaster, with episodes of relief on hopes of a peace deal. If prices remain at current levels well beyond the winter, they may take their toll on sentiment and growth. That would put us closer to the ECB’s adverse scenario, and raise risks of a fourth hike (not more), but with weaker growth, we think. Consequently, we still expect a cutting cycle to start in 2027, but perhaps at a swifter pace than we currently assume. Related to that, there are other non-linearities that are key for an ECB October move and, hence, why we don’t see it happening. For an October move we would need to see a sense of urgency and/or that the central bank feels too far from the endpoint (the desired terminal rate of the hiking cycle). Going back to Lagarde’s speech at the Watchers conference the ECB would need to perceive that we are now in the scenario that requires a forceful adjustment. Recent ECB speak, including from Lagarde herself, suggests we are still in the measured adjustment scenario. Can we move there before the October meeting? That would require a sense that non- linear dynamics are being triggered or a much higher probability that they will be triggered- To us that would require at least one of two ingredients. While front-end pricing already reflects the possibility of this tightening scenario (a policy rate of 3.50% has been priced in by December 2027), the 2s10s curve remains a long way off. This lag has been a feature of previous cycles, however, with the trough typically reached 12 months after the first rate hike (versus 6–8 months in 10s30s). Also notable, the curve did not re-steepen even as the front end priced in an end to the Middle East conflict back in June, suggesting greater stability in the curve than front-end pricing. Current market pricing of 3.50% may be more a function of positioning and stop-outs than a reflection of the consensus that the ECB will reach 3.50%. Investor feedback is indeed vehemently skewed towards disbelief that the ECB could go as high as 3.00%, while a policy rate above 3.00% is largely seen as tipping the economy into a recession. Despite pricing in a 3.50% policy rate, the market is barely pricing in any rate cuts thereafter, and the curve remains much steeper than in a 150bp tightening scenario. The inflation market is also inconsistent with the ECB’s ‘severe’ scenario (Figure 3). This suggests that, should this scenario materialize, the pricing of rate hikes may intensify further, or at a minimum the curve should flatten further. -125 -100 -75 -50 -25 0 25 50 7

The result is a weaker pass-through from trade surpluses and exporter conversion into net RMB demand. Nor is RMB Beijing’s preferred tool for economic rebalancing, in our view. China’s large current-account surplus is also the external counterpart of a widening domestic saving- investment gap. As we argued here, the post-housing equilibrium is characterized by “structurally high saving, weaker investment demand, and a lower equilibrium interest rate”, which together have pushed the economy toward a larger external surplus and a weaker real exchange rate. Engineering rapid RMB appreciation would therefore treat the symptom rather than the underlying imbalance: it would tighten financial conditions, compress exporters’ RMB margins and add to disinflation at a time when domestic demand remains soft. A more durable rebalancing requires stronger household income and consumption, lower precautionary savings and firmer domestic investment demand; RMB appreciation should follow that reflation and rebalancing, rather than substitute for it.

records.text: M Idea 2 Fundamentals offer little relief from tightening expectations A perfect storm in the rates market The rates market is caught in a perfect storm. Resilient growth, sticky inflation, concerns over government restrictions in energy markets, a newly hawkish Fed, corporate issuance, persistent fiscal deficits, and questions surrounding a Treasury that has become less regular and predictable have all combined to push Treasury yields significantly higher. Since March, the yield on the 2y, 5y, and 10y US Treasury note has risen between 120- 150bp. Much of this rise has come from expectations for monetary tightening. Following the Fed's 25bp rate hike in September, markets are pricing in almost 100bp more in additional policy rate increases. We do not see the Fed delivering this much policy rate tightening in our baseline, but we are hard pressed to see any fundamental drivers that will make this clear to markets for some time. The Fed path certainly contains hikes, but how many is uncertain With the understanding that financial markets price a continuum of outcomes, our conversations with clients in recent weeks have centered on three outcomes. The first looks like the median forecast from the September FOMC meeting: a Fed that recalibrates policy by raising its policy rate 50-75bp to lean against second round effects from supply shocks on inflation. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 September 2026 Citi Research 37 UK Like the euro yield forecasts, the main change this month is a new house view on policy rates. Citi now expects the BoE to hike twice to 4.25% by 1Q27 before reversing with cuts later in 2027. This fits with the idea that the BoE is reluctant to hike and will do so only as insurance which can be removed should the inflation threat dissipate. The result is an upward revision to our yield projections, led by the front-end. This still results in a bullish view vs prevailing yield levels given the market has moved to price in around four BoE rate hikes, which we think is an overshoot. For 10yr gilt yields, we forecast 5.15% for 4Q26 up from 5% previously. Away from natural gas prices and the front-end, another bearish risk comes from the 28 October Budget. The sell-off in yields makes the challenge of restoring headroom much harder. If it is allowed to slip, the gilt market may take it as a can kick and hit to fiscal credibility. The importance and linkage of yields to headroom amplifies near-term risk for gilts, especially as higher energy prices could add to the fiscal spend at the Budget. However, gilt valuations already look relatively cheap vs net supply metrics vs Bunds. The relatively supportive issuance trend for gilts may be protected should any increase in the funding need at the Budget be met by Treasury bills. Morgan What does this mean for options markets? Given the current levels of implieds and the current jump frequency, markets have to deliver less on non-jump days to break even (Fig- ure 9). For example, given a 10% jump frequency for 2-year tails, they need to deliver about 6bp on non-jump days for positions to break even. This number decreases significantly as the jump frequency increases, creating a risk to short-gamma positions. Therefore, as we approach NFP next week, and with geopolitical uncertainty still in the background, we recommend patience before initiating outright shorts even at these levels. However, for investors who would like to initiate shorts, we recommend anchoring them in 30-year tails, as 30-year tails have been delivering the least amount of volatility on non-jump days and have a lower jump frequency than the other tails . We prefer pairing shorts in 6M expiries with longs in 1Y expiries, vega-neutral, for soft bearish gamma exposure in 30-year tails. Additionally, the implied vol differential has declined substantial- ly this week and is near YTD highs ( Figure 10 ). Therefore, we recommend selling 6Mx30Y straddles versus buying vega-neutral 1Yx30Y straddles, delta hedged daily (see Trade recommendations ).

records.text: 4 UK Watch | 23 September 2026 We expect headline inflation to rise to 4% early next year and stay persistently high for a few months, which can increase risks of threshold and second round effects (4% is where the BoE has previously warned about risks of threshold and non-linear effects, whereby attentiveness to inflation rises). Our energy price forecasts and futures (even with the recent declines) are close to the BoE’s adverse scenario in the near term (with gas higher), even if our forecasts/ futures don’t point to the same persistence (Exhibit 3 and Exhibit 4) and second round effects remain limited. In this scenario we think it would be difficult for the BoE to hold out from raising rates. At the same time, the BoE moved decisively hawkish in the Sept. meeting and looked more open to hiking to guard against the risks of second round effects, if high energy prices persist. records.text: 25 September 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 11 research shows that Europe as a region holds little comparative advantage in the field of AI and is still not specialized in producing pieces for the AI value chain (Figure 13). This has two implications: i) an AI-dominated global cycle will be less beneficial to European economic growth than it can be in other parts of the world, ii) European spending on AI tends to leak abroad (Figure 14). Beyond direct trade channels, Europe also experiences the indirect side effects of the global AI phenomenon, notably in the form of imported inflationary pressures for electronic components and a higher global interest rate environment. n Competitiveness concerns have not disappeared. Despite some recent improvement, corporate perception of external competitiveness remains close to historical lows ( Figure 15). This is particularly true in Germany, where competitiveness measures continue to signal structural challenges. Moreover, the second China shock, characterised by an intensification of the Chinese competition in global manufacturing and export markets, could place additional pressure on European exporters and, ultimately, on euro area growth (Figure 9 above). Economic growth is likely to improve further next year, once the inflow of EU funds becomes more visible. We believe Hungary should be able to regain access to RRF grants, cohesion funds, and SAFE loans. We continue to think that rather than the level of openings themselves, details of labor market flows from the JOLTS report are the more useful signals for labor market dynamics. Given strong payroll job growth in August, there should either be an increase in hiring in JOLTS data (more positive signal for stronger labor market) or a decline in separations like layoffs or quits (a slightly less positive signal). If the difference in August hires less separations is not quite as strong as 162k August payrolls, there could be revisions lower to August payrolls and/or weaker September job growth. While the level of JOLTS openings is not necessarily a useful signal of demand for workers, changes in openings could be a reflection of whether demand is picking up or not. So far, demand seems stable and moving sideways. But the trend of job openings could be an increasingly important signal, especially as the ratio of job openings to unemployed workers tends to lead trends in wage growth by a few months. Our energy price forecasts and futures (even with the recent declines) are close to the BoE’s adverse scenario in the near term (with gas higher), even if our forecasts/ futures don’t point to the same persistence (Exhibit 9 and Exhibit 10) and second round effects remain limited. In this scenario we think it would be difficult for the BoE to hold out from raising rates. The tightening would be seen as insurance/risk management to guard against the risks of material second round effects, especially ahead of and around 2027 pay settlements being set. We also think that insurance tightening would serve as a signal that the BoE is serious about guarding against upside inflation risks and is not behind the curve, especially in the context of other central banks raising rates. Moreover, stronger growth so far lowers the inflation growth trade-off for the BoE. At the same time, the BoE moved decisively hawkish in the Sept. meeting and looked more open to hiking to guard against the risks of second round effects, if high energy prices persist. We also made the case last week that the signaling from the September FOMC meeting indicated that this was likely the first in a series of hikes. If this is indeed the case, history would indicate that it’s very unlikely rates will pause here. The move in 10-year yields has been textbook in nature, tracking the average behavior observed during historical tightening cycles. However, it’s notable that the curve flattening has been more decisive than in the average cycle, and more closely resembles the behavior of the curve around the onset of the 2022 cycle than the shallower 1999 or 2016 cycles. If we extend out the curve, it’s notable that amid the underperformance of the belly this week, the intermediate sector no longer appears expensive, with 10-year yields appearing only 9bp too low in our fair value model. Alongside the retracement in front- end valuations, we think both of these factors reduce some of the headwinds for the Treasury market over the near term and could provide support to yields. However, next week’s employment report looms large, and the risk of a stronger September reading is rising, which could justify markets pricing in a high probability of an October hike. Despite this anemic income growth, real consumption growth has generally held in, growing above 2% and probably closer to 3.5% in the middle half of the year. The only way to make this math work is through a reduction in the personal saving rate. This decline in the saving rate has met two interpretations. In the benign version, soaring household wealth—partly driven by AI enthusiasm in equity markets—has motivated a lower saving rate through the usual wealth effects. In the more con- cerning version, the only way consumers can keep spending through the latest jump in headline inflation is by borrowing or dipping into savings, perhaps in an unsustainable way. In this note, we argue that much of the trend decline in the saving rate over the past few years is the normal wealth effect. This should be fine so long as there isn’t a major set- back in equity markets. However, the acceleration in the decline in the saving rate over the past six months is likely due to consumers maintaining spending habits despite a high- er cost of living. This too could end up well, if energy prices return to near pre-war levels. But sustained high pump prices could eventually lead to a rebalancing of income away from consumption and back to saving. records.text: European Watch | 24 September 2026 3 Overall, the updated guidance is consistent with a central bank that has become more confident in the recovery and somewhat less comfortable with the inflation outlook, leading us to expect a more extended tightening cycle than previously anticipated. Norges Bank: a 25bp hike, with a higher-for-longer rate outlook Norges Bank surprised us with a 25bp rate hike, with market expectations broadly split ahead of the meeting. At 4.5%, the policy rate is now at its highest level since the post- pandemic years. Following the hike delivered in May, Norges’s decision in September effectively reverses the rate cuts implemented in 2025. The policy rate path has been revised higher over 2027-29, reinforcing a “higher-for-longer” outlook. The projected peak in the policy rate has been raised to 4.60% (from 4.55% in June), preserving a modest tightening bias consistent with inflation risks remaining skewed to the upside. That said, we believe rates have probably peaked and do not expect further tightening from Norges Bank. However, persistently high energy prices and the prospect of a more hawkish global central bank backdrop in the short term could still create conditions for one additional hike by 1Q27. Cross-Asset Research US Midterms: Priced for Gridlock Midterm elections often command investors' attention, but their impact on fixed income markets has historically been muted. In the aftermath, markets typically refocus on growth, inflation, and monetary policy. We assess the implications of the 2026 election across main fixed income asset classes. Key Takeaways: • Divided government remains our base case and would likely leave the policy backdrop broadly unchanged. • The elections matter primarily through fiscal optionality. A Republican sweep would preserve the potential for additional fiscal expansion, while a divided government would constrain it. • Across markets, the biggest surprise scenario would be a Republican sweep, which would likely support growth, pressure rates higher, and create the most risk-on outcome for credit. records.text: Putting it together: equity vol carry remains the core The framework offers a mixed scorecard, but the implications for vol premia are clear. Negative equity/rates correlation strengthens some arguments for a richer rates VRP , but does not overturn the structural case for a richer equity VRP . Fat tails and jump risk increase the compensation rates volatility sellers should demand as inflation rises. Spot/vol beta suggests equity volatility becomes relatively less reactive to selloffs, but short equity vol losses still remain more aligned with broader risk-off episodes than rates volatility losses. Equity volatility also becomes harder to forecast at shorter horizons, arguing for embedding more premium, all else equal. Supply and demand provide another reason equity VRP may remain robust. When bonds cease to hedge equity risk, investors arguably become more reliant on explicit equity protection. Greater demand for equity options can sustain equity VRP , offsetting some of the weakening suggested by spot/vol beta behaviour in negative correlation regimes. Inflation may dampen equity volatility's response to selloffs, but it can simultaneously increase investors' willingness to pay for protection against them. Recent rates VRP suggests option pricing has adapted to the changing risk environment. It is challenging to say whether these revisions will become less meaningful over time: on the income side, the comprehensive updates typical- ly involve new methodologies, as opposed to the routine incorporation of better data. Consequently, the BEA might eventually run out of improvements to make, in which case the smaller revisions of recent years could become the new normal. The saving rate has steadily drifted down over the last few years, leading to concerns that consumer spending could eventually slow. Soaring wealth is likely one reason for a sav- ing rate decline, along with higher gas prices since March. But the saving rate also has a strong tendency to be revised up, especially via positive income revisions (Figure 1), which if repeated would suggest recent spending growth is more durable. Receipts on assets were a key source of upward revi- sion in last year’s annual GDP (NIPA) update, and we see reasons why they could be revised higher again either in the annual update that is being released next week or in future updates. With the region producing 3 mbd, exports amount to 43% of Gulf Coast distillate output—an enormous share—and far more than existing pipelines could redirect to the East Coast, a region most reliant on foreign imports. Gulf refiners can ship diesel by sea, but movements between US ports are subject to the Jones Act, which requires a US-built, US-owned and coastwise-qualified vessel. A Jones Act waiver introduced on March 17 and extended through November 15 helped relieve this constraint, driving a surge in waterborne petroleum shipments from the Gulf Coast to the East Coast from 0.6 mbd in February to a record 0.8 mbd in May, including 0.15 kbd of diesel. With logistical constraints eased, surplus Gulf Coast barrels would flow to the East Coast and Midwest. Even then, nearly 1.1 mbd of diesel would still need to find a home. For the first few weeks, that home is relatively straightforward: rebuilding depleted inventories. At a 1.1 mbd build, US diesel inventories could return to their five-year average within two weeks. If the ban lasted 30 days, it would add around 30 million barrels to storage, lifting inventories to about 140 mn bbls—elevated, but still within levels the US system has carried historically. Fat tails: rates tails fatten as bonds stop hedging Equities exhibit their fattest tails precisely when bonds still hedge. We begin with the most basic building blocks: the distribution of returns. Splitting sixty years by equity/rates correlation quintiles, we find that equity return kurtosis is highest in the two most positive correlation regimes. This is counter-intuitive: a liquid, reliable hedge might be expected to dampen equity extremes. The data says otherwise. The explanation is more likely positioning than macro. It is tempting to read the result through the lens of growth versus inflation shocks, but equity/rates correlation is a state variable rather than a shock identifier, and negative-correlation periods have contained plenty of growth-driven stress. A more plausible explanation lies in portfolio construction. When bonds function as a dependable hedge, investors are willing to run greater leverage and larger equity allocations. To close, NY Fed SOMA manager Roberto Perli reiterated the Desk’s ample-reserves objec- tive and emphasized that RMPs are a flexible tool (not on a preset course) calibrated to reserve demand, reserve-supply forecasts, and money market conditions. He highlighted that the market absorbed heavy net bill issuance in July–August with little impact on money market rates and said the Desk is watching how markets handle potential renewed T-bill supply in October. In our view, while money markets are likely to firm modestly in the fourth quarter versus the prior couple of months, we do not expect material funding pressures that would warrant the Fed re-engaging in RMPs this year. Perli also contrasted the Fed’s securities-led framework (marginal reserves supplied mainly via outright purchases such as T-bill RMPs) with repo-led approaches (BoE/ECB). In a repo-led framework, routine access to central bank liquidity at near-market rates can allow banks to operate with a smaller precautionary reserves buffer, potentially reducing the need for the central bank to provision reserves ex ante to absorb shocks. It could also shorten the duration (and interest-rate risk) of the central bank balance sheet. At the same time, a repo- led framework relies more explicitly on central bank liquidity operations, raising design choices around how directly the central bank supplies liquidity versus how much

It is our understanding that the more recent RDMICH bond had more investors involved in the primary process than RPLDCI and thus reason for different index providers to draw this line in the sand differently, but this shows the frailty of this criteria altogether. Our view is that when there is public disclosure pointing to limited syndication, this should be supplemented with some sort of objective criteria. Those criteria could be spread related. For example, if a bond issued with limited syndication tightens more than say 5% of its issuance spread over the first five days then it should be excluded; if not, it should be included, so long as its secondary market volumes are in line with similar size/rating broadly syndicated, registered securities. Or to keep it simple, benchmark indices could tighten their definition of limited syndication to exclude just deals with very little immediate secondary liquidity, or provide the marketplace with objective criteria to define this constraint, such as a requirement to syndicate to X number of investors per Y billion of bonds. The macro mod- el draws on a longer history and a broader set of housing- market information, but its reliance on shelter’s historical per- sistence could make it slow to recognize a structural change in rent-setting behavior. On balance, we place somewhat more weight on the macro model and use the new-lease rent model to gauge risks. Both models point to further shelter cooling in 2027, but the macro model implies less near-term relief for core inflation. The Zillow model also suggests that the moderation may prove temporary if new-lease rent growth remains near 3%. Risks to the outlook With the Fed raising rates last week and likely to tighten fur- ther before year-end, monetary policy itself could slow shelter disinflation. Dias and Duarte (2019) find that contractionary policy temporarily puts upward pressure on rents as home- ownership and rental vacancies decline. Our earlier estimates imply that a 50bp increase in the fed funds rate raises shelter inflation by about 0.25 percentage point over the following year, even as core CPI excluding shelter is largely unrespon- sive in the short run. Mingyue Xin | Strategist | +44-20-754-10002 Note: This note was originally published on 21 September 2026. Recent central bank QT decisions and potential reviews of the investment frameworks of major institutional investors have brought renewed attention to shifts in the price -insensitive investor base and their potential impact on global term premia (TP). In today's CoTD, we use the historical relationship between our US-Germany composite 5s10s term premium and free float to estimate the increase in free-float debt associated with a 1bp increase in term premium, and put the magnitude into context by comparing it with major central bank QT programmes and foreign holdings of USTs. Over 2004Q1 -2025Q4, the relationship implies that a 1bp increase in the composite term premium is associated with around a 0.23ppt increase in free float. records.text: M Idea 2 Higher on All Components Our EA September inflation forecasts | Headline up to 3.7%Y and core to 2.6%Y: September could bring another uptick of headline inflation (3.7%Y) with strength from all components including an increase in core (2.6%Y from 2.4%Y). We forecast energy inflation to once again move up sharply (17.8%Y from 14.3%Y), primarily due to higher fuel prices. The uptick in wholesale natural gas price should also increasingly feed through to retail gas and electricity tariffs. Food inflation could move up slightly (1.2%Y from 1.1%Y) as negative base effects from last year become less flattering. We expect services inflation to rise to 3.1%Y from 3.0%Y because of a rebound in tourism-related items after a soft August print. But we expect non-tourism services inflation to continue moving sideways. We also foresee an increase in goods inflation (1.4%Y from 1.2%Y), reflecting ongoing IT- related price pressures ("chipflation") and lubricants inflation (which is part of goods as per Eurostat classification). Despite the expected increase in inflation across all items, we stress idiosyncratic factors dominate and we continue to expect limited evidence of indirect or second-round impacts from energy costs. records.text: res could ripple out toward rental households. Affordability for rental households behaves differently from ownership households. When rents are increasing, they increase for almost all rental households eventually given typical 12- or 24- month leases. Renters don't benefit from the lock-in effect like seasoned homeowners do. In fact, affordability challenges in the ownership market can result in households that are effectively stuck renting. That trapped demand could actually put upward pressure on rents. In the years since the pandemic we have seen a substantial gap form between weaker new lease growth and stronger renewal rent growth. According to the Joint Center for Housing Studies, the number of rental households who are cost burdened - defined as paying more than 30% of your income on shelter - has risen from 46.3% in 2019 to 49.4% in 2024. The number that are severely cost burdened, or pay more than 50% has risen from 23.9% to 26.2%. Record new supply in the multifamily space has gone a long way toward mitigating upward pressure on rents in recent years, but as housing affordability deteriorates anew, that release valve might not be as available this time around. It is true that supply is still elevated relative to history, and that 5+ unit housing starts have rebounded somewhat this year, but they are still down 22% since local peaks in 2022. The decline in starts has allowed the number of units under construction to decline by 33% from recent peaks ( Exhibit 23 ).

records.text: . The main point is to highlight that, if decision -makers and investors believe AI to be a “winner takes most” set -up, then it becomes plausible to expect aggregate overinvestment. Crucially, such overinvestment is not reflective of a bubble or a lack of eco nomic benefits from AI. Rather, it is driven by the disproportionate advantage of being the dominant market leader. Rate market implications The “traditional” textbook impact of a new technology is to raise the equilibrium rate. Initially, higher capex shifts the savings/investment balance and pushes equilibrium rates higher. Subsequently, increased productivity results in higher growth and higher wages, which ultimately leads to higher consumption. So far, we have sided with the traditional textbook view, arguing that equilibrium rates were likely to reverse most of their post -GFC decline. We have highlighted both tails of AI (a bubble or a significant impact on the labour market) as risks to this view. This note highlights a third risk: rational overinvestment. If the AI race is genuinely a “winner takes most” set -up, one could expect a reassessment of the profitability of aggregate capex without denying the significant economic benefits of AI. If that occurs, the ensuing capex slowdown could result in lower rates. Appendix Let each firm i choose investment xᵢ at unit cost to compete for a fixed prize V. The distinction is not cyclical versus defensive in the abstract; it is whether earnings growth is accelerating fast enough, off a cheap enough starting valuation, to offset the multiple compression. Cyclical value has both. Capital goods and technology have the growth but carry higher valuations and so more duration risk. Defensives have neither, and take the full brunt of the discount rate. Positioning Stay with companies whose beta to rising yields is lowest because their valuations are cheaper and their earnings carry more cyclicality and growth - enough to offset the valuation drag. In a market where the proportion of the index able to sustain positive performance narrows with every further move higher in yields, the bar for owning long- duration defensives is now considerably higher than it looks on a static valuation screen. This effectively builds domestic inventories without requiring direct government purchases and without immediately passing costs through to downstream consumers. At the same time, inventories located inside US borders become available for use during foreign supply disruptions. A Global Oversupply, But Much of It Is Unavailable The implication is a reduction in available inventories outside the US. While global inventories remain comfortable on paper, a growing share is being concentrated in US warehouses, reducing liquidity in the rest of the market and leaving less material readily available (Exhibit 6). The tightening in available ex-US inventories came as investor interest broadened beyond gold into silver, platinum, palladium, and even copper (Exhibit 7, Left Panel). records.text: ving a lot of the growth This tailwind for broader manufacturing and capex should remain as long as the AI/tech buildout continues. That should increase demand for non-tech capex, and support the S in I/S ratios as inventories build. That should keep capex intentions bright, fuel credit expansion and demand for C&I loans, in addition supporting the actual capex broadening underway across sectors. This analysis also highlights a broader theme: the expansion's general reliance on AI. Real income growth is flat to negative. But, AI-driven equity wealth gains continue to support consumption. Aside from the household sector, government is not exactly in expansion mode here, at least not on a whole government basis. Some components of government are expanding (defense investment, also supporting manufacturing) while other parts of government are being cut or other spending is being flatlined. Currently, fiscal policy's support for the expansion is in the process of flipping from fiscal support to fiscal drag. Net exports have turned structurally negative because we import so much of the AI/tech related investment. Residential investment is languishing under this level of interest rates. Then the remaining segment of GDP growth, business investment and inventories, are being broadly supported by the direct and indirect demand stemming from the AI buildout. The singular nature of the driving shock, AI, is both unusual and exceptional at the moment.

In a traditional sense, with a Phillips Curve coefficient of 0.3 would imply the interest rate sensitive sectors would need to send the unemployment rate to 8% to get inflation from over 3% down to 2.0%. Perhaps the setting of the funds rate is a signal to guide and anchor inflation expectations? Possible, but that may not be the level of interest rates, but a change in the rate needed to demonstrate conviction, a completely different mechanism and one orthogonal to the concept of the neutral rate. What mechanism the new Chairman has in mind is something he has not yet articulated. The other unknown is the speed he deems sufficient to get inflation to 2.0%. What if some neutral rate is changing over that horizon? Back when the mid- point of the target range for the federal funds rate was 4.375%, the FOMC made a lot of progress on inflation. Core inflation fell to 2.6% and headline PCE inflation fell to 2.3% in April 2025, prior to the liberation day tariff announcements. Is that still above the “Wicksellian” rate? How far above? The market does not seem to think a 4.375% funds rate is sufficiently restrictive any longer, pricing in a 4.8% funds rate, or roughly the target range reaching 4.75% to 5.00%, compared to the current 3.75% to 4.00%. records.text: US Economics Weekly 25 September 2026 Citi Research 12 Initial Jobless Claims – Citi: 203k, median: NA, prior: 197k Continuing Claims – Citi: 1725k, median: NA, prior: 1719k Initial and continuing jobless claims have been very low throughout the year but have fallen to even lower levels in recent weeks following the Labor Day holiday. We expect initial claims to rise modestly to 203k the week of September 25 and continuing claim to rise to 1725k the week of September 19. If continuing claims remain at very low levels, this could suggest a renewed decline in the unemployment rate within a few months. While continuing claims should correspond more concurrently with labor market conditions in the monthly employment reports, recent patterns have implied continuing claims leading the unemployment rate. Some of the decline in continuing claims could reflect increased hiring, but could also just reflect that initial claims have been very low (fewer flows onto unemployment insurance in the first place). records.text: US Economic Perspectives23 September 2026 ab 5 We can put some structure on this and estimate spillover empirically Are these anecdotes reflected somewhere in the national accounts data? Recall Solow's quip that you could see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics. While we should be wary of torturing the data too early, some basic manipulation of the NIPA's Business Fixed Investment (BFI) account might be informative. We leverage an innovation from a classic paper on investment that warned about spillovers from housing just before the GFC. (4) The intuition is straightforward. Consider forecasting growth in non-residential BFI (NRBFI) from its own history. A first-order auto-regression run over the past 40 years produces a parameter of 0.5, meaning that if NRBFI growth is above its long-run mean, that momentum persists next period by half (auto-regression and predictability are two sides of the same coin). But where does that momentum come from? We can decompose NRBFI's growth rate into the sum of the contributions of its subsectors: machinery, transportation equipment, info processing equipment, etc…. Then, instead of regressing NRBFI growth on lagged NRBFI as in the standard auto-regression, we regress it on the lagged contributions of the sectors/categories that add up to it. New Zealand Our longstanding dovish view on the RBNZ remains unchanged. We believe 2.75% is terminal in this cycle. Our view is based on the fact that neutral policy rates are lower than what the RBNZ is estimating. We see neutral in the range of 2.5%- 2.75%, rather than 3% or higher. Consequently, we should see a slowdown in activity indicators over the coming weeks and months that will likely prevent the RBNZ from hiking further. The election, although the Governor Breman has stated has no impact on policy, adds to policy uncertainty in our view. A possibility of a dual mandate once again will likely grip the minds of the MPC the next time they meet. If the MPC was to hold, we may see a split vote once again, with the hawkish external members opting for a hike. Overall, our base case remains unchanged that terminal in NZ is 2.75%, however, we do acknowledge the risk to our view is skewed towards more hikes. Source: Citi Research, Banxico, Bloomberg Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg CLP Esteban Tamayo USDCLP Forecasts: 0-3m 940, 6-12m 940 Chile’s macro backdrop has become increasingly characterized by weak domestic growth rather than inflation concerns, supporting a largely stable FX outlook over the forecast horizon. The September IPoM delivered a sharp downgrade to growth and investment projections, confirming that investment has emerged as the economy’s principal constraint and pushing any meaningful recovery further into 2027. While inflation remains above target, the BCCh’s policy discussion has shifted away from tighter policy and toward the implications of weaker activity, reducing support from domestic rate expectations. At the same time, external fundamentals remain constructive. Copper prices continue to provide an important terms-of-trade cushion, fiscal credibility remains intact, and Chile retains strong external buffers, including its IMF Flexible Credit Line. In our view, these supportive external factors should largely offset domestic growth headwinds. As a result, we expect USDCLP to remain broadly stable around 940 over both the 0-3 month and 6–12-month

records.text: US Economics Weekly25 September 2026 ab 33 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Employment report: should be more good news We expect nonfarm payroll employment expanded 95K in September, with private employment rising 90K and government employment rising 5K. September employment reports have displayed notable acceleration in job gains in recent years, surprised on the upside the last four years in a row, and risk being biased upward by seasonal adjustment. The September increase would come on the heels of a substantial swing in employment between July and August, which resulted from poorly identified 4- 5 week adjustments in highly seasonal sectors like leisure and hospitality and local government education. The uniqueness of the 2026 calendar setup has introduced substantial volatility, with May employment pulled forward from June, for another example. Smoothing through those four months' volatility, the average pace of job gains sits at roughly 70K jobs added per month. We expect average hourly earnings climbed 0.21% in September, held down slightly by the calendar set-up. Absent revision that would leave the year-over-year change at 3.1%, back down to the pre-Covid years' range and negative in real terms. We expect average weekly hours dipped in September, just enough to move the rounded workweek down from 34.4 to 34.3 hours, and still consistent with aggregate slack along that margin. Using the most recent data we have from the US census bureau, 65% of households are homeowners. 40% of those households, or 26% of the total, do not have a mortgage and are therefore likely in a rather comfortable situation when it comes to cost of shelter. Over 50% of mortgaged homeowners, or 20% of total households, have a mortgage rate locked in below 4% and are thus similarly in a good affordability boat. That leaves the 35% of households that are renters, half of which we know are already cost burdened, and the 10% of the population that are homeowners but have a mortgage above 6% in a more precarious affordability situation.
